AMGR-001.description: Implement a SessionSearch tool call that replaces scripts/session-search.sh and scripts/session-search-skill.md with a native Rust implementation. Re-uses the existing persistence layer (MessageStore, HistoryStore, BlobStore) to provide search_history, show_session, recent_sessions, and context_search actions. This tool will also be used by an upcoming compaction refactor to access conversation history programmatically. Agent orchestration (spawn/close/list/message/DeepSearch) is deferred to a separate future AgentManager card.

examples.text: Agent calls SessionSearch(action='recent', count=5) and gets back 5 sessions with name, work unit ID, first/last user message previews, timestamps, message count, project path — enough to triage which session to dig into

Agent calls SessionSearch(action='search', query='RLM-001', context_turns=3) and gets back matches across all content (user inputs, assistant responses, tool calls) with 3 surrounding turns of context per match, grouped by session

Agent calls SessionSearch(action='show') with no session_id and gets back the current session's full conversation with blob-resolved content and reassembled streaming chunks, each message truncated at 5000 chars
Agent calls SessionSearch(action='search', query='DeepSearch', last_hours=24, all_projects=true) and gets back matches from all projects in the last 24 hours, not just the current project
Agent calls SessionSearch(action='search', query='authentication') and gets no matches — tool returns 'No matches found' as structured result, not an error

questions.answer: Split. SessionSearch is its own tool (AMGR-001). Agent orchestration (spawn/close/list/message/DeepSearch) becomes a separate future card.
questions.text: @human: Should AgentManager be one tool with action dispatch, or split into 2-3 separate tools (SessionSearch + AgentSpawn + AgentMessage)? Single tool is simpler for LLM discovery but mixed concerns.

rules.text: Session search must use the existing Rust persistence layer (MessageStore, HistoryStore, BlobStore) — no subprocess to Python or bash
Session search replaces scripts/session-search.sh and scripts/session-search-skill.md entirely — these files become deprecated
Split. SessionSearch is its own tool (AMGR-001). Agent orchestration (spawn/close/list/message/DeepSearch) becomes a separate future card.
SessionSearch output must be usable programmatically (structured data) — not just formatted text — to support compaction and other internal consumers
Streaming chunk reassembly (porting the Python logic from session-search.sh) must reconstruct readable text from [Thinking:...], [Tool:...], and raw SSE fragments
search_history searches ALL persisted content — user inputs, assistant responses, tool calls, tool results, thinking chunks — not just user input history
Search matching uses the ripgrep libraries (grep-regex, grep-searcher, grep-matcher) already bundled in codelet/tools — same engine as the Grep tool
Search defaults to current project sessions only, with an optional flag to search across all projects
Search results include all available metadata per match — session ID, session name, timestamp, role, turn index, matched content preview, surrounding context, project path, provider, message count
Time filtering supports both absolute (after/before ISO timestamps) and relative (last_hours/last_days) parameters — whichever is easiest for the LLM to express in the moment
show_session truncates individual messages at 5000 chars (matching existing tool output conventions), with optional user_only filter and max_turns limit

Three actions: search (keyword search with configurable context_turns around matches), show (load specific session by ID), recent (list recent sessions for discovery) — context_search merged into search as a parameter
All actions have sensible defaults with optional overrides — search defaults to limit=20 matches, recent defaults to count=10, show defaults to all turns with 5000 char truncation per message

SessionSearch replaces the step-by-step Bash workflow from session-search-skill.md (recent → search → show → drill deeper) — the agent follows the same iterative pattern but via native tool calls instead of Bash subprocess

recent action returns: session name, work unit ID (if attached), first/last user message previews, timestamps, message count, and project path — optimized for the LLM to triage which session is relevant
show action defaults to current session if no session_id is provided — 'current' is also accepted as an explicit keyword. The tool resolves it internally via its session_id constructor parameter.
Error handling is simple and direct — empty results return 'No matches found', non-existent session IDs return an error, no suggestion engine or fallback heuristics

AMGR-007.description: Implement an AgentManager tool that allows AI agents to spawn subordinate sessions, manage their lifecycle, send messages between sessions, and set roles. The spawner is always the supervisor — they own the subordinate's lifecycle and close it when done. Spawned sessions are regular agent_loop sessions (not the old supervisor_agent_loop). Subordinates use SessionSearch to pull context from their supervisor when needed, and message to push results back or interrupt. Any session can have a role set (a string acting as system prompt overlay). The old supervisor_agent_loop, ObservationBuffer, automatic observation/injection pipeline, /supervisor command, and supervisor TUI management screens are removed.

examples.text: Supervisor calls AgentManager(action='spawn', role='You are a security reviewer. Analyze code for vulnerabilities, injection risks, and auth bypass.') → returns { session_id: 'uuid' }. Then sends a message with the actual task.

Supervisor spawns a worker, then sends AgentManager(action='message', session_id='worker-id', message='Review src/auth/ for SQL injection vulnerabilities and report back'). The worker receives this as its first prompt and starts working.

Subordinate finishes its task and calls AgentManager(action='message', session_id='supervisor-id', message='Found 2 SQL injection vulnerabilities in query_builder.rs lines 45 and 89. See my analysis.') to report results back.

Subordinate needs context from supervisor — calls SessionSearch(action='show', session_id='supervisor-id', max_turns=10) to see what the supervisor is working on, then adjusts its own work accordingly.

Supervisor calls AgentManager(action='set_role', session_id='my-session-id', role='You are a senior engineer focused on performance optimization') — sets a role on its own session as a system prompt overlay.
User types /role in the TUI — a dialog pops up to enter a role string for the current session. This is the TUI equivalent of AgentManager(action='set_role').
Supervisor is done with a worker — calls AgentManager(action='close', session_id='worker-id') to terminate it and clean up.

Supervisor spawns 3 workers for parallel tasks — a security reviewer, a test writer, and a documentation updater. Each gets a role and a message with their specific task. Supervisor polls them via list/get_status and collects results via messages.

Worker subordinate discovers something urgent — calls AgentManager(action='message', session_id='supervisor-id', message='URGENT: The database migration will drop the users table. Stop the deploy.') to interrupt the supervisor.

rules.text: AgentManager is a single tool with action dispatch — spawn, list, message, set_role, close, get_status — same pattern as SessionSearch and Bridge
The spawner is always the supervisor — they own the subordinate's lifecycle and are responsible for closing it when done
spawn creates a new subordinate session running a regular agent_loop — NOT the old supervisor_agent_loop. Every spawned session is a normal session.
spawn accepts an optional role (string — system prompt overlay for the subordinate). The subordinate always starts idle and waits for a message from the supervisor to begin work.
The spawned subordinate inherits the supervisor's model automatically — no model parameter on spawn

A role is a string that acts as a system prompt overlay for a session — any session can have a role, not just spawned ones. set_role changes the role on any session. In the TUI, /role opens a dialog to set the role on the current session.
Subordinates use SessionSearch to pull context from their supervisor when they need it — no automatic streaming of observations. Context is pulled, not pushed.
Subordinates use the message action to send results back to the supervisor or to interrupt the supervisor when needed
message works between any two sessions — supervisor to subordinate, subordinate to supervisor, or between any two sessions that know each other's IDs. Any-to-any.
close terminates a subordinate session — only the spawner (supervisor) or the user can close it. Close cleans up the parent-child ownership relationship.

The old supervisor_agent_loop, ObservationBuffer, automatic observation/injection pipeline, broadcast subscription for observation, breakpoint detection — all removed. These are replaced by explicit pull (SessionSearch) and push (message) patterns.

The /supervisor TUI command and supervisor management screens (SupervisorTemplateList, SupervisorCreateView, SupervisorTemplateForm) are removed. Replaced by /role command (opens a role dialog for the current session) and AgentManager tool for spawning/managing subordinates.
All actions return JSON. On error: { error: true, code: 'session_not_found' | 'permission_denied' | 'invalid_parameter' | 'delivery_failed', message: string }

message supports an optional context array of session history references — specific turns, turn ranges, or search queries. Resolved at send time so the receiver gets self-contained content. Graceful degradation for missing sessions and zero-match queries.

Resolved message context uses XML-style format: <agent-message from="session-id" role="role"> wraps delivery, <quoted-context> with <from session="id" turns="N-M"> blocks for referenced history. Warnings inline for missing sessions or zero-match queries.
Messages queue in an mpsc channel (capacity 16). No interruption of LLM generation — message waits and is picked up on next iteration. delivery_failed error when channel is full.

The tool module lives at codelet/tools/src/ and is registered in all providers' create_rig_agent() alongside SessionSearch and DeepSearch. AgentManager and SessionSearch are independent — neither imports the other.

AMGR-009.description: Implement the AgentManager tool module with handler-delegated pattern and the core lifecycle actions: spawn (create subordinate session with optional role), list (all sessions with relationships), get_status (detailed session info), close (terminate subordinate, spawner-only). Spawned sessions run regular agent_loop. Spawn inherits supervisor's model. Registered in all providers.

examples.text: Agent calls AgentManager(action='spawn') with no role — gets back { session_id: 'uuid' }. Subordinate inherits the spawner's model and starts idle.
Agent calls AgentManager(action='spawn', role='You are a security reviewer') — gets back { session_id: 'uuid' }. Subordinate has the role set as system prompt overlay.
Agent calls AgentManager(action='list') — returns { sessions: [...] } with all active sessions showing their session_id, name, role, status, spawner_id, subordinate_ids.

Agent calls AgentManager(action='get_status', session_id='valid-uuid') — returns full status object. Agent calls with session_id='nonexistent' — returns { error: true, code: 'session_not_found', message: '...' }.
Spawner agent calls AgentManager(action='close', session_id='subordinate-uuid') — returns { closed: true, session_id: '...' }. ChainOfCommand is cleaned up, session is destroyed.
Non-spawner agent calls AgentManager(action='close', session_id='other-session') — returns { error: true, code: 'permission_denied', message: '...' }. Only the spawner can close.
Agent calls AgentManager(action='spawn') 3 times — creates 3 subordinate workers. Agent calls list — sees all 3 with spawner_id pointing back to the agent's session.
Agent calls AgentManager(action='invalid_action') — returns { error: true, code: 'invalid_parameter', message: 'Unknown action: invalid_action' }.

rules.text: AgentManagerTool follows the handler-delegated pattern: tool struct in codelet-tools with static HashMap<Uuid, Handler>, handler closure created in codelet-napi with persistence access
spawn action creates a new subordinate BackgroundSession running regular agent_loop, inherits the spawner's model, registers relationship in ChainOfCommand via add_supervisor()
spawn accepts an optional role string (system prompt overlay). The subordinate starts idle and waits for a message — no initial prompt is sent
list action returns all sessions with their session_id, name, role, status, spawner_id, and subordinate_ids — no access control

get_status action takes a session_id and returns detailed info: session_id, role, status, model, spawner_id, subordinate_ids, pending_messages. Returns error with code session_not_found if ID is invalid.

close action takes a session_id and terminates the subordinate. Only the spawner (supervisor) can close a session — returns error with code permission_denied otherwise. Cleans up ChainOfCommand relationships.
All actions return JSON. Error responses use shape: { error: true, code: string, message: string }. Error codes: session_not_found, permission_denied, invalid_parameter
The tool is registered in all 5 providers' create_rig_agent() with .tool(AgentManagerTool::new(session_id)) alongside SessionSearch and DeepSearch
Handler is registered in agent_loop() before run via set_agent_manager_handler(session_id, Some(handler)) and cleaned up after via set_agent_manager_handler(session_id, None)
Actions use serde tagged dispatch: #[serde(tag = "action", rename_all = "snake_case")] on AgentManagerAction enum

AMGR-009.title: Core AgentManager tool — spawn, list, get_status, close

userStory.action: spawn subordinate sessions, list all sessions, get session status, and close subordinates via a single AgentManager tool
userStory.benefit: I can create and manage worker agents for parallel tasks without manual session management

architectureNotes.text: Add Message variant to AgentManagerAction enum in types.rs: Message { session_id: String, message: String }. Add MessageDelivered variant to AgentManagerResult.

Handler implementation in agent_manager_handler.rs: Message action looks up target session by ID from SessionManager, calls session.receive_incoming_message() with IncomingMessage { source_session_id, role_name, message, images: None }. Uses try_send which returns TrySendError::Full for channel-full case.
The sender's role is obtained from the calling session's role field (Option<String> on BackgroundSession, simplified from SupervisorRole in AMGR-008). If None, pass empty string as role_name.

No new channels or select branches needed — the existing incoming_message_rx branch in agent_loop's tokio::select! already handles delivery to the target. Messages are formatted via format_incoming_message() before being sent to the LLM.

AMGR-010.description: Implement the message action for AgentManager. Any session can send a plain text message to any other session by ID. Messages queue in an mpsc channel (capacity 16), no interruption of LLM generation, delivery_failed when full. Covers supervisor→subordinate, subordinate→supervisor, and peer-to-peer messaging.

examples.text: Supervisor spawns subordinate, then sends message(session_id=subordinate, message='Analyze auth.rs for security issues') — gets { delivered: true, session_id: 'subordinate-uuid' }
Subordinate sends message back to its spawner with results — message(session_id=spawner, message='Found 2 SQL injection vulnerabilities') — gets { delivered: true }
Agent sends message to nonexistent session_id — gets { error: true, code: 'session_not_found', message: '...' }
Agent sends 17 messages rapidly to a target that is busy processing — first 16 succeed, 17th gets { error: true, code: 'delivery_failed', message: '...' }
Two subordinates of the same supervisor send messages to each other (peer-to-peer) — both deliveries succeed, no spawner relationship required
Agent calls message action without session_id — gets { error: true, code: 'invalid_parameter', message: 'session_id is required' }
Target session receives message while idle — message appears as next input and triggers agent processing with formatted sender info

rules.text: Any session can send a message to any other session by ID — no access control on sending (supervisor→subordinate, subordinate→supervisor, peer-to-peer)
Messages are delivered through the target session's existing incoming_message channel (mpsc, capacity 16) — reuses the IncomingMessage infrastructure
Messages queue if the target is mid-generation — no interruption of LLM processing. Picked up on next agent_loop iteration via tokio::select!
If the incoming_message channel is full (16 pending messages), the send fails with error code delivery_failed
Message action requires both session_id (target) and message (text content) parameters. Missing either returns error code invalid_parameter
Success response shape: { delivered: true, session_id: 'target-id' }. Error response shape: { error: true, code: string, message: string }
The message is delivered as an IncomingMessage with source_session_id set to the sender's session ID and role_name set to the sender's role (or empty if no role)
Sending a message to your own session ID is allowed (self-messaging) — no special case needed

AMGR-010.title: Agent messaging — plain, bidirectional, any-to-any

userStory.action: send plain text messages to other agent sessions
userStory.benefit: agents can coordinate work, delegate tasks, and report results back

architectureNotes.text: Add optional context field to AgentManagerAction::Message variant: context: Option<Vec<ContextReference>>. Add ContextReference enum with three variants: Turns { session_id, turns }, TurnRange { session_id, start_turn, end_turn }, Query { session_id, query }.

Context resolution logic lives in agent_manager_handler.rs as a new resolve_context() function. It uses persistence::load_session() and persistence::get_session_messages_full() — the same persistence layer as SessionSearch. For the search query variant, reuse grep-regex matching (same engine as SessionSearch's handle_search).

The resolved context is prepended to the IncomingMessage.message field before delivery — the existing receive_incoming_message() API stays unchanged. The message body sent to the channel is: sender's text + \n\n<quoted-context>...</quoted-context>. The entire message including resolved context goes through the existing format_incoming_message() pipeline.

Add MessageDeliveredWithContext variant to AgentManagerResult to include context_resolved count. When context is provided: use MessageDeliveredWithContext { delivered: true, session_id, context_resolved }. When context is omitted: use existing MessageDelivered { delivered: true, session_id } for backward compat.

AMGR-011.description: Extend the message action to support an optional context array of session history references. Three variants: specific turns, turn ranges, search queries. Resolved at send time using SessionSearch persistence layer. Graceful degradation for missing sessions and zero-match queries. XML-style format for resolved context blocks.

examples.text: Agent sends message with context=[{session_id: 'supervisor-id', turns: [1, 2]}] — receiver gets the message text plus <quoted-context><from session="supervisor-id" turns="1-2">[1] user: ...[2] assistant: ...</from></quoted-context>
Agent sends message with context=[{session_id: 'worker-id', start_turn: 0, end_turn: 5}] — receiver gets turns 0 through 5 from the worker's session history inline with the message
Agent sends message with context=[{session_id: 'peer-id', query: 'SQL injection'}] — receiver gets matching turns from the peer's session containing 'SQL injection' references
Agent sends message referencing a session that was deleted — gets { delivered: true, context_resolved: 0 } and the receiver sees a warning in the quoted-context block

Agent sends message with context=[{session_id: 'worker-id', query: 'nonexistent phrase'}] — query matches nothing, receiver sees '⚠ No matches for query' in the quoted block, but the sender's message text is still delivered

Agent sends message with mixed context array — [{session_id: 'A', turns: [3]}, {session_id: 'B', query: 'auth'}] — both references are resolved and appear as separate <from> blocks inside a single <quoted-context>
Agent sends message without context (or context=[]) — behaves exactly like AMGR-010 plain text delivery, response has no context_resolved field

rules.text: The message action accepts an optional context array alongside the existing session_id and message parameters. Each element is a context reference object.

Three context reference variants are supported: (1) specific turns { session_id, turns: [42,43,44] }, (2) turn range { session_id, start_turn: 10, end_turn: 15 }, (3) search query { session_id, query: 'SQL injection' }. All three can be mixed in a single context array.

Context references are resolved at send time in the handler — the persistence layer (load_session, get_session_messages_full) is accessed to fetch actual message content. Resolved content is appended after the sender's message text before delivery.

Resolved context is formatted in XML-style blocks: <quoted-context><from session="id" turns="N-M">[N] role: content\n[N+1] role: content</from></quoted-context>. Each reference becomes a separate <from> block inside the <quoted-context> wrapper.

Graceful degradation for errors: if a referenced session doesn't exist, the <from> block contains a warning '⚠ Session {id} not found' but the message still delivers. If a search query matches nothing, the block contains '⚠ No matches for query "{term}"'. The sender's message text is always delivered regardless of resolution failures.

The MessageDelivered response includes a context_resolved count: { delivered: true, session_id: 'target', context_resolved: 2 }. This tells the sender how many context references were successfully resolved (vs. degraded with warnings).
When context is omitted or empty, the message action behaves identically to AMGR-010 — plain text delivery with no context resolution. This is backward compatible.

Turn indices are 0-based, matching the position in the session's ordered message list (same indexing as SessionSearch show). Out-of-range turn indices are silently skipped — if turns [1, 999] are requested and the session only has 5 messages, only turn 1 is included.

Blob references in resolved messages are transparently resolved — if a message's content contains a blob:sha256: reference, it's fetched from BlobStore and the actual text content is used in the quoted context.

AMGR-011.title: Message context resolution

userStory.action: attach session history references when sending messages to other agents
userStory.benefit: the receiving agent gets self-contained context without needing follow-up SessionSearch calls

architectureNotes.text: RoleDialog component at src/components/RoleDialog.tsx — wraps base Dialog, uses useMultiLineInput hook for text editing, implements Tab-based focus cycling (textarea → OK → Cancel → textarea)
set_role action dispatched in agent_manager handler — calls session_set_role(session_id, role_name, None, None) NAPI binding; empty role calls session_clear_role or sets empty
/role slash command integrated in AgentView.tsx following /thinking pattern — checks currentSessionId, opens dialog or shows status message

AMGR-012.description: Implement set_role action for AgentManager (set/change a role string on any session as a system prompt overlay) and the /role TUI command (opens a dialog to set the role on the current session). Replaces the old /supervisor command and supervisor template screens.

examples.text: User types /role → dialog opens with empty textarea → types 'code-reviewer' → presses Tab → focus moves to OK button → presses Enter → role is set to 'code-reviewer'

Session has role 'architect' → user types /role → dialog opens with 'architect' pre-populated in textarea → user edits to 'senior architect' → presses Tab then Enter on OK → role updated to 'senior architect'
Session has role 'reviewer' → user types /role → dialog opens with 'reviewer' → user clears the text area → presses Tab then Enter on OK → role is removed/cleared
User types /role → dialog opens → user presses ESC → dialog closes, role unchanged
User types /role → dialog opens → user presses Tab → OK button highlighted → presses Tab again → Cancel button highlighted → presses Tab → focus back to textarea
User types /role with no active session → status message 'Start a session first to set a role.' displayed, no dialog
Agent calls set_role action with role='test-helper' and no session_id → role set on caller's own session → response: { session_id: 'own-id', role: 'test-helper' }
Agent calls set_role with session_id='sub-123' and role='code-reviewer' → role set on subordinate session → response: { session_id: 'sub-123', role: 'code-reviewer' }
Agent calls set_role with role='' (empty string) → role cleared → response: { session_id: 'target-id', role: null }
Agent calls set_role with session_id='nonexistent' → error response: { error: true, code: 'session_not_found', message: '...' }
Agent calls get_status for session with role='architect' → response includes role: 'architect' field
Agent calls list → sessions with roles show role field in their entries
In the dialog text area: cursor is visible, Enter creates newline, arrow keys navigate, backspace deletes — standard multi-line editing using useMultiLineInput hook

rules.text: /role command opens a modal dialog with a multi-line text area (6 fixed visible lines) pre-populated with the current role text if one exists
Dialog has OK/Cancel buttons at the bottom — Tab cycles focus between the text area and the button row, left/right arrows navigate between OK and Cancel when buttons are focused
Enter key inserts a newline in the text area (when text area is focused). When button row is focused, Enter activates the selected button
Submitting with an empty text area clears/removes the role from the session
ESC dismisses the dialog without making any changes (handled by base Dialog component)
Dialog uses cyan border color and the base Dialog component from src/components/Dialog.tsx
set_role AgentManager action sets or replaces the role on a target session — empty/null role clears it
set_role action defaults session_id to caller's own session when not specified
Role appears in get_status and list action responses
/role requires an active session — shows status message if no session exists

AMGR-012.title: Role management — set_role action and /role TUI command

userStory.action: set or edit a role on any session via a /role TUI dialog or the AgentManager set_role action
userStory.benefit: customize the system prompt overlay for sessions to specialize their behavior

AMGR-013.description: When AgentManager spawn action tries to inherit the spawner's model, it calls current_provider_name() which returns the internal ProviderType name (e.g. 'claude', 'gemini') but then passes this to create_session_with_id() which expects the models.dev registry name (e.g. 'anthropic', 'google'). The model string becomes 'claude/claude-opus-4-6' instead of 'anthropic/claude-opus-4-6', causing: 'Unknown provider: claude. Available providers: anthropic, ...'. This affects ALL providers with name mismatches: claude→anthropic, gemini→google.

examples.text: Anthropic: selected_model_string() returns 'anthropic/claude-opus-4-6' → passed directly → spawn succeeds
Google: selected_model_string() returns 'google/gemini-2.5-pro' → passed directly → spawn succeeds
OpenAI: selected_model_string() returns 'openai/gpt-4o' → passed directly → spawn succeeds

rules.text: handle_spawn must receive the full model string from ProviderManager::selected_model_string() which already has the correct registry format (e.g. 'anthropic/claude-opus-4-6')
No provider name mapping/translation is needed — the original model string is passed through directly to create_session_with_id
The fix is in create_handler and handle_spawn in agent_manager_handler.rs — accept a single Option<String> model string instead of separate provider_id + model_id

AMGR-013.title: AgentManager spawn fails — current_provider_name() returns internal name 'claude' but create_session_with_id expects registry name 'anthropic'

AMGR-014.description: When AgentManager spawns a subordinate session via handle_spawn, no persistence manifest is created for it. This means the subordinate's messages are not persisted to disk, making its conversation history unsearchable via SessionSearch. Normal sessions have their persistence created by TypeScript before calling create_session_with_id, but subordinate sessions are created entirely in Rust.

examples.text: Parent session spawns subordinate, sends it a task. Parent then uses SessionSearch to find the subordinate's conversation — subordinate shows up in 'recent' and its messages appear in 'search'
Subordinate processes a message from parent. The user and assistant messages are persisted to disk and can be loaded by load_session()
Persistence manifest creation fails (e.g. disk full). Spawn still succeeds but logs a warning. Session works for the current run but history won't survive restart

rules.text: Subordinate sessions must have a persistence manifest created before the in-memory session, so messages are stored on disk
The manifest ID must match the subordinate session UUID so persistence and in-memory session are linked
The provider field in the manifest should be extracted from the model string (e.g. 'anthropic/claude-opus-4-6' → 'anthropic')
If manifest creation fails, the session should still be created (degraded mode — works but not searchable)

AMGR-014.title: Spawned subordinate sessions not searchable — no persistence manifest created

userStory.action: search the conversation history of spawned subordinate sessions
userStory.benefit: I can review what my subordinate agents discussed and find relevant information across all sessions

architectureNotes.text: The handler in agent_manager_handler.rs must subscribe to each target session's supervisor_broadcast channel (tokio::broadcast::Receiver<StreamChunk>) and use tokio::select! to wait for SessionStateChange(Idle) events rather than polling get_status()

The handler must be async — unlike other AgentManager actions which are sync closures, await_idle needs to .await on broadcast receivers and tokio::time::timeout. The AgentManagerHandler type signature may need to return a Future or the handler dispatch must special-case await_idle as async

For multi-session await, spawn one tokio::spawn per target session, each subscribing to that session's broadcast channel. Use tokio::select! with a shared deadline (Instant + Duration) to cancel all remaining waiters when timeout expires. Use a JoinSet or select_all pattern.

The call() method in AgentManagerTool (mod.rs) currently calls execute_agent_manager() synchronously. For await_idle, it needs an async path. Options: (A) make execute_agent_manager async, (B) add a separate execute_agent_manager_async for await_idle, (C) pass a oneshot::Sender into the handler and await the receiver in call(). Option B is cleanest — minimal blast radius.
The interrupt check should use the calling session's interrupt_notify (Arc<Notify>) as a cancellation signal in the tokio::select! alongside the broadcast receivers and timeout
Result type: add AwaitResult variant to AgentManagerResult containing results: Vec<AwaitSessionResult> where each entry has { session_id, status: idle|timed_out|destroyed|interrupted }

AMGR-015.description: Add an `await_idle` action to the AgentManager tool that allows a supervisor agent to efficiently wait for one or more subordinate sessions to reach idle state. This replaces the anti-pattern of polling get_status in a loop with sleep/delay between calls. Uses the existing supervisor_broadcast channel and SessionStateChange events for zero-polling notification-based waiting with configurable timeout.

examples.text: Supervisor spawns 3 workers, sends tasks, calls await_idle with all 3 session IDs, all 3 finish within timeout → result shows all 3 as `idle`
Supervisor calls await_idle on a single session that is already idle → returns immediately with `idle` status, no wait
Supervisor calls await_idle with timeout=10 on a session that takes 30s → after 10s returns with that session marked as `timed_out`
Supervisor calls await_idle on 3 sessions, 2 finish quickly and 1 times out → result shows 2 as `idle` and 1 as `timed_out`
Supervisor calls await_idle with a non-existent session ID → immediate error response with session_not_found code
Supervisor calls await_idle on a session that gets destroyed mid-wait → that session resolves as `destroyed`, remaining sessions continue being awaited
User presses Esc while supervisor is awaiting 3 sessions (1 already idle, 2 still running) → returns partial result: 1 idle, 2 interrupted
Supervisor calls await_idle with a single string session_id (not array) → works the same as passing a single-element array
Supervisor calls await_idle with timeout omitted → waits indefinitely until session becomes idle

rules.text: The action name must be `await_idle` and be added to the AgentManagerAction enum alongside spawn/list/get_status/close/message/set_role
The `session_id` parameter accepts either a single session ID string or an array of session ID strings to await multiple agents simultaneously
Must use notification-based waiting (subscribe to supervisor_broadcast channel for SessionStateChange events), NOT polling with sleep
If a target session is already idle at call time, it is immediately resolved without waiting
The result must report which sessions became idle and which timed out, using a structured JSON response
If a target session is destroyed while being awaited, it counts as resolved (not an error) with a `destroyed` status
The await must be interruptible — if the calling session is interrupted (Esc), the await should cancel and return partial results
Non-existent session IDs must return an immediate error (session_not_found), not wait until timeout
Pre-tool hooks (HOOK-013) must be checked before execution, consistent with all other AgentManager actions
An optional `timeout` parameter (in seconds) sets a maximum wait duration; if omitted, waits indefinitely until all sessions are idle

AMGR-015.title: AgentManager await_idle action — efficient blocking wait for subordinate agents to finish

userStory.action: await one or more subordinate agents becoming idle
userStory.benefit: I can coordinate parallel work without wasteful polling or sleep loops

architectureNotes.text: Primary change in codelet/cli/src/interactive/stream_loop.rs — wrap stream.next() in tokio::time::timeout inside the inner streaming loop
DeepSearch wall-clock timeout in codelet/napi/src/deep_search_handler.rs — wrap build_and_run_agent() call in tokio::time::timeout
Drop guard for agent_loop in codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs — ensure set_status(Idle) executes even on panic via a struct that implements Drop
The stall timeout error should be a distinct error type (not reuse network/truncation errors) so error_classifiers.rs does not accidentally catch and retry it
The tokio::select! in the stream loop already has an interrupt_notify branch — the timeout can be added as another branch in the same select

AMGR-016.description:
When a subordinate agent spawns a DeepSearch sub-agent and that DeepSearch stalls or errors without returning a result, the subordinate gets stuck permanently in 'running' state. The await_idle caller times out but the subordinate never transitions to idle.

Observed behavior:
- Agent 179f28e7 was dispatched with a research task using DeepSearch
- DeepSearch returned its result (visible as turn 10, role=user)
- The agent never produced an assistant response after that — stuck in 'running' forever
- await_idle with 600s timeout returned 'timed_out' for this agent
- Other agents with identical roles and similar DeepSearch tasks completed fine

Expected behavior:
- If a DeepSearch (or any tool) returns but the agent's LLM response fails/stalls, there should be a timeout mechanism that detects the hang and either retries or marks the agent as errored
- The spawner should be able to detect this state (stuck after tool result returned but no generation happening) vs normal 'running'

Possible causes:
1. LLM API returned an error/timeout after the DeepSearch result was injected but the error was swallowed
2. The agent's generation got stuck in an infinite loop or deadlock
3. No watchdog/heartbeat mechanism exists to detect stalled generations

Suggested fix areas:
- Add a generation timeout per turn (e.g., if no tokens received for 120s after tool result, abort and mark errored)
- Add a 'stalled' or 'errored' status to AgentManager get_status
- Make await_idle distinguish between 'still working' and 'stuck/errored'
- Consider a heartbeat mechanism where running agents periodically confirm they're making progress

examples.text: LLM SSE stream stalls after DeepSearch result is injected — stream.next() blocks for 120s — timeout fires — agent transitions to Idle — error message emitted — await_idle caller gets idle result
LLM generates tokens normally — each token resets the idle timeout — no timeout fires — agent completes and transitions to Idle normally
LLM pauses for 60s between tokens (slow generation) — timeout is 120s — no timeout fires — agent completes successfully
DeepSearch sub-agent's LLM stalls during its own generation — wall-clock timeout (300s) fires — parent agent receives timeout error as tool result string — parent continues processing
Network error during streaming triggers existing NET-001 retry logic — stall timeout does NOT interfere — retries succeed — agent completes normally
Stream loop panics during processing — drop guard fires — agent_loop sets status to Idle — await_idle returns idle
LLM starts responding with tokens, then stops mid-sentence for 120s — stall timeout fires — partial text is preserved in history — agent transitions to Idle

rules.text: stream.next().await in the stream loop must be wrapped in a tokio::time::timeout so that stalled SSE streams are detected and aborted
The idle timeout resets on every received streaming chunk (token, tool_call, etc.) — only fires when no data arrives for the full duration
When the idle timeout fires, the stream loop must break and return Err so the outer agent_loop sets status to Idle
The timeout duration should be configurable but default to 120 seconds
After a stall timeout, the error emitted to the UI must clearly indicate it was a stall (not a network error or API error)
The existing error classifier cascade must NOT catch stall timeouts — stall is a distinct terminal error that always breaks the loop
DeepSearch sub-agent execution must be wrapped in a wall-clock timeout (default 300s) so stalled sub-agents don't block the parent forever
The agent_loop post-stream cleanup (set_status(Idle) + emit Done) must ALWAYS execute even if the stream loop panics — use a drop guard or equivalent

AMGR-016.title: Subordinate agent hangs indefinitely when DeepSearch sub-agent fails to return

userStory.action: detect and recover when a subordinate agent's LLM generation stalls indefinitely
userStory.benefit: subordinates don't hang forever and I get clear error feedback instead of silent timeouts

architectureNotes.text: Instrumentation API: profile_scope!("label") macro is the primary call site marker. Compiles to `let _guard = ProfileScope::enter(concat!(module_path!(), "::", "label"));` which on Drop accumulates elapsed nanos into ScopeMetrics. The label MUST be a &'static str (compile-time concat) so the registry never allocates on the hot path

Initial instrumentation targets (must be wired during implementing — not optional): codelet/tools/src/bridge_relay.rs relay_loop outer loop, connect_and_relay inbound for-loop, connect_and_relay outbound select! arms (one label per arm: control_recv, stream_recv, subordinate_recv, shutdown_recv); codelet/napi/src/agent_manager_handler.rs handle_await_idle outer loop and join_set.join_next branches, spawn_subordinate_forwarding_task recv loop; codelet/napi/src/scheduler/engine.rs spawn_scheduler tick loop; codelet/napi/src/scheduler/loop_store.rs register_with_task_and_idle_check inner loop

Channel instrumentation: introduce TrackedBroadcast<T>, TrackedMpsc<T>, and TrackedUnboundedMpsc<T> wrapper types in codelet/tools/src/profile/channels.rs that delegate to the tokio primitives but register themselves in a global ChannelRegistry on construction (with a stable name) and unregister on Drop. Migrate supervisor_broadcast in codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs:509, OUTBOUND_CONTROL_SENDERS in bridge_relay.rs, and SUBORDINATE_CHUNK_SENDERS in bridge_relay.rs to use these wrappers

Tokio runtime metrics: use tokio's experimental tokio::runtime::Handle::current().metrics() (requires `tokio_unstable` cfg flag in build.rs) to populate the runtime section. If tokio_unstable is not enabled, the runtime section degrades gracefully to {worker_threads: <known>, alive_tokio_tasks: null}

Process metrics: use the existing dependency tree where possible — RSS via mach2::task on macOS, /proc/self/status on Linux, GetProcessMemoryInfo on Windows. Wrap in a single get_process_metrics() helper in codelet/common/src/process_metrics.rs to avoid duplicating platform code

AgentManager dispatch: extend AgentManagerAction enum in codelet/tools/src/agent_manager/types.rs with `Profile { duration_secs: Option<u32>, top_n: Option<usize>, label_prefix: Option<String> }`. Profile is ASYNC (it awaits tokio::time::sleep for the duration of the window), so it dispatches through the existing async handler in codelet/napi/src/agent_manager_handler.rs::create_async_handler — NOT through the sync handler. The handler validates duration_secs is in range 1..=60 (defaulting to 10), then awaits ProfileSession::run(duration_secs, top_n, label_prefix)

Gating mechanism: ProfileRegistry exposes `static PROFILING_ACTIVE: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false)`. The profile_scope!() macro expands to `let _guard = if PROFILING_ACTIVE.load(Ordering::Relaxed) { Some(ProfileScope::enter(concat!(module_path!(), "::", $label))) } else { None };` — when inactive this is one Relaxed atomic load + branch (sub-1ns on aarch64). ProfileSession::run() does: (1) compare_exchange(false, true, AcqRel, Acquire) — return error if Err, (2) call registry.reset_all() to zero counters and capture baseline metrics, (3) tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_secs(duration_secs)).await, (4) capture end metrics and build result, (5) store(false, Release) on PROFILING_ACTIVE, (6) return result. The Acquire/Release pairing ensures all counter writes during the window are visible to the result-building code

Module path: codelet/tools/src/profile/ — new submodule containing registry.rs (ProfileRegistry singleton with DashMap<&'static str, ScopeMetrics> and PROFILING_ACTIVE: AtomicBool), scope.rs (ProfileScope RAII guard + profile_scope!() macro), session.rs (ProfileSession::run() — the time-bounded capture orchestrator), result.rs (ProfileResult, ScopeReport, ChannelReport types), and channels.rs (instrumented broadcast/mpsc wrappers used by bridge_relay and session_manager)

rig::tool::Tool integration: extend AgentManagerTool::call() in codelet/tools/src/agent_manager/handler.rs to handle AgentManagerAction::Profile by awaiting ProfileSession::run(duration_secs, top_n, label_prefix). The handler must use the same singleton ProfileRegistry instance as the NAPI dispatch path so both call paths see the same counters and the same PROFILING_ACTIVE gate

TypeScript binding: AgentManager tool wrapper in src/tools/agentManager.ts must add `profile` to the action union and forward duration_secs, top_n, and label_prefix parameters to the NAPI handler. Add the profile action to the JSON schema in src/tools/agentManagerSchema.ts so AI agents see it in their tool catalog. Document in the schema that the call BLOCKS for duration_secs (default 10) — agents must expect a long-running tool call and not interpret the wait as a hang

AMGR-017.description: Extend the AgentManager tool with a new `profile` action that returns runtime diagnostic information from the Rust side (codelet-napi) — thread counts, tokio task metrics, channel queue depths, lock contention indicators, and hot-loop counters. This is needed to diagnose CPU spikes like the runaway tokio worker thread accumulation observed during PROV-053 / PROV-054 sessions, where 9+ tokio workers became permanently pegged at 99% CPU with no symbols available in the stripped SEA binary. The action must be a first-class AgentManager command (NOT a separate NAPI binding) so any agent can query it at runtime via the same dispatch path as spawn/list/await_idle, and so it works in production builds without requiring debug symbols or external profilers like dtrace/sample.

examples.text: An AI agent debugging a CPU spike calls AgentManager profile duration_secs=10. The call blocks for 10 seconds while instrumentation is active. The result returns: scopes_by_calls[0] = { label: 'bridge_relay::subordinate_forwarding::recv_loop', call_count: 24_800_000, total_self_ms: 9840, calls_per_sec: 2_480_000, currently_executing_at_end: 9 } — pinpointing the runaway loop spinning at 2.4M calls/sec with 9 concurrent instances at the moment the window closed

An AI agent calls AgentManager profile (default duration_secs=10) and the runtime section of the result shows alive_tokio_tasks_start=12 and alive_tokio_tasks_end=47 — the agent immediately sees that 35 tokio tasks accumulated during the 10-second window, confirming a task leak

An AI agent narrows in on a suspect module by calling AgentManager profile duration_secs=5 label_prefix='handle_await_idle'. After the 5-second window the result contains only scopes whose label starts with that prefix — letting the agent confirm or rule out the await_idle loop without sifting through hundreds of unrelated entries

While an AI agent has a profile session running (started 3 seconds ago, 7 seconds remaining) a second AgentManager profile call from any other agent returns an immediate error response: { error: 'profile_session_active', started_at: '2026-04-07T14:12:30Z', ends_in_secs: 7 } — the second agent waits 7 seconds and retries rather than overlapping windows that would corrupt counters

An AI agent calls AgentManager profile duration_secs=10 and inspects the channels section of the result: it sees supervisor_broadcast_<id> with sender_count=1, receiver_count=9, queued_at_end=128, lagged_during_window=42_000 — the agent concludes broadcast subscribers cannot drain fast enough and follows the lead to the subordinate forwarding loop

A subordinate LLM agent invokes the AgentManager rig::tool::Tool with action=profile and duration_secs=10 directly via tool_use. It awaits the 10-second blocking response, parses the structured JSON, finds scopes_by_calls[0].currently_executing_at_end=9, and decides to call AgentManager close on the runaway sibling — the entire diagnostic loop happens autonomously without human intervention

questions.answer: Opt-in per call site via profile_scope!("label") macro at known hot loops only — NOT auto-instrument-all-functions. Rationale: (1) sub-1ns cost when PROFILING_ACTIVE=false means we don't need to be stingy, but covering every fn would balloon the registry with thousands of irrelevant entries that drown out signal during a 10-second window, (2) the goal is diagnosing runaway loops, which are already a small known set (bridge_relay, await_idle, scheduler, forwarding) — instrumenting those plus any new loop added later via PR review is sufficient, (3) opt-in keeps the result payload small so it fits comfortably in a single tool-call response without truncation
questions.text: @human: Should the proc-macro-based instrumentation cover ALL functions in codelet/tools and codelet/napi automatically (via #[instrument] on every fn), or should it be opt-in per call site so we keep the registry small and only profile the loops we care about?

questions.answer: No persistence — snapshots are in-memory only, ephemeral, scoped to the AI tool-call lifetime (5-10 second windows). The bounded LRU snapshot store (max 32) lives in process memory and is dropped on restart. This is a tool for AI agents to diagnose runtime issues during a session, not a long-term observability system for humans.
questions.text: @human: Should snapshots be persisted to disk (e.g. ~/.fspec/profile-snapshots/<id>.json) so they survive process restarts and can be diffed across runs, or kept in-memory only?

questions.answer: Flat scopes only — NO parent/child nesting. Rationale: (1) flame-graph nesting adds ~50ns per enter/exit and requires per-thread scope-stack tracking (thread-local storage with push/pop), which is more state to manage and more places for bugs to hide, (2) the diagnostic question we're answering is 'which loop body is spinning' not 'what is the call tree' — flat call_count and total_self_ms answer the spin question directly, (3) the labels are namespaced by module_path!() at compile time (e.g., 'bridge_relay::subordinate_forwarding::recv_loop'), so a human reader can already see the hierarchy from the label string without runtime parent/child tracking, (4) flat scopes serialize trivially as a sorted list, no tree-walking in the response builder
questions.text: @human: Do you want flame-graph-style parent/child scope nesting (where ProfileScope::enter inside another ProfileScope is recorded as a child), or flat scopes only? Nesting is more powerful but adds ~50ns per enter/exit and complicates the response shape.

rules.text: AgentManager exposes a new `profile` action alongside spawn/list/get_status/close/message/set_role/await_idle, dispatched through both the NAPI handler path and the rig::tool::Tool trait so any caller (TUI, subordinate, supervisor, MCP, LLM tool_use) can invoke it

Functions and async loop bodies are instrumented with a `#[profile_loop]` proc-macro (or manual `ProfileScope::enter("label")` RAII guard) that increments a per-label call counter, accumulates wall-clock self time in nanoseconds, and tracks max iteration time — stored in a global ProfileRegistry

Every long-running async loop in codelet/tools/src/bridge_relay.rs (relay_loop, inbound_handle for-loop, outbound select! loop, subordinate forwarding loop), codelet/napi/src/agent_manager_handler.rs (await_idle outer loop, spawn_subordinate_forwarding_task receive loop), codelet/napi/src/scheduler/engine.rs (30s tick loop), and codelet/napi/src/scheduler/loop_store.rs (per-entry interval loop) MUST be instrumented with a unique label so each loop iteration is counted individually

ProfileRegistry stores per-label metrics: { call_count: AtomicU64, total_self_ns: AtomicU64, max_iter_ns: AtomicU64, last_seen_unix_ms: AtomicU64, currently_executing: AtomicI32 } — all updates use Relaxed atomics so instrumentation overhead is < 100ns per call

Profiling can be disabled at compile time via a `profile` Cargo feature flag (default on for dev/release, off for tiny builds) — when off, the macro/RAII guards expand to no-ops and the registry is omitted, so there is zero overhead

The profile action takes a `duration_secs` integer parameter (range 1-60, default 10) specifying the length of the profiling window in seconds — instrumentation is active only during this window and returns aggregated results when it closes, mirroring how `sample(1)` and `perf record` operate as bounded captures rather than always-on systems

Instrumentation is gated by a single global PROFILING_ACTIVE: AtomicBool flag in the ProfileRegistry — when false (the steady state), the profile_scope!() macro performs only one Relaxed atomic load and a branch-not-taken (~1ns), so leaving instrumentation compiled in costs effectively zero. Counter increments and timing only occur when the flag is true

Only one profile session may run at a time. Starting a profile uses an atomic compare-and-swap on PROFILING_ACTIVE from false→true; if a session is already active, the second call returns an error of the form `{ error: "profile_session_active", started_at: <iso8601>, ends_in_secs: <n> }` rather than waiting in line or stomping the existing session

Profile session lifecycle: (1) compare-and-swap PROFILING_ACTIVE to true, (2) reset all per-scope counters to zero and capture process/runtime baseline metrics, (3) tokio::time::sleep(duration_secs), (4) capture process/runtime end metrics and channel stats, (5) set PROFILING_ACTIVE to false, (6) return aggregated result. The profile call BLOCKS the calling agent for the full duration — this is intentional and the caller should expect it

Profile result shape: { duration_secs, started_at, ended_at, process: { pid, rss_bytes_start, rss_bytes_end, total_threads_start, total_threads_end }, runtime: { worker_threads, alive_tokio_tasks_start, alive_tokio_tasks_end }, scopes_by_calls: [top N scopes sorted by call_count desc], scopes_by_self_ms: [top N scopes sorted by total_self_ms desc], channels: [{ name, sender_count, receiver_count, queued_at_end, lagged_during_window }] }. Each scope entry includes { label, call_count, total_self_ms, max_iter_ms, calls_per_sec, currently_executing_at_end }

Optional `top_n` parameter (default 20, max 200) caps how many scopes appear in scopes_by_calls and scopes_by_self_ms. Optional `label_prefix` parameter filters scopes to those whose label starts with the given string before sorting/truncation — both filters apply at result-build time, never on the hot path

The profile action is read-only with respect to session state — it must not spawn new tokio tasks during the window (sleep + atomic counters only), must not mutate any AgentManager session, and must not allocate on the hot path. Total instrumentation overhead during an active window must remain under 5% of CPU even at multi-million-calls-per-second hot loops

No persistence — profile results live only in the tool-call response. There is no on-disk snapshot store, no LRU cache of past sessions, no ~/.fspec/profile-snapshots/ directory. Each profile call is a fresh capture. This is a tool for AI agents to diagnose runtime issues during a session, not a long-term observability system for humans

Opt-in per call site via profile_scope!("label") macro at known hot loops only — NOT auto-instrument-all-functions. Rationale: (1) sub-1ns cost when PROFILING_ACTIVE=false means we don't need to be stingy, but covering every fn would balloon the registry with thousands of irrelevant entries that drown out signal during a 10-second window, (2) the goal is diagnosing runaway loops, which are already a small known set (bridge_relay, await_idle, scheduler, forwarding) — instrumenting those plus any new loop added later via PR review is sufficient, (3) opt-in keeps the result payload small so it fits comfortably in a single tool-call response without truncation

Flat scopes only — NO parent/child nesting. Rationale: (1) flame-graph nesting adds ~50ns per enter/exit and requires per-thread scope-stack tracking (thread-local storage with push/pop), which is more state to manage and more places for bugs to hide, (2) the diagnostic question we're answering is 'which loop body is spinning' not 'what is the call tree' — flat call_count and total_self_ms answer the spin question directly, (3) the labels are namespaced by module_path!() at compile time (e.g., 'bridge_relay::subordinate_forwarding::recv_loop'), so a human reader can already see the hierarchy from the label string without runtime parent/child tracking, (4) flat scopes serialize trivially as a sorted list, no tree-walking in the response builder

architectureNotes.text: Backward compatibility: existing scopes_by_calls and scopes_by_self_ms fields remain in ProfileResult with the same shape; new fields (samples_by_thread, hot_stacks, sampling) are additive so existing tool-call consumers do not break.

Noise frame blocklist lives in session.rs: NOISE_FRAME_PREFIXES = ['libsystem_', '__pthread_', '_pthread_', '_dyld_', '_os_', '__os_unfair_', '_uv_', '_uv__', 'libuv', 'libgcc', 'libc', '_napi_register_module_v1', 'napi_', '__tsan', '__asan']. A symbol is considered noise if any prefix is a substring of its demangled name. The match uses str::contains for portability across macOS's underscore-prefixed mangling convention.

hot_stacks uses a HashMap<Vec<String>, StackAggregate> keyed by the first 6 meaningful symbol names in each resolved stack. Each StackAggregate accumulates sample_count and tracks the originating thread_name. At build time the map is sorted by sample_count desc and truncated to top_n. File/line metadata is captured from the leaf meaningful frame only — full per-frame metadata is dropped to keep the payload under the 1MB tool response limit.

cpu_cores_consumed is computed as total_samples * (1.0 / SAMPLE_FREQUENCY_HZ) / duration_secs. For a fully CPU-saturated single thread at 250Hz over 10s you'd expect ~2500 samples, giving cpu_cores_consumed ≈ 1.0. Two saturated workers would give ~2.0. This lets the agent immediately judge 'is the process actually hammering or is it mostly idle' without parsing individual sample counts.

The resolved_rust_samples / unresolved_samples split uses a simple heuristic: a sample is 'resolved' if its attributed non-noise frame has file.is_some() AND filename doesn't end with '.c' or 'Unknown'. This gives a tight signal — if it's <10% the build is almost certainly stripped.

AMGR-018.description: The AMGR-017 profile action returns garbage because (1) the release build strips symbols so backtrace-rs can't resolve internal Rust functions, (2) run_pprof_window only looks at the leaf frame and collapses every call chain that ends in the same leaf, (3) it double-counts inlined symbols, and (4) it discards thread_name, full stack, file/line metadata that pprof-rs already captures. Fix the release profile to retain debug info, rewrite run_pprof_window to walk leaf->root skipping OS/libuv/napi noise frames, emit per-thread sample distribution, emit top-N hot stacks with file:line, emit a sampling-quality report so agents can detect when debug info is missing, and add a focus filter argument.

examples.text: AI calls AgentManager profile duration_secs=10. The subordinate_forwarding task is in a tight recv loop on a tokio worker. samples_by_thread[0] = {thread_name:'tokio-runtime-worker-3', sample_count:2400, cpu_ms:9600}. hot_stacks[0].frames[0] = {symbol:'codelet_napi::agent_manager_handler::spawn_subordinate_forwarding_task::{{closure}}', file:'codelet/napi/src/agent_manager_handler.rs', line:243}. The agent immediately sees exactly which function is hot and on which worker.

AI calls profile duration_secs=10 on a binary built with the old strip='symbols' profile. Response.sampling.debug_info_available=false, sampling.resolved_rust_samples=8, sampling.unresolved_samples=2076, and a human-readable hint is embedded. The AI reports back 'cannot diagnose — need rebuilt binary with debug info' instead of chasing phantom _napi_register_module_v1 hot spots.

AI suspects the subordinate forwarding task and calls profile duration_secs=10 focus='spawn_subordinate_forwarding_task'. hot_stacks contains only stacks that touched that function; samples_by_thread shows which workers ran it; scopes_by_calls sums the attributed samples only within that call chain — letting the AI confirm or rule out the suspect in one call.

AI profiles an idle process. samples_by_thread shows every worker with <5 samples, scopes_by_calls top entry is a tokio::runtime::park or epoll_wait, and sampling.cpu_cores_consumed is 0.02. The AI confirms there is no CPU hammering — the old bug would have reported _napi_register_module_v1 as the hot spot regardless.

AI profiles a process hot on three different code paths. hot_stacks[0..3] show three distinct stacks each with different leaf symbols but NOT merged together, and scopes_by_calls attributes each via walking-leaf-to-root, giving three separate attribution entries instead of the old behavior of collapsing them all into a single shared wrapper frame.

Inlined double-count fix verified: AI profiles a synthetic workload where compiler inlines 4 helpers into a single frame. Old code would credit 4 symbols per sample (4x inflation); new code credits the outermost symbol only, so scopes_by_calls total_self_ms matches real wall-clock CPU burn within sampling error.

rules.text: The release build must retain line-table debug info (debug=1) and NOT strip symbols, so backtrace-rs can resolve internal Rust functions
run_pprof_window walks each stack leaf-to-root and attributes the sample to the first non-noise frame (skipping libsystem, libuv, pthread, dyld, _os_, __os_unfair, and NAPI C-export wrapper frames)
When a physical stack frame contains multiple inlined symbols, only the outermost symbol is credited with the sample (no double-counting)
ProfileResult includes samples_by_thread: a Vec<ThreadSampleReport> listing every thread that produced samples, sorted by sample_count desc, each with thread_name, thread_id, sample_count, and cpu_ms

ProfileResult includes hot_stacks: a Vec<StackReport> listing the top-N unique call stacks by sample_count, each stack truncated to the first 6 meaningful frames with {symbol, file, line} and carrying thread_name

ProfileResult includes sampling: a SamplingReport with total_samples, resolved_rust_samples, unresolved_samples, cpu_cores_consumed (derived from total samples and duration), and debug_info_available (false when < 10% of samples resolved to Rust symbols)

A new focus: Option<String> argument drops any sample whose stack does not contain a frame whose symbol contains the focus substring — applied before per-leaf attribution so hot_stacks, scopes_by_calls and samples_by_thread all reflect the narrowed view
The noise-frame blocklist is a compile-time static array in session.rs so the filter cost is one substring scan per frame; adding a new noise prefix is a single source edit
The TypeScript tool binding in src/tools/agentManager.ts and its JSON schema accept the new focus parameter and document it in the action description

Changing strip from 'symbols' to 'none' and adding debug=1 + split-debuginfo='packed' to [profile.release] retains line-table DWARF in a sibling .dSYM bundle on macOS without ballooning the .node binary size

BRIDGE-001.description:
Create a Bridge Rig Tool that the AI agent can call to connect sessions to external WebSocket endpoints.

**This is a RIG TOOL like WebSearch, Read, Bash - NOT NAPI bindings!**

**Tool Location:** `codelet/tools/src/bridge.rs`

**Tool Actions (like WebSearch):**
- `connect` - Connect to a WebSocket endpoint URL
- `disconnect` - Disconnect from a specific endpoint
- `list` - List active bridge connections with status

**How it works:**
1. Agent calls `Bridge` tool with action `connect` and URL
2. Bridge subscribes to session's `watcher_broadcast` channel
3. Bridge connects as WebSocket client to the endpoint
4. Outbound: StreamChunks are serialized to JSON and sent to endpoint
5. Inbound: Messages from endpoint are injected into session's input channel

**Integration:**
- Uses existing `subscribe_to_stream()` from WATCH-003
- Uses existing `watcher_input_tx` for input injection from WATCH-006
- Tool manages global connection state (like WebSearch's browser state)

**Message Format:**
- Outbound: `{"type": "chunk", "session_id": "...", "data": <StreamChunk>}`
- Inbound: `{"type": "input", "session_id": "...", "message": "..."}`

examples.text: Agent calls Bridge(action: 'connect', url: 'ws://localhost:8080') → Returns 'Connected to ws://localhost:8080'
Agent calls Bridge(action: 'connect', url: 'ws://invalid:9999') → Returns error 'Connection refused'
Agent calls Bridge(action: 'list') → Returns '[{url: ws://localhost:8080, state: connected, buffered: 0}]'
Agent calls Bridge(action: 'disconnect', url: 'ws://localhost:8080') → Returns 'Disconnected from ws://localhost:8080'
Agent connects to two endpoints → Both receive all StreamChunks as JSON messages
Endpoint sends {type: 'input', session_id: '...', message: 'build the app'} → Agent receives 'build the app' as user input
Connection drops → Bridge buffers messages, reconnects → Buffered messages delivered to endpoint
Agent calls Bridge(action: 'list') during reconnect → Returns '[{url: ws://localhost:8080, state: reconnecting, buffered: 5}]'

questions.answer: Relay everything including thinking/reasoning. The bridge is a dumb pipe - the endpoint decides what to display.
questions.text: Should thinking/reasoning be relayed, or only final assistant responses?

questions.answer: Buffer messages when the external endpoint is unreachable, then deliver when connection is restored.
questions.text: What happens when bridge is connected but external platform is unreachable? Buffer messages or drop them?

rules.text: Bridge is a Rig Tool in codelet/tools/src/bridge.rs - implements rig::tool::Tool trait
Tool has three actions: connect (URL), disconnect (URL), list
connect action: validates URL, creates WebSocket client connection to endpoint, subscribes to session broadcast, returns connection status
disconnect action: closes WebSocket connection, stops relaying, returns confirmation
list action: returns all active bridge connections with URL, state (connecting/connected/reconnecting/disconnected), buffer size
Multiple bridges can connect to same session simultaneously (agent calls connect multiple times)
Bridge acts as WebSocket CLIENT - connects outbound to endpoint URL (endpoint is server)
Outbound messages: JSON envelope {type: 'chunk', session_id, data: StreamChunk}
Inbound messages: JSON envelope {type: 'input', session_id, message: string} - injected into session's input channel
Auto-reconnect on disconnect with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s... max 30s)
Buffer outbound messages when endpoint unreachable, deliver when reconnected
Buffer max 1GB - if exceeded, drop connection and return error
Tool needs session context to access watcher_broadcast and watcher_input_tx - passed via FacadeWrapper like FspecTool

BRIDGE-002.description:
Create a standalone TypeScript WebSocket endpoint that bridges codelet sessions to Telegram via BotFather Bot API.

**Location:** `bridge/telegram-endpoint.ts` (single file)

**Architecture:**
1. WebSocket server that codelet's BridgeManager connects to
2. Receives raw StreamChunks (text, thinking, tool_call, tool_result, done, error)
3. Formats and truncates messages for Telegram's 4096 char limit
4. Sends to Telegram chat via Bot API
5. Receives Telegram messages and sends back to codelet as input

**Message Flow:**
- Inbound from codelet: `{type: 'chunk', session_id, data: StreamChunk}`
- Outbound to codelet: `{type: 'input', session_id, message: string}`

**Telegram Integration:**
- Uses `node-telegram-bot-api` npm package
- Bot token from BotFather stored in `.env` file
- Supports MarkdownV2 formatting for code blocks
- Handles message chunking for long responses

**Key Features:**
- Smart truncation (preserve beginning and end)
- Code block preservation with syntax markers
- Thinking content formatted with 💭 prefix
- Tool outputs show tool name and truncated result
- Chat session tracking (which Telegram chat to send to)

BRIDGE-006.description: Enhance the Telegram bridge with content-aware chunking that respects natural content boundaries. Currently, telegram-endpoint.ts uses simple idle-based buffering (800ms/3500 chars) that can break messages mid-sentence. This story adds: (1) Boundary detection - flush at sentences, paragraphs, headings, code blocks instead of arbitrary limits, (2) Content summarization - condense thinking blocks to indicators like '🤔 Analyzing...' and tool output to summaries like '📄 Read file.ts (245 lines)', (3) Markdown validation - ensure each chunk has balanced markers before sending.

When a table would exceed 4096 chars, it is split BEFORE the table starts (at paragraph boundary), not mid-table

When multiple thinking chunks arrive in succession, they flow as continuous content between the single <think> and </think> tags - NOT multiple separate '🤔' messages

rules.text: Messages must never break mid-sentence - chunks should end at sentence boundaries (., !, ?) when possible
Code blocks (``` ... ```) must be sent as complete units, never split across messages
Tool output (especially file reads) should be summarized with key info, not sent verbatim - e.g., '📄 Read file.ts (245 lines)'
Each message must have valid, complete markdown - no unclosed backticks, bold markers, etc.
Messages must respect Telegram's 4096 character limit - split at nearest logical boundary before limit
Paragraph breaks (double newlines) are preferred chunking points
Headings (# ## ###) should start new chunks, not appear mid-chunk
Base64 images are too large for Telegram (4096 char limit). Show placeholder like '📷 [image referenced]' or skip entirely. Current code already handles photo uploads separately.
Markdown tables (| delimited rows) must be sent as complete units - never split mid-row or between header and data rows
Thinking blocks should be streamed with content wrapped in <think>...</think> tags - first thinking chunk gets <think> prefix, last gets </think> suffix, content flows naturally between

Rust is a pure emitter - ZERO knowledge of which session is active/attached/viewed. No attachment state whatsoever.

architectureNotes.text:
Standalone TypeScript file at bridge/relay-endpoint.ts with two WebSocket connections: (1) relay-client WS that connects TO the relay server, (2) local WS server that accepts codelet BridgeTool connections.

ONE UNIFIED COMMAND EXECUTION PATH:
ALL messages (input, control, command, chunk, connected) flow through the bridge WebSocket ↔ codelet bridge_relay.rs using the InboundMessage/OutboundMessage/StreamChunk event system. The relay endpoint is a PURE PROTOCOL TRANSLATOR — it translates relay protocol format (camelCase, {data:{}} envelope) to fspec flat InboundMessage format and vice versa. It does NOT call fspecCallback directly.

COMMAND FLOW:
1. Relay sends {type:command, session_id, request_id, data:{command, args}} to relay endpoint
2. Relay endpoint translates to InboundMessage {type:'command', session_id, request_id, command, args_json} and forwards to codelet bridge WS
3. bridge_relay.rs receives 'command' InboundMessage and emits FspecCommandRequest StreamChunk into the session
4. GlobalSessionStreamManager intercepts FspecCommandRequest, calls fspecCallback (same path as LLM Fspec tool)
5. FspecCommandResult StreamChunk flows back through session broadcast channel
6. bridge_relay.rs intercepts FspecCommandResult (does NOT forward as regular chunk), formats as commandResponse OutboundMessage with matching request_id
7. Relay endpoint translates OutboundMessage to relay protocol format and sends to relay

KEY TYPES:
- FspecCommandRequest (StreamChunk type in codelet/napi/src/types.rs) — emitted by bridge_relay.rs when command arrives, AND by session_manager.rs when LLM invokes Fspec tool
- FspecCommandResult (StreamChunk type) — result flowing back, intercepted by bridge_relay.rs for commandResponse
- InboundMessage (bridge_relay.rs) — extended with 'command' type, request_id, command, args_json fields
- OutboundMessage (bridge.rs) — extended with optional request_id for commandResponse messages
- fspecCallback (src/utils/fspec-callback.ts) — the shared in-process command executor, called ONLY by GlobalSessionStreamManager

Uses 'ws' npm package for both client and server.

BRIDGE-015.description: Create a new bridge endpoint (alongside the existing Telegram endpoint) that connects fspec to the platform-agnostic relay server. Unlike the Telegram endpoint which translates to Telegram Bot API, this endpoint speaks the relay protocol directly — handling the 5 session-scoped message types (input, sessionControl, command, commandResponse, chunk) plus auth handshake. The key new capability vs Telegram: handling 'command' messages by forwarding them through bridge_relay.rs into the FspecCommandRequest/FspecCommandResult StreamChunk event system, where GlobalSessionStreamManager calls fspecCallback — the same path used when the LLM invokes the Fspec tool. The relay endpoint is a PURE PROTOCOL TRANSLATOR and does NOT call fspecCallback directly. This is the fspec-side counterpart to MOBILE-010 in the fspec-mobile project.

examples.text: Endpoint starts, connects to relay ws://relay.example.com, sends auth with channel_id and api_key, receives authSuccess with instances list

Relay sends {type:input, session_id:X, data:{message:'fix bug', images:[...]}} → endpoint translates to flat InboundMessage {type:input, session_id:X, message:'fix bug', images:[...]} → forwards to codelet WS
Relay sends {type:sessionControl, session_id:X, data:{action:interrupt}} → endpoint translates to {type:control, session_id:X, action:interrupt} → forwards to codelet WS

Relay connection drops → endpoint logs warning, attempts reconnection with exponential backoff, re-authenticates on reconnect

Two codelet BridgeTools connect simultaneously with different session_ids (session-A, session-B). Relay sends input for session-A → endpoint routes to session-A's WS connection only. Relay sends input for session-B → endpoint routes to session-B's WS connection only.

Relay sends {type:command, session_id:X, request_id:R1, data:{command:'board', args:{}}} → endpoint translates to InboundMessage {type:'command', session_id:X, request_id:R1, command:'board', args_json:'{}'} → forwards to codelet WS → bridge_relay.rs emits FspecCommandRequest StreamChunk → GlobalSessionStreamManager calls fspecCallback → FspecCommandResult flows back through broadcast channel → bridge_relay.rs sends {type:'commandResponse', session_id:X, request_id:R1, data:{command:'board', success:true, result:{...}}}

Relay sends command that takes 45 seconds → bridge_relay.rs emits FspecCommandRequest → fspecCallback execution exceeds pipeline timeout (same timeout as LLM-invoked Fspec tool) → FspecCommandResult with error flows back through broadcast channel → bridge_relay.rs sends commandResponse with success:false and timeout error preserving request_id

Relay sends command for unknown fspec command → command flows through bridge_relay.rs → FspecCommandRequest → fspecCallback returns error → FspecCommandResult with success:false flows back → bridge_relay.rs sends commandResponse with error message and preserved request_id

rules.text: Endpoint is a standalone WebSocket server in bridge/ directory (like telegram-endpoint.ts), started independently
Endpoint connects to the relay server as a WebSocket CLIENT (relay is the server), unlike Telegram where fspec connects TO the endpoint
Auth handshake: endpoint sends {type:auth, data:{channel_id, api_key}} on connect and waits for authSuccess/authError before processing messages
chunk and connected messages pass through from fspec to relay with no transformation needed
sessionControl from relay must be renamed to 'control' and data unwrapped when forwarding to fspec bridge

Relay protocol uses camelCase message types (sessionControl, commandResponse) matching the mobile app implementation, and wraps payloads in {data:{...}} envelope. fspec InboundMessage uses flat fields (message, action) and 'control' instead of 'sessionControl'. Endpoint translates between these formats in both directions. NOTE: Part 3 architecture notes use snake_case (session_control, command_response) but the actual implementations use camelCase.

Endpoint supports multiple concurrent codelet sessions. Each codelet BridgeTool connects to the local WS server and identifies itself with a session_id via the connected message. Endpoint maintains a session_id→WebSocket map for routing inbound relay messages to the correct codelet connection.
Endpoint initiates periodic ping messages to the relay server to keep the connection alive (same pattern as mobile app). Relay responds with pong. Ping interval is 30 seconds.

Configuration via env vars: RELAY_URL (full WebSocket URL including path, e.g. ws://relay.example.com/v1/ws), RELAY_CHANNEL_ID, RELAY_API_KEY, WEBSOCKET_PORT (local port for codelet BridgeTool connections, default 8080)

StreamChunk data from fspec is forwarded to the relay without internal field transformation. fspec uses {type: 'tool_call'} (snake_case), mobile currently expects {chunkType: 'toolCall'} (camelCase). Messages from relay targeting an unknown or disconnected session_id are logged as warnings and silently dropped. No error response is sent back to the relay for session-scoped messages (input, sessionControl).

Must handle all 5 message types: input (session→fspec), sessionControl (session→fspec), command (session→fspec), commandResponse (fspec→client), chunk (fspec→client). ALL message types are session-scoped. Commands provide a separate channel within the session for fspec CLI operations, distinct from the agent conversation (input/chunk).

command messages are session-scoped and use request/response pattern with request_id correlation. Commands flow through the session's bridge WebSocket to Rust bridge_relay.rs, which channels them through the FspecCommandRequest/FspecCommandResult StreamChunk event system via fspecCallback. The relay endpoint does NOT call fspecCallback directly — it is a pure protocol translator.

InboundMessage in bridge_relay.rs must be extended to support 'command' type with request_id, command name, and args_json fields. When bridge_relay.rs receives a command InboundMessage, it emits a FspecCommandRequest StreamChunk into the session. GlobalSessionStreamManager handles it by calling fspecCallback. The FspecCommandResult StreamChunk flows back through the session's broadcast channel. bridge_relay.rs intercepts FspecCommandResult chunks (does NOT forward them as regular chunks) and sends a commandResponse OutboundMessage with the matching request_id back through the bridge WebSocket.

commandResponse uses canonical format: {type:'commandResponse', request_id, session_id, data:{command, success, result, error}} where success and error are derived from fspec's FspecCommandResult. OutboundMessage must be extended to support request_id for commandResponse messages.

Command execution timeout is handled within the FspecCommandRequest/FspecCommandResult pipeline — the same mechanism and timeout that applies when the LLM invokes the Fspec tool. The relay endpoint does not implement its own timeout via Promise.race.
