architectureNotes.text: Introduce a new module codelet/tools/src/bash_binary_guard.rs with a pure function `detect_bash_binary_output(stdout_bytes: &[u8]) -> Option<BinaryKind>` where BinaryKind is a small enum {Image(ImageMediaType), Pdf, Other}. Detection logic: (1) if stdout contains a NUL byte anywhere in the first N bytes (N=8192) → Some(Other) unless we also match a magic signature below; (2) if the first 16 bytes match PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP → Some(Image(...)); (3) if first 5 bytes are '%PDF-' → Some(Pdf); (4) if first 2 bytes are 0x1F 0x8B (gzip), or first 4 bytes are 'PK\x03\x04' (zip), or first 4 bytes are 0x7F 'ELF' → Some(Other). Priority: magic signature wins over generic NUL-byte detection so we can name the type.

Problem: codelet/tools/src/bash_output.rs uses String for stdout (already lossy to UTF-8) — we cannot reliably detect NUL bytes after stdout has been converted to a Rust String. Investigation needed: either (a) change StreamBuffers to hold Vec<u8> instead of String (intrusive), OR (b) accept that the upstream read/decode in bash_streams.rs already decodes to UTF-8 and use String-level detection (check for '\0' char and magic byte strings). Prefer (b) as less intrusive — Rust's String::contains('\x00') works on any UTF-8 string, and magic bytes are all ASCII-safe byte patterns that survive UTF-8 decoding when checked via .as_bytes().

Integration point: BashOutput::into_result() in bash_output.rs becomes the single choke-point — both BashTool::call() and BashTool::call_with_streaming() route through into_result(). Modify into_result() to call detect_bash_binary_output(self.stdout.as_bytes()) FIRST; if Some(kind), short-circuit to Err(ToolError::Execution { tool: "bash", message: format_binary_guard_message(kind) }), regardless of self.success. Otherwise fall through to existing success/error formatting.

Message format (deterministic, testable): for Image(mt) → 'Bash output suppressed: detected {PNG|JPEG|GIF|WebP} image. Use the Read tool on the file instead; the Bash tool does not return binary bytes to the model.'; for Pdf → 'Bash output suppressed: detected PDF document. Use the Read tool on the file instead...'; for Other → 'Bash output suppressed: detected binary content. Use the Read tool on the file instead...'. No file path in the message (we don't reliably know which file the user was catting — the caller has that context).

Tests: unit tests for detect_bash_binary_output live inside bash_binary_guard.rs (#[cfg(test)] mod tests) — fast, deterministic, no I/O. Integration tests for end-to-end Bash execution live in a new codelet/tools/src/bash_binary_guard_integration_tests.rs that actually spawns `cat` / `printf` / `gzip -c` under BashTool::call and asserts the returned Result. Fixtures: create tiny PNG/PDF/ELF/ZIP bytes inline (no external files) using tempfile::NamedTempFile so tests are hermetic.

BUG-142.description: Parent: BUG-138. When a script runs bash like `cat /tmp/icon.png` (or `hexdump`/`xxd`/`base64` on binaries) through the Bash tool under any provider (Rhai-scripted or not), detect binary output and return a structured error that tells the model to use Read instead. Don't fabricate mock content. Scope: codelet/tools/src/bash.rs output post-processing, feature file, tests with PNG, PDF, ELF, ZIP fixtures.

examples.text: Given cat /tmp/icon.png (a valid PNG) succeeds with exit 0, when Bash tool returns, then the caller receives ToolError::Execution whose message contains 'detected PNG image' and 'use the Read tool instead' — the PNG bytes themselves are never in the returned output

Given cat /tmp/doc.pdf (a valid PDF) succeeds with exit 0, when Bash tool returns, then the caller receives ToolError::Execution whose message contains 'detected PDF document' and 'use the Read tool instead'

Given cat /bin/ls (an ELF binary) succeeds with exit 0, when Bash tool returns, then the caller receives ToolError::Execution whose message contains 'detected binary content' (no specific type since ELF is not a known image/pdf) and 'use the Read tool instead'
Given echo 'hello 👋 world — accents: café' succeeds, when Bash tool returns, then output is returned normally (no false-positive binary detection from emoji/UTF-8 multi-byte chars)

Given printf '\x00\x01\x02\x03hello' succeeds with exit 0 (raw bytes including a NUL), when Bash tool returns, then the caller receives ToolError::Execution with 'detected binary content' and 'use the Read tool instead' — the raw bytes are not forwarded

Given cat /tmp/missing.png fails with exit 1 and stderr 'cat: /tmp/missing.png: No such file or directory' (no stdout), when Bash tool returns, then the caller receives the usual exit-code-1 ToolError::Execution with the stderr diagnostic preserved (no binary-guard triggered because stdout is empty)

Given `hexdump -C /tmp/icon.png | head -5` succeeds and produces TEXT output (hex dump is text, not binary), when Bash tool returns, then the output is returned normally (the hexdump lines are text — no false positive even though the source file is binary)

Given `gzip -c /tmp/big.log` succeeds with exit 0 and prints gzip-compressed bytes to stdout (magic: 0x1F 0x8B), when Bash tool returns, then the caller receives ToolError::Execution with 'detected binary content' and 'use the Read tool instead'

Given `{ printf 'header\n'; cat /tmp/icon.png; }` succeeds with exit 0 (mixed text prefix then binary payload — stdout contains NUL bytes), when Bash tool returns, then the caller receives ToolError::Execution with 'detected binary content' and 'use the Read tool instead' (the text prefix is discarded because the payload is binary)

Given call_with_streaming() executes `cat /tmp/icon.png` with a stream_callback, when the command completes with exit 0, then: (a) the stream_callback MAY have received intermediate chunks during execution (not guarded — UI streaming is out of scope), BUT (b) the FINAL returned Result is ToolError::Execution with the binary-guard message — the caller never sees the binary bytes in the buffered return value

rules.text: Binary output is detected when captured stdout contains NUL bytes (0x00) OR when its leading bytes match a known binary magic signature (PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP/PDF/ELF/ZIP/GZIP), evaluated on the raw byte buffer before UTF-8 truncation

When binary output is detected, the Bash tool MUST return a ToolError::Execution whose message is a structured, actionable directive: (a) names the offending command, (b) identifies the detected binary type when known (e.g. 'PNG image'), (c) instructs the agent to use the Read tool on the same file instead, and (d) does not forward any of the binary bytes to the model

Detection applies to BOTH the non-streaming call() path and the call_with_streaming() path — in both cases the final buffered stdout is checked before being returned to the caller (streaming callbacks to the UI are not affected; only the returned buffered output is replaced)
Detection applies ONLY to stdout — stderr content is left unchanged (stderr is expected to be text diagnostics, and some programs emit mixed stderr legitimately)

Text output containing occasional high-bit UTF-8 sequences (emoji, accented chars, CJK) MUST NOT be classified as binary — detection uses NUL-byte presence AND magic-byte matching, not simple non-ASCII heuristics

Binary detection runs regardless of exit status — a command that prints binary and exits 0 is still intercepted; a command that prints binary and fails (exit!=0) returns the binary-guard error instead of the usual format_error() (the guard takes precedence because forwarding binary garbage helps no one)

If the detected binary magic signature maps to a known ImageMediaType or PDF, the error message explicitly names the type (e.g. 'detected PNG image' / 'detected PDF document') so the agent knows which Read mode to use; for unknown binaries (ELF/ZIP/generic) the message says 'detected binary content' without fabricating a type

The guard is triggered regardless of which command produced the bytes — `cat /tmp/icon.png` → triggers; `base64 -d <<< 'iVBORw0...'` → triggers; `printf '\x00\x01\x02'` → triggers; `curl -o - binary.bin` → triggers. The mechanism is content-based, not command-name-based

BUG-144.description: During compaction, when a PromptCancelled error occurs inside StreamingError, the error chain is destroyed by anyhow::anyhow!("Streaming error: {e}") formatting which converts the typed error into a bare string. This makes extract_prompt_cancelled() unable to downcast the error, causing classify_compaction_branch to return NotCompaction, falling through the generic cascade and terminating the session. The compaction_needed flag and CMPCT-032 safety net are both bypassed.

examples.text: User cancels a prompt during compaction operation — session terminates instead of gracefully handling the cancellation
After fix with Error::from(e), extract_prompt_cancelled() should return Some when PromptCancelled flows through the production path
Existing test detects_streaming_error_wrapped_prompt_cancelled uses .into() which preserves types, but production uses anyhow::anyhow!(...) which destroys types — test is a false positive

questions.answer: Use anyhow::Error::from(e) without context — the StreamingError Display impl already includes 'Streaming error' prefix so no context is needed, and this avoids breaking string-based classifiers
questions.text: Should we use Error::from(e) or Error::from(e).context("Streaming error")? The former is safer for string-based classifiers but loses the explicit prefix; the latter preserves prefix but may break classifiers that search for "Streaming error" patterns.

rules.text: anyhow::anyhow!("Streaming error: {e}") destroys the typed error chain by formatting via Display into a bare string — only the Display output is captured, not the original type

architectureNotes.text: Root cause (verified by reading codelet/rpc-types/src/lib.rs on 2026-05-21): the file uses two distinct attribute spellings. Struct-level (containers): `#[cfg_attr(feature = "napi", napi_derive::napi(object))]` (45 sites, lines 35, 72, 90, 132, 190, 210, 235, 283, 295, 314, 339, 360, 373, 381, 389, 397, 406, 415, 422, 430, 445, 453, 465, 477, 505, 516, 537, 547, 561, 573, 587, 602, 611, 623, 635, 644, 655, 668, 683, 700) — these resolve correctly because the path `napi_derive::napi` is fully-qualified. Field-level (per-field js_name renames): `#[cfg_attr(feature = "napi", napi(js_name = "..."))]` (34 sites) — these FAIL because the bare attribute identifier `napi` is the napi crate name, not an attribute in scope. Rust's compiler explicitly reports: `napi is in scope, but it is a crate, not an attribute`. There is currently NO `use napi_derive::napi;` and NO `#[macro_use] extern crate napi_derive;` at the top of lib.rs.

Fix decision (chosen 2026-05-21): add a single feature-gated `use napi_derive::napi;` import at the top of codelet/rpc-types/src/lib.rs:

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "napi")]
#[allow(unused_imports)]
use napi_derive::napi;
```

Rationale: (a) smallest possible diff — one 3-line addition versus rewriting 34 field-level cfg_attr sites; (b) keeps the default build untouched (the use is gated behind `feature = "napi"`, so no `napi-derive` import sneaks in when the feature is off); (c) matches what real napi crates do (`napi_derive::napi` is intended to be a bare attribute imported via use); (d) `#[allow(unused_imports)]` is required because the struct-level sites already use the fully-qualified `napi_derive::napi(...)` form, which means the `use` is technically only needed for the field-level shorthand — depending on resolution order Rust may not flag it but the allow makes the intent explicit and survives future refactors. Alternative considered & rejected: qualifying every field-level site (34 edits, much larger diff, easy to drift).

Empirical follow-up (2026-05-21, post-attempted-fix): the originally-proposed 3-line `use napi_derive::napi;` fix is INSUFFICIENT. Rust REFUSES to expand a field-level `#[cfg_attr(feature = "napi", napi(js_name = "..."))]` whose meta resolves to a proc-macro attribute. Tested in this order:

1. Baseline (pre-fix): `cargo build -p codelet-napi --features noop` → 34 errors `cannot find attribute napi in this scope` (napi is in scope only as a CRATE, not an attribute).

2. Added `#[cfg(feature = "napi")] #[allow(unused_imports)] use napi_derive::napi;` at lib.rs top → SAME 34 errors changed shape to `expected non-macro attribute, found attribute macro napi` — now napi IS in scope as a proc-macro attribute, but Rust disallows attribute macros at field positions.

3. Tried `#[cfg(feature = "napi")] #[macro_use] extern crate napi_derive;` instead → SAME 34 errors, same `expected non-macro attribute` message.

4. Additionally changed all 40 struct-level uses from `napi_derive::napi(...)` → bare `napi(...)` (mirroring the codelet/napi pattern that DOES work because that crate's #[napi(...)] uses are on item-level fn declarations, not on STRUCT FIELDS) → SAME 34 errors.

ROOT CAUSE OF ATTEMPTED-FIX FAILURE: Rust's attribute resolution runs after `cfg_attr` expansion but BEFORE outer-struct proc-macro invocation. So when the parent `#[napi(object)]` proc-macro on the struct hasn't yet had a chance to consume the field-level `#[napi(...)]` attributes during its expansion, Rust pre-validates the resolved field-level attribute — and `napi` resolves to an attribute proc-macro that cannot be applied to a field (because attribute macros only attach to items: fns, structs, enums, etc.). The canonical napi-rs pattern (`#[napi(object)] struct X { #[napi(js_name = "x")] pub y: T }` with `#[macro_use] extern crate napi_derive`) works because the WHOLE struct is passed as a TokenStream into the proc-macro BEFORE Rust resolves field-level attrs, and the macro strips/consumes them during expansion. But that flow is bypassed when `cfg_attr` is involved — `cfg_attr` is a built-in attribute that expands earlier in the pipeline, producing a 'resolved' attribute that Rust validates eagerly. So the bug is ROOTED IN the `cfg_attr` pattern, not in scope.

IMPLICATIONS for the architecture note: the previously-proposed 3-line fix is wrong. The actual minimal-correct fix requires removing `cfg_attr` from the field-level renames. Options under evaluation: (a) move each field-level `#[cfg_attr(feature = "napi", napi(js_name = "..."))]` to a CFG-gated pair of fields (one with the napi attr inline, one without), (b) replace `napi(js_name = "x")` with `serde(rename = "x")` if napi-derive honors serde renames (must verify against napi-derive v3 docs), (c) split the structs into two parallel definitions in two modules (one cfg(feature=napi), one cfg(not(feature=napi))). Option (b) is the smallest viable diff IF napi-derive v3 honors serde renames — verify before committing. Option (a) is provably correct but adds 34*2 = 68 lines of attribute decorations. Option (c) is the safest but adds ~500 lines of struct duplication.

Option (a) cfg-gated field pairs EMPIRICALLY FAILS (tested on WorkUnitInfo, 2026-05-21). When two `pub work_type: String,` fields are present — one gated `#[cfg(feature = "napi")]`, one gated `#[cfg(not(feature = "napi"))]` — the parent `napi_derive::napi(object)` proc-macro sees BOTH variants in the input TokenStream because cfg-on-FIELDS is evaluated AFTER the parent attribute macro expands. Result: 6 errors per duplicated field (E0416 `identifier bound more than once in the same pattern`, E0025 `field bound multiple times`, E0062 `field specified more than once`). So Option (a) does not work.

DECISION SUMMARY:
- Option (a) cfg-gated field pairs: FAILS (proc-macro sees both variants)
- Option (b) replace napi(js_name="x") with serde(rename="x"): CHANGES THE WIRE SHAPE on tarpc/embedded transports. The current code intentionally keeps Rust snake_case for serde JSON and only camelCase-renames for the JS surface. Adopting (b) means all transports get camelCase, which may BREAK existing JSON-RPC consumers. Needs verification of every consumer.
- Option (c) full struct duplication (one in `mod napi_shapes { #[cfg(feature = "napi")] }`, another in `mod wire_shapes { #[cfg(not(feature = "napi"))] }`): WORKS but adds ~500-700 LOC of struct duplication for 20 affected structs.
- Option (d) WAIT for napi-rs upstream fix (GH issue #2635 https://github.com/napi-rs/napi-rs/issues/2635 confirms this is a known false-positive). Hold until upstream lands.

RECOMMENDED PATH (subject to user confirmation):
Option (b) — change `napi(js_name="X")` to `serde(rename="X")` AND verify napi-derive v3 respects serde renames at the TS surface. IF napi-derive v3 honors `#[serde(rename)]` on object fields, the diff is just 34 line modifications (no insertions). IF napi-derive v3 ignores serde renames, fall back to Option (c). The wire-shape change on tarpc/embedded must be verified as backwards-compatible — but actual usage is currently limited to scenarios that already round-trip serde JSON, so a careful audit of the 23 StreamChunk variants + 20-ish object structs is feasible.

This BUG-146 was originally scoped as a 1-point 'tiny scoping fix' but its real scope is closer to 5-8 points (verify napi-derive behaviour, choose strategy, modify 34+ sites, update integration tests, verify all transport consumers). Estimate revised from 1 → 5.

BUG-146.description: When `codelet-rpc-types` is compiled with the `napi` feature enabled (which happens transitively when building `codelet-napi`, including under `--features noop`), 34 errors of the form `error: cannot find attribute 'napi' in this scope` are emitted from `codelet/rpc-types/src/lib.rs`. The cause: struct-level decorations correctly use the absolute path `#[cfg_attr(feature = "napi", napi_derive::napi(object))]`, but field-level decorations use the bare `#[cfg_attr(feature = "napi", napi(js_name = "..."))]` without bringing `napi_derive::napi` into attribute scope. The fix is to either (a) add `#[cfg_attr(feature = "napi", macro_use)] extern crate napi_derive;` (legacy) or (b) `#[cfg(feature = "napi")] use napi_derive::napi;` at the top of `lib.rs`, or (c) qualify every field-level use as `napi_derive::napi(js_name = ...)`. Affected lines: 40, 58, 217, 426, 457, 459, 461, 471, 473, 705, 707, 712, 714, 718, 720, 722, 726, 728, 730, 734, 736, 738, 749, 756, 771, 775, 779, 783, 787, 791, 793, 799, 804, 806 (34 occurrences). This BLOCKS RPC-043's `scenario_codelet_napi_builds_with_noop_feature` assertion. Discovered 2026-05-21 while attempting the RPC-043 7-module split — pre-existing bug, not introduced by RPC-043.

CMPCT-002.description:
When compaction is triggered during Gemini continuation (empty tool_use), the current code errors out. This should be handled gracefully by breaking out of the continuation loop and returning a signal to trigger compaction, then retrying the turn.

## Current Behavior
- Logs error: 'Compaction triggered during Gemini continuation - not yet supported'
- Returns Err() which fails the session
- User loses work in progress

- Break out of continuation loop gracefully
- Save any partial progress (continuation_text)
- Return a signal indicating compaction is needed
- Calling code triggers compaction and retries the turn

## Implementation
1. Add StreamLoopResult::NeedsCompaction variant
2. Change error case to return this signal
3. Handle signal in calling code to trigger compaction

## Research
See attached research document analyzing how OpenCode and VTCode handle this.

CMPCT-005.description:
Replace the current LLM-based batch anchor detection and narrative summary compaction with a three-layer architecture that uses in-view DAG construction.

Key insight: instead of running compaction in a background process with separate LLM calls, the agent itself builds the hierarchical summary DAG in the same conversation view using /clear + SessionSearch + a new inject_summary tool. The agent IS the summarizer — zero marginal LLM cost.

Verified: /clear only clears in-memory state (messages, turns, token_tracker). It never touches the on-disk persistence layer. All pre-clear messages remain fully searchable via SessionSearch (which reads from the JSONL message store, not in-memory state).

Layer 0 — Structurally Lossless Trimming: Before DAG construction, deterministically strip mechanical bloat from SessionSearch results (raw tool outputs replaced with condensed references, file contents from Read replaced with path references, base64 data stripped, verbose Edit parameters collapsed). Zero LLM cost, fully reversible from persisted originals. CMV (Santoni 2026) shows 20-86% token reduction from this alone. Trimming is applied automatically during DAG construction only via an implicit compaction_in_progress flag on BackgroundSession.

Layer 1 — In-View DAG Construction: When compaction triggers, the flow is: (1) /clear (context emptied, persistence intact), (2) agent retrieves previous history via targeted SessionSearch calls (with Layer 0 trimming applied to results), (3) agent writes hierarchical DAG summary with D0 (detailed: files, decisions, errors), D1 (arc-level: attempts, outcomes), D2 (durable: architecture, milestones) depth levels, each with turn range references for future SessionSearch drilldown, (4) agent calls inject_summary to pin the DAG and drop all builder turns. The agent has full judgment over what to keep — it knows which decisions are still in effect, which explorations were dead ends, and what the current work state is.

Layer 2 — Emergency Threshold Compaction: Existing threshold trigger as safety net. Auto-triggers /clear and instructs the agent to build its DAG via SessionSearch. Never drops below system reminders + injected DAG + last user message.

New tool required: inject_summary(content) — pins DAG content as system-level message (wrapped in <system-reminder type=compaction-dag>), drops all builder turns using the same partition_for_compaction() → clear → restore pattern as execute_compaction(), returns injected token count and remaining budget. Builder turns remain on disk (persisted during streaming) and are recoverable via SessionSearch.

This replaces the current expensive batch system (2 large LLM calls per compaction, 50k+ tokens) with zero-marginal-cost agent-driven summarization. Inspired by CMV, LCM, Focus, ACON, HiAgent, SimpleMem, H-MEM research (see attachments).

CMPCT-006.description:
Create `codelet/core/src/compaction/trimmer.rs` — a deterministic, zero-LLM-cost content transformer that strips mechanical bloat from StoredMessage content before the agent sees it during DAG construction.

## Research Foundation

This implements the core insight from CMV (Santoni, Imperial College London, arXiv:2602.22402, Feb 2026): the highest-ROI intervention for context management is stripping raw tool outputs BEFORE any lossy compression. CMV demonstrates 20% mean token reduction (up to 86% for tool-heavy sessions) from structurally lossless trimming alone — preserving every user message and assistant reasoning verbatim while replacing verbose tool parameters/results with compact references.

The Deep Agents SDK (LangChain) validates the same principle: structured tool output replacement is economically viable even under prompt caching, with break-even within 10 turns for mixed tool-use sessions (39% average reduction per CMV).

## What To Build

A `Trimmer` struct with a `trim_message(stored_msg: &StoredMessage) -> String` method that applies deterministic transformation rules:

| Content Type | Trim Action | Replacement |
|---|---|---|
| Read tool results (file content) | Replace with reference | `[file: {path}, {lines} lines, {tokens} tok — use Read to retrieve]` |
| Write tool parameters (full content) | Replace with reference | `[Write: {path}, {lines} lines — file persisted to disk]` |
| Edit tool parameters (old_string/new_string) | Condense | `[Edit: {path} — replaced {old_len} chars with {new_len} chars]` |
| Bash tool output (stdout/stderr) | Truncate head+tail | First 10 lines + `... ({N} lines omitted)` + last 5 lines + exit code |
| Base64 image data | Strip entirely | `[image: {W}x{H}, {bytes} bytes, from {path}]` |
| Search/Grep tool output | Truncate matches | First 10 matches + `... ({N} more matches)` |

**Key constraint:** Trimming NEVER touches user messages or assistant reasoning text. Only structured tool parameters and tool result outputs are transformed.

## Codebase Integration Points

- **Input type:** `StoredMessage` from `codelet/napi/src/persistence/` — has `role: String`, `content: String`, and `metadata: HashMap<String, Value>`. The metadata field contains tool information (tool name, input parameters) serialized from `AssistantContent::ToolUse`.
- **Output:** Transformed content `String` — the trimmed version of `stored_msg.content`.
- **Caller:** Will be invoked from `session_search_handler.rs` (see CMPCT-010) via `resolve_message_content()` when the `compaction_in_progress` flag is set.
- **Re-export:** Add `pub mod trimmer;` and `pub use trimmer::Trimmer;` to `codelet/core/src/compaction/mod.rs`.

## Files To Create

- `codelet/core/src/compaction/trimmer.rs` — Trimmer struct and all transformation rules
- `codelet/core/src/compaction/__tests__/trimmer.test.rs` — Comprehensive tests

## Files To Modify

- `codelet/core/src/compaction/mod.rs` — Add module declaration and re-export

## Acceptance Criteria

- Each trimming rule from the table has a dedicated unit test
- User messages pass through completely unchanged
- Assistant reasoning text passes through completely unchanged
- Messages without tool metadata pass through unchanged
- Token count of trimmed output is measurably smaller than input
- All trimming is fully reversible by re-reading the persisted originals via SessionSearch

CMPCT-007.description:
Extend `codelet/core/src/compaction/model.rs` with a `StructuralAnnotation` enum for per-turn inline signal detection. These annotations provide zero-cost metadata that the agent can reference during DAG construction to identify important turns without reading full content.

## Research Foundation

This preserves the correct insight from CMPCT-004 (per-turn structural signal detection) while reframing it as metadata rather than content. ACON (Kang et al., KAIST/Microsoft, arXiv:2510.00615, Oct 2025) demonstrates that preserving WHY decisions were made — not just WHAT tool was called — is critical for continuation quality. The annotations capture structural milestones (fspec status changes, error resolutions, file modifications) that the agent can use as navigation aids during SessionSearch retrieval.

HiAgent (Hu et al., ACL 2025, aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1575) validates that agent-controlled compression boundaries based on structural signals (subgoal completions) produce better results than external heuristics. Our annotations provide these structural signals.

## What To Build

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum StructuralAnnotation {
    /// fspec milestone reached (from Fspec tool call with specific command)
    FspecMilestone {
        command: String,     // e.g., "update-work-unit-status"
        args: Vec<String>,   // e.g., ["AUTH-001", "implementing"]
    },
    /// Error was resolved (previous failure + current file modification + all-success)
    ErrorResolution {
        failed_tool: String,
        resolved_file: String,
    },
    /// File modification (from Edit/Write tool calls)
    FileModification {
        path: String,
        operation: FileOp, // Created, Modified, Deleted
    },
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum FileOp {
    Created,
    Modified,
    Deleted,
}
```

## Codebase Integration Points

- **Location:** `codelet/core/src/compaction/model.rs` — alongside existing `ConversationTurn`, `ToolCall`, `ToolResult`
- **Deprecations:** `PreservationContext` and `BuildStatus` (currently at lines 220+ of model.rs) become `#[deprecated]` — subsumed by agent judgment during DAG construction. These contain flaky heuristics like `detect_build_status()` matching substrings "pass"/"fail" against arbitrary tool output.
- **Kept unchanged:** `TokenTracker` — tracks API-level token usage, orthogonal to compaction strategy.
- **Re-export:** Update `codelet/core/src/compaction/mod.rs` to export `StructuralAnnotation` and `FileOp`.
- **Consumer:** The per-turn annotation detector (CMPCT-011) will attach these to persisted messages during the stream loop. The agent sees them via SessionSearch metadata during DAG construction.

## Files To Modify

- `codelet/core/src/compaction/model.rs` — Add StructuralAnnotation enum, FileOp enum, deprecate PreservationContext/BuildStatus
- `codelet/core/src/compaction/mod.rs` — Update re-exports

## Acceptance Criteria

- FileOp enum covers Created, Modified, Deleted
- PreservationContext and BuildStatus marked #[deprecated]
- All existing tests still compile (deprecated items still usable with warnings)

CMPCT-008.description:
Create `codelet/tools/src/inject_summary.rs` — the Rig Tool definition for `inject_summary`, following the same handler-dispatch pattern used by `SessionSearchTool` (codelet/tools/src/session_search/) and `FspecTool` (codelet/tools/src/fspec.rs).

## Research Foundation

This tool is the mechanism through which the agent completes its self-directed compression cycle. Focus (Verma, arXiv:2601.07190, Jan 2026) demonstrated that agents with explicit compression primitives (`start_focus`/`complete_focus`) achieve 22.7% token reduction with zero accuracy loss. Our `inject_summary` is the single completion primitive — the agent calls it after building its DAG to pin the summary and discard builder turns.

LCM (Ehrlich & Blackman, Voltropy PBC, Feb 2026) provides DAG navigation tools (`lcm_describe`, `lcm_grep`, `lcm_expand_query`). In our design, `inject_summary` replaces the need for these — the agent writes the entire hierarchical DAG itself and pins it via this tool, while SessionSearch handles all retrieval.

## What To Build

A tool struct implementing the Rig `Tool` trait with:

```rust
Tool name: "inject_summary"
Tool description: "Pin a hierarchical DAG summary as system-level content, dropping all builder turns from the active context. Call this after building your session summary via SessionSearch. The content is wrapped as a system-reminder (type: compaction-dag) and persisted across future compactions."

Parameters:
  content: String (required) — The DAG summary content to inject

Return:
  injected_tokens: u64 — Token count of the injected DAG
  remaining_budget: u64 — Available context budget after injection
```

## Handler Pattern (from codebase)

The tool does NOT perform the session manipulation directly. Following the pattern established by `SessionSearchTool` and `FspecTool`:

1. Tool definition and JSON schema live in `codelet-tools` crate
2. A handler type alias is defined: `pub type InjectSummaryHandler = Arc<dyn Fn(String) -> InjectSummaryResult + Send + Sync>;`
3. A global handler registry (like `set_session_search_handler()` in `codelet/tools/src/lib.rs` at line ~112) stores per-session handlers
4. The actual session manipulation code lives in the NAPI handler (CMPCT-009)
5. When `call()` is invoked, the tool dispatches to the registered handler

See `codelet/tools/src/fspec.rs` for the cleanest example of this pattern: `FspecTool` defines the schema, `set_fspec_handler_for_session()` manages the registry, and the actual logic is in `codelet/napi/src/fspec.rs`.

See `codelet/tools/src/session_search/mod.rs` for the SessionSearch equivalent: `SessionSearchTool` defines the schema, `set_session_search_handler()` manages the registry, and the actual persistence access is in `codelet/napi/src/session_search_handler.rs`.

## Files To Create

- `codelet/tools/src/inject_summary.rs` — Tool struct, parameter/result types, handler type alias, global handler registry

## Files To Modify

- JSON schema for parameters validates correctly

- Tool returns error when no handler is registered (like SessionSearchTool does)
- Tool is registered in the tool list (lib.rs exports)

CMPCT-009.description:
Create `codelet/napi/src/inject_summary_handler.rs` — the NAPI handler that performs the actual session manipulation when the agent calls `inject_summary`. Register the handler in the agent loop setup alongside SessionSearch and Fspec handlers.

## Research Foundation

This implements the "partition → clear → restore → inject" pattern that makes the agent the sole authority over its own context compression. Focus (Verma, arXiv:2601.07190, Jan 2026) showed that agent autonomy over compression (22.7% token reduction, zero accuracy loss) outperforms external compression. HiAgent (Hu et al., ACL 2025) showed 2× success rate improvement when agents control their own memory boundaries.

The key insight from SimpleMem (Liu et al., ICLR 2026 Workshop LLA, arXiv:2601.02553) applies here: semantic density gating should be performed by the entity with the most context — which is the agent itself. inject_summary is how the agent's judgment materializes as persistent context.

## What To Build

A handler closure that captures `BackgroundSession`'s inner `Session` and, when invoked with DAG content:

1. **Partitions** `session.messages` using `partition_for_compaction()` from `codelet_cli::session::system_reminders` — cleanly separates system reminder messages (identified by `<system-reminder>` XML tags in `UserContent::Text`) from all other messages.

2. **Clears** `session.messages` entirely.

3. **Restores** only the system reminder messages (from step 1).

4. **Appends** the DAG content as a new `Message::User` wrapped in `<system-reminder>` with `<!-- type:compaction-dag -->` marker — making it part of the stable prefix for prompt caching and preserved through future compactions.

5. **Resets** `session.turns` to empty and updates `session.token_tracker` display values to reflect the new context size.

6. **Returns** `{ injected_tokens: u64, remaining_budget: u64 }` to the agent.

**Future integration note:** CMPCT-010 will add a `compaction_in_progress` flag to BackgroundSession. When that work is done, the inject_summary handler will be extended to clear that flag after injection completes, so subsequent SessionSearch calls return full (untrimmed) content.

## Existing Pattern to Follow

This is essentially the same mechanism as `execute_compaction()` in `codelet/cli/src/interactive_helpers.rs` (lines 170-303), which already does:
- `partition_for_compaction(&session.messages)` → extract system reminders
- `session.messages.clear()` → clear all messages
- `session.messages.extend(system_reminders)` → restore system reminders
- Append summary as `Message::User` → add compaction result

The difference: `inject_summary` replaces the LLM-generated summary with the agent-written DAG and skips kept-turns reconstruction (the DAG IS the kept context).

## Registration Point

In `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs`, the agent loop setup (around line 5365) already registers handlers:
```rust
// AMGR-001: Register SessionSearch handler for this session
let session_search_handler = crate::session_search_handler::create_handler(...);
codelet_tools::set_session_search_handler(session.id, Some(session_search_handler));
```

Add inject_summary handler registration immediately after, following the same pattern.

## Persistence Note

Builder turns (the SessionSearch calls and agent reasoning during DAG construction) ARE persisted to disk as they stream — `persist_user_message()` and `persist_assistant_message()` fire during normal agent execution. The builder turns are only dropped from the in-memory `session.messages`, not from the on-disk JSONL store. They remain recoverable via SessionSearch.

## Files To Create

- `codelet/napi/src/inject_summary_handler.rs` — Handler function `create_handler()` returning `InjectSummaryHandler` closure

## Files To Modify

- `codelet/napi/src/lib.rs` — Add module declaration
- `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs` — Register handler in agent loop setup (~line 5368), clean up handler on session teardown (~line 5576)

## Acceptance Criteria

- Handler correctly partitions, clears, restores system reminders, and injects DAG
- DAG content is wrapped in `<system-reminder><!-- type:compaction-dag -->` markers
- Builder turns are dropped from in-memory messages but NOT from persistence
- Token tracker is recalculated to reflect new context size
- Handler is registered and cleaned up alongside SessionSearch handler
- Returns accurate injected_tokens and remaining_budget values

CMPCT-010.description:
Extend `codelet/napi/src/session_search_handler.rs` to apply Layer 0 structurally lossless trimming to SessionSearch results during DAG construction. Add a `compaction_in_progress` flag to `BackgroundSession` that controls when trimming is active.

## Research Foundation

CMV (Santoni, Imperial College London, arXiv:2602.22402, Feb 2026) demonstrates that trimming applied to tool outputs before the agent processes them yields 20-86% token reduction. The critical insight is WHERE trimming happens: not on the stored data (originals are sacred), but on the RETRIEVAL PATH — the data the agent sees during DAG construction. This is "Option A" from the design document: implicit trimming via session state flag.

SimpleMem (Liu et al., ICLR 2026 Workshop LLA) validates this approach conceptually: their "Semantic Structured Compression" stage distills interactions into compact indexed units during the write phase. Our trimming serves the same purpose during the read/retrieval phase.

## What To Build

### 1. BackgroundSession Flag

Add `compaction_in_progress: Arc<AtomicBool>` field to `BackgroundSession` in `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs` (alongside existing fields like `compaction_progress: RwLock<Option<CompactionProgress>>`).

- Default: `false`
- CMPCT-010 only adds the field and wires it to SessionSearch. The actual set/clear lifecycle (setting to true when compaction begins, clearing after inject_summary) is handled by CMPCT-011 which orchestrates the full compaction flow.

### 2. Extended create_handler()

Modify `create_handler()` in `session_search_handler.rs` (currently at line 35) to accept an additional `Arc<AtomicBool>` parameter:

```rust
pub fn create_handler(
    project_path: PathBuf,
    compaction_trimming: Arc<AtomicBool>,
) -> SessionSearchHandler {
```

The handler closure already captures `project_path` — extend it to also capture `compaction_trimming`.

### 3. Conditional Trimming

When `compaction_trimming.load(Ordering::Relaxed)` is `true`:

- In `handle_show()`: After `resolve_message_content()` returns content for each `StoredMessage`, pass it through `Trimmer::trim_message()` (from CMPCT-006) before building `SessionMessage` results.
- In `handle_search()`: After `resolve_message_content()` returns content for each `StoredMessage`, pass it through `Trimmer::trim_message()` before building `SearchMatch` results.

When `false`: Pass content through unchanged (current behavior).

### Key Integration Points in session_search_handler.rs

- `handle_show()` iterates `StoredMessage`s and calls `resolve_message_content()` to get the content string. Trimming is applied to this resolved content.
- `handle_search()` similarly resolves content for matching messages. Trimming is applied before content appears in `SearchMatch`.
- `resolve_message_content()` itself handles blob dereferencing — trimming is applied AFTER blob resolution.

### Registration Update

In `session_manager.rs` around line 5365, where `create_handler()` is called:
```rust
// Before:
let session_search_handler = crate::session_search_handler::create_handler(
    std::path::PathBuf::from(&session.project),
);

// After:
let session_search_handler = crate::session_search_handler::create_handler(
    std::path::PathBuf::from(&session.project),
    session.compaction_in_progress.clone(),
);
```

## Files To Modify

- `codelet/napi/src/session_search_handler.rs` — Extend `create_handler()` signature, add conditional trimming in `handle_show()` and `handle_search()`
- `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs` — Add `compaction_in_progress` field to `BackgroundSession`, pass to `create_handler()`

## Acceptance Criteria

- `compaction_in_progress` flag defaults to `false`
- When flag is `false`, SessionSearch returns full untrimmed content (regression test)
- When flag is `true`, SessionSearch returns trimmed content via Trimmer
- Trimming is applied after blob resolution (correct ordering)
- Thread-safe: AtomicBool with Relaxed ordering is sufficient (single writer, single reader)

CMPCT-011.description:
Rewrite `execute_compaction()` in `codelet/cli/src/interactive_helpers.rs` to trigger the in-view DAG construction flow instead of the batch LLM approach. Create the compaction system instruction that guides the agent through DAG construction. Wire per-turn structural annotation detection into the stream loop.

## Research Foundation

This is the core integration card — where the three-layer architecture comes together. It implements the central thesis validated across all seven research papers:

- **LCM** (Ehrlich & Blackman, Voltropy PBC, Feb 2026): Hierarchical summary DAG with D0/D1/D2 depth levels. LCM-augmented agents outperform Claude Code on OOLONG long-context evaluation from 32K to 1M tokens.
- **Focus** (Verma, arXiv:2601.07190, Jan 2026): Agent-autonomous compression — the agent decides when and what to compress. 22.7% token reduction with identical accuracy.
- **HiAgent** (Hu et al., ACL 2025): Subgoal-based hierarchical working memory management — 2× success rate, 3.8 fewer steps.
- **ACON** (Kang et al., KAIST/Microsoft, arXiv:2510.00615, Oct 2025): Compression guidelines embedded in system instructions yield 26-54% peak token reduction while maintaining task performance.
- **H-MEM** (Sun & Zeng, arXiv:2507.22925, Jul 2025): Multi-level semantic abstraction with positional index routing — hierarchical organization is a NECESSARY CONDITION for robust long-term reasoning.

## What To Build

### 1. Rewrite execute_compaction()

Currently at `codelet/cli/src/interactive_helpers.rs` lines 170-310, `execute_compaction()` does:
1. `partition_for_compaction()` → separate system reminders
2. Create LLM prompt function via provider
3. Calculate summarization budget
4. Convert messages to turns
5. Call `compactor.compact()` → batch LLM anchor detection + LLM summary generation
6. Reconstruct messages: system reminders + kept turns + summary + continuation

New flow:
1. Set `compaction_in_progress` flag to `true` (triggers Layer 0 trimming in SessionSearch)
2. Execute `/clear` (clears in-memory context, reinjects system reminders, preserves persistence)
3. Inject compaction system instruction as the next user message — tells the agent to build its DAG via SessionSearch and call `inject_summary`
4. Return control to the agent loop — the agent takes over from here
5. Agent calls SessionSearch (gets trimmed results via Layer 0), builds DAG, calls inject_summary
6. `inject_summary` handler (CMPCT-009) performs the partition→clear→restore→inject and clears the flag

### 2. Compaction System Instruction

The system instruction that's injected after `/clear` to guide the agent. Must be concise (consumes context during rebuild):

```
Your context window was getting full. Your conversation history has been preserved on disk and is fully searchable via SessionSearch. Build a hierarchical summary DAG of your session:

1. Search strategically (not linearly):
   - SessionSearch(show, max_turns: 10) for recent context
   - SessionSearch(search, query: "error|failed|fix") for error resolutions
   - SessionSearch(search, query: "decision|chose|architecture") for decisions
   - SessionSearch(search, query: "TODO|blocker|question") for open items

2. Write a structured summary with depth levels:
   - D2 (Durable): Architecture decisions, milestones still in effect
   - D1 (Arc): What was attempted, outcomes, current work state
   - D0 (Detailed): Exact files, decisions, errors from recent work
   - Include [SessionSearch: turns X-Y] references for future drilldown

3. Call inject_summary(content) with your complete DAG to pin it and continue working.
```

### 3. Per-Turn Structural Annotation Detection

In `codelet/cli/src/interactive/stream_loop.rs`, after each completed turn:
- Inspect the turn's tool calls for fspec commands → `FspecMilestone`
- Detect error→success transitions → `ErrorResolution`
- Track Write/Edit tool calls → `FileModification`
- Attach annotations to the turn's metadata (zero cost, inline)

## Codebase Flow

```
stream_loop.rs (per-turn annotation detection)
  → compaction_hook detects threshold exceeded
  → execute_compaction() [rewritten]
    → set compaction_in_progress flag
    → clear_history() [existing, session_manager.rs:1574]
    → inject system instruction as user message
    → return to agent loop
  → agent calls SessionSearch (trimmed via CMPCT-010)
  → agent calls inject_summary (handled by CMPCT-009)
    → clears flag, pins DAG, drops builder turns
  → agent continues working normally
```

## Files To Modify

- `codelet/cli/src/interactive_helpers.rs` — Rewrite `execute_compaction()` for in-view flow
- `codelet/cli/src/interactive/stream_loop.rs` — Add per-turn structural annotation detection, modify compaction trigger to use new flow
- `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs` — Modify `session_compact()` to trigger in-view flow

## Files To Create

- `codelet/core/src/compaction/annotation_detector.rs` — Per-turn inline structural annotation detection logic

## Acceptance Criteria

- execute_compaction() no longer makes any separate LLM calls
- Agent receives compaction system instruction and can build DAG via SessionSearch
- inject_summary is called and context is properly reconstructed
- Per-turn annotations are detected inline (zero cost)
- Post-compaction context contains: system reminders + injected DAG only
- Agent can continue working normally after compaction
- Wall-clock compaction time is <5 seconds (no LLM wait)

CMPCT-012.description:
Modify the existing `CompactionHook` threshold trigger to use the in-view DAG construction flow instead of the batch LLM pipeline. This is the Layer 2 safety net — it fires when context hits 85-90% capacity and the agent hasn't proactively managed its context.

## Research Foundation

ACON (Kang et al., KAIST/Microsoft, arXiv:2510.00615, Oct 2025) demonstrates that compression guidelines optimized via failure analysis yield 26-54% peak token reduction while maintaining task performance. The emergency threshold acts as the failure-analysis trigger — when the agent doesn't compress proactively, the threshold forces it.

Focus (Verma, arXiv:2601.07190, Jan 2026) describes a "sawtooth" context pattern where context grows during exploration and collapses during consolidation. The emergency threshold prevents the sawtooth from hitting the ceiling by forcing a consolidation when the agent fails to initiate one.

## What To Build

### Current Flow (to be replaced)

In `codelet/core/src/compaction_hook.rs`, the `CompactionHook` detects when context usage exceeds the threshold. The post-stream-loop logic in `stream_loop.rs` checks `compaction_needed` and calls `execute_compaction()` which runs the batch LLM pipeline.

### New Flow

When the threshold is exceeded:
1. Auto-trigger `/clear` (same as manual, preserves persistence)
2. Set `compaction_in_progress` flag to `true`
3. Inject the compaction system instruction (same instruction as CMPCT-011)
4. The last user message is re-appended after the instruction so the agent knows what to resume
5. Agent builds DAG via SessionSearch, calls `inject_summary`, then continues

### Minimum Preserved Context

After emergency compaction, context contains at minimum:
- System reminders (CLAUDE.md, environment, fspec workflow)
- Injected DAG summary
- Last user message (so the agent knows what to do next)

Never drops below this floor.

### Proactive /compact Command

Also wire up a `/compact` slash command that the agent can call proactively when it notices context pressure. This triggers the same in-view flow but without the emergency urgency — the agent initiates it on its own terms.

## Codebase Integration Points

- `codelet/core/src/compaction_hook.rs` — Threshold detection logic (keep as-is, it's orthogonal)
- `codelet/cli/src/interactive/stream_loop.rs` — Post-turn compaction trigger (modify to use new flow)
- `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs` — `session_compact()` NAPI binding (modify to use new flow)

## Files To Modify

- `codelet/cli/src/interactive/stream_loop.rs` — Modify threshold-triggered compaction to use in-view flow
- `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs` — Modify `session_compact()` to use in-view flow

## Acceptance Criteria

- When context exceeds 85-90% threshold, in-view DAG construction is triggered (not batch LLM)
- Last user message is preserved through emergency compaction
- Post-compaction context contains: system reminders + DAG + last user message
- /compact slash command triggers same flow proactively
- CompactionHook threshold detection logic is unchanged
- No separate LLM calls during emergency compaction
- Agent can resume working after emergency compaction without losing current task

CMPCT-013.description:
Remove the old batch LLM-based compaction infrastructure after the in-view DAG construction flow is validated and stable. This is the final migration phase — pure deletion, zero new functionality.

## Research Foundation

The old system embodies every antipattern identified by the research:

- **Flat summarization** contradicts H-MEM (Sun & Zeng, arXiv:2507.22925): hierarchical memory organization is a NECESSARY CONDITION for robust long-term reasoning. The old `generate_llm_summary()` produces flat prose.
- **External compression** contradicts Focus (Verma, arXiv:2601.07190) and HiAgent (Hu et al., ACL 2025): agents that control their own compression outperform agents compressed externally. The old system compresses the agent without its input.
- **Flaky heuristics** contradicts ACON (Kang et al., arXiv:2510.00615): `detect_build_status()` matching substrings "pass"/"fail" against arbitrary tool output produces silent misclassifications (false positives on "password", "bypass", `DB_PASS`). `extract_goal_from_message()` matching action verbs like "build", "remove", "please" in user messages.
- **Expensive batch calls** contradict CMV (Santoni, arXiv:2602.22402): the highest-ROI intervention is structural trimming (20-86% reduction at zero cost), not expensive LLM summarization.

CMPCT-016.description:
Research card documenting the gaps between the LCM paper (Ehrlich & Blackman, Voltropy PBC, Feb 2026) and our current DAG compaction implementation (CMPCT-005 through CMPCT-013), with a concrete implementation plan to close those gaps.

## Problem

The current implementation was *inspired by* LCM but diverges from it in critical ways that limit quality, reliability, and lossless retrievability. The most important gap — identified during review — is that DAG summary nodes contain **free-text breadcrumbs** (`[SessionSearch: turns X-Y]`) rather than **structured, machine-readable references** that can be automatically resolved. The AgentManager already has a working pattern for structured context references (`<from session="..." turns="...">`) that should be reused.

## Gap Analysis: LCM Paper vs. Current Implementation

### Gap 1: No Structured References (CRITICAL)

**LCM:** Every summary node maintains deterministic, engine-enforced pointers (foreign keys) to the original messages it summarizes. `lcm_expand(summary_id)` can programmatically expand any summary back to its constituent messages. The engine inserts IDs as a *post-processing step* independent of model output.

**Current:** The agent writes free-text markdown with `[SessionSearch: turns X-Y]` hints. These are not machine-parseable. There is no expand tool. The agent must manually re-call SessionSearch to drill down. Nothing enforces that references are correct or present.

**Fix:** Adopt the AgentManager context reference pattern. DAG content should contain structured `<ref>` blocks that SessionSearch (or a new expand tool) can resolve:

```xml
<dag-node depth="D2" turns="1-120">
Architecture: JWT + Redis + bcrypt for auth
Switched from node-redis to ioredis (connection reliability)
</dag-node>
```

The `turns` attribute uses the same compact format as AgentManager (`"1-3"` for ranges, `"1,3,5"` for non-contiguous). These are resolvable by SessionSearch via the existing `resolve_turns_context()` infrastructure already built for AgentManager.

### Gap 2: No Incremental Condensation (D0→D1→D2 Promotion)

**LCM:** Uses incremental compaction — only messages outside the 'fresh tail' are eligible. When enough leaf summaries accumulate, they are synthesized into condensed (higher-order) summaries. The DAG grows incrementally over time.

**Current:** Every compaction cycle rebuilds the entire DAG from scratch via SessionSearch. Previous DAG content survives in context as a `<system-reminder type=compaction-dag>` block, but there's no mechanism to incrementally update it. The agent re-reads everything and writes a new DAG each time.

**Fix:** When a previous compaction-dag exists in context, the compaction instruction should tell the agent to *extend* the existing DAG rather than rebuild from scratch. The previous D2/D1 nodes should be preserved (they're already durable summaries), and only the fresh conversation since the last compaction needs to be summarized into new D0 nodes. D0 nodes from the previous cycle that are no longer recent can be promoted to D1. This is analogous to LCM's condensation mechanism but agent-driven rather than engine-driven.

### Gap 3: No Guaranteed Convergence / Escalation

**LCM:** Three-Level Summarization Escalation (Figure 3 in paper): Level 1 (Normal: preserve_details) → Level 2 (Aggressive: bullet_points, half budget) → Level 3 (DeterministicTruncate: 512 tokens, no LLM). Guaranteed to converge because Level 3 requires no LLM.

**Current:** If the agent produces a DAG that's too large, or fails to call inject_summary at all, there's no fallback. The `compaction_in_progress` flag stays true, SessionSearch stays trimmed, and context keeps growing until the emergency threshold fires again — creating an infinite loop of failed compactions.

**Fix (Implemented — CMPCT-020):** Three-attempt escalation using stream attempt counting (not turn counting):
- Attempt 1: Normal DAG construction — agent gets one full stream to build DAG and call inject_summary
- Attempt 2: If attempt 1 failed, inject COMPACTION_ESCALATION_MESSAGE and run another stream
- Attempt 3: If attempt 2 also failed, engine deterministically extracts partial dag-node blocks or creates minimal fallback DAG, force-injects it, clears compaction_in_progress. No LLM call — guaranteed convergence.

Attempt-based counting is more precise than turn-based counting because it only escalates when the system actually tried to compact and failed, rather than counting turns that may not involve compaction activity.

### Gap 4: No Scoped Search Within DAG Nodes

**LCM:** `lcm_grep(pattern, summary_id?)` can search within the scope of a particular summary node's constituent messages. This prevents the agent from searching across the entire history when it only needs detail within one arc.

**Fix:** If DAG nodes have structured `<dag-node turns="80-120">` references, SessionSearch could accept an optional scope parameter that restricts search to those turn ranges. This is a natural extension of the existing regex search. Alternatively, the agent can manually specify turn ranges in SessionSearch queries — no new tool needed, just better system instruction guidance.

### Gap 5: No File ID Propagation Through DAG

**LCM:** When messages referencing files are compacted, the resulting summary node retains the file IDs. After multiple rounds of compaction, the model retains awareness of all files encountered.

**Current:** The trimmer replaces file content with `[file: path, lines]` references during DAG construction (Layer 0), but these references are in the *trimmed SessionSearch results*, not in the DAG itself. After inject_summary drops the builder turns, the file references only survive if the agent explicitly mentioned them in its DAG summary.

**Fix:** The compaction instruction should explicitly tell the agent to include an 'Active Files' section listing all files modified/read in the summarized turns. The structured DAG format should have a `<files>` block that's engine-extracted from structural annotations (FileModification annotations already track this).

### Gap 6: No Soft/Hard Threshold Distinction

**LCM:** Two thresholds — τ_soft (triggers async compaction, non-blocking) and τ_hard (blocks until compaction completes). Below τ_soft, zero overhead.

**Current:** Single threshold that triggers the in-view DAG construction. The agent must stop its current work and build the DAG before continuing. This is always blocking.

**Fix:** Implement τ_soft as an early warning that tells the agent (via system reminder or annotation) that compaction will be needed soon, giving it a chance to finish its current logical unit of work before the hard threshold forces compaction. This is a UX improvement, not architectural.

## Implementation Approach

The fixes should be implemented as children of this card, prioritized by impact:

1. **Structured DAG references** (Gap 1) — Highest impact. Reuse AgentManager's `<from>/<quoted-context>` XML pattern. Update compaction system instruction to tell agent to write `<dag-node>` blocks with turn attributes. Add optional expansion via SessionSearch.

2. **Incremental condensation** (Gap 2) — High impact. When previous DAG exists, instruction tells agent to extend rather than rebuild. Preserve existing D2/D1 nodes.

3. **Convergence guarantee** (Gap 3) — Safety-critical. Add attempt-count watchdog + deterministic force-inject fallback.

4. **File tracking through DAG** (Gap 5) — Medium impact. Engine-side: extract file list from structural annotations. Agent-side: instruction mandates Active Files section.

5. **Scoped search** (Gap 4) — Nice-to-have. Instruction-level fix initially, engine support later.

6. **Soft threshold** (Gap 6) — Nice-to-have UX improvement.

CMPCT-031.description:
Currently parse_tool_result_content in codelet/patches/rig-core/src/agent/prompt_request/streaming.rs only rejects oversized IMAGE and PDF payloads. Plain text tool results are wrapped verbatim as ToolResultContent::text(result) with zero size bound. Any tool that returns a very large text payload (validate-tags returning 3000+ lines, cargo clippy with 3193 lines, find/grep with many results, etc.) bloats chat_history and forces the compaction system to discard the full payload before it can retry.

Fix: add a MAX_TOOL_RESULT_TEXT_BYTES constant (e.g. 64 KiB or 32 KiB) in parse_tool_result_content. When a text tool_result exceeds the bound, replace it with a truncation marker: {"status":"truncated","original_bytes":N,"max_bytes":M,"preview":"<first 2 KB>","suffix":"<last 512 bytes>","hint":"re-run the tool with a narrower query or use --failures-only / --summary flags"}. This keeps the compaction retry path stable even when an agent re-invokes a verbose tool during DAG rebuild.

Dependency: VAL-006 (primary root-cause fix) should land first; this is defense-in-depth so future verbose tools can't regress the same cascade.

A tool returning exactly 64 KiB of text (equal to the bound) is stored verbatim — bound is inclusive of equality and triggers truncation only when original_bytes > MAX
A tool returning an oversized IMAGE is still rejected by the existing image size check — the new text bound does not bypass or replace the image bound
The truncation marker JSON is valid UTF-8 and self-describing so the model can reason about it (preview + suffix give visual anchors; original_bytes and max_bytes make the reason obvious)

The bound applies AT the point of content ingestion (parse_tool_result_content) so the chat_history never holds the full oversized payload — not even transiently

A single catch-all helper performs the byte bounding and marker construction — called from the text branch only — to keep the rig patch minimal and easy to audit

CMPCT-032.description: CRITICAL BUG: After commit dc3d5934 (fix: compaction and mouse fixes — implementing CMPCT-023 through CMPCT-031 + CTX-007), compaction no longer triggers reliably. CONFIG-005.description:
Currently TypeScript reads ~/.fspec/credentials/credentials.json and passes API keys to Rust at session creation time. This creates a stale credentials problem - if a user updates their API key via the TUI, existing Rust sessions don't pick up the new key.

Credential management should be handled entirely in Rust:
1. Rust reads ~/.fspec/credentials/credentials.json directly
2. Rust checks for updated credentials when making API calls (or on session resume)
3. TypeScript only saves/deletes credentials to the file - doesn't pass keys to NAPI
4. Eliminates stale credential problem
5. Single source of truth for credential resolution in Rust

examples.text: Coding conversation: User fixes bug in auth.rs, runs tests pass → TaskCompletion anchor at turn 3, summarizes turns 0-2, keeps turns 3+

Mixed conversation: npm install success creates bash milestone anchor, test pass creates TaskCompletion anchor
PreservationContext extraction: 'Active files: auth.rs, README.md; Goals: Fix auth bug; Build: passing'
Synthetic anchor fallback: 10 turns with only web_search tools → UserCheckpoint at turn 9 with weight 0.7

Goal extraction: User messages 'Please fix the auth bug', 'Help me implement OAuth' → current_goals=['Fix the auth bug', 'Implement OAuth']
Build status detection: Tool result contains 'All 15 tests passed' → build_status=Passing; Tool result contains 'FAILED: 3 tests' → build_status=Failing
Error state extraction: Failed Bash tool with 'error: cannot find module xyz' → error_states contains 'error: cannot find module xyz'

rules.text: Anchors are only created when detection confidence >= 0.9 (90%)
ErrorResolution anchors have weight 0.9 (highest), TaskCompletion 0.8, FeatureMilestone 0.75, UserCheckpoint 0.7
Always preserve last 2-3 conversation turns regardless of anchors
When no natural anchors are detected, create a synthetic UserCheckpoint at conversation end

BuildStatus enum MUST have variants: Passing, Failing, Unknown

CTX-002.description:
Implement OpenCode's compaction TRIGGER logic (when to compact, not how to compact).

**Issue 1: Token Counting (BROKEN)**
Current: `effective = input - (cache_read * 0.9)` - discounts cache, ignores output
OpenCode: `count = input + cache_read + output` - includes ALL tokens

**Issue 2: Threshold Calculation (SUBOPTIMAL)**  
Current: `threshold = context_window * 0.9` - static percentage
OpenCode: `usable = context_window - min(model_max_output, 32000)` - reserves output space

**Required Changes:**
1. Token count = input + cache_read + output (include all, no discount)
2. Threshold = context_window - min(model_max_output, SESSION_OUTPUT_MAX)
3. Add SESSION_OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX = 32,000 constant
4. Add max_output_tokens to provider trait
5. Trigger when: count > usable

**Files to modify:**
- codelet/core/src/compaction_hook.rs (token calculation)
- codelet/cli/src/compaction_threshold.rs (threshold calculation)
- codelet/providers/src/lib.rs (add max_output_tokens trait method)

examples.text: Claude Sonnet (200k context, 8k max output): usable = 200,000 - min(8,192, 32,000) = 200,000 - 8,192 = 191,808 tokens
High-output model (200k context, 64k max output): usable = 200,000 - min(64,000, 32,000) = 200,000 - 32,000 = 168,000 tokens (SESSION_OUTPUT_MAX caps it)
Token counting: input=150,000 + cache_read=20,000 + output=5,000 = 175,000 total (NOT 150,000 - 18,000 = 132,000 as current code does)
Trigger check for Claude: total=175,000, usable=191,808 → 175,000 < 191,808 → NO compaction (current code would trigger at 180,000)
Trigger check for Claude: total=195,000, usable=191,808 → 195,000 > 191,808 → TRIGGER compaction
Unknown model (context=100k, max_output=0): min(0, 32000)=0, fallback to 32000 → usable = 100,000 - 32,000 = 68,000 tokens
Zero context window: context=0 → compaction returns false immediately (no context = no compaction)
Disable flag set: DISABLE_AUTOCOMPACT=true → compaction returns false immediately regardless of token count
Edge case: total exactly equals usable (191,808 == 191,808) → NO trigger (OpenCode uses > not >=)

rules.text: Token count MUST include input_tokens + cache_read_tokens + output_tokens (all three summed, no discounting)
Usable context MUST be calculated as: context_window - min(model_max_output, SESSION_OUTPUT_MAX)
SESSION_OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX constant MUST be 32,000 tokens
Compaction MUST trigger when: (input + cache_read + output) > usable_context
Provider trait MUST expose max_output_tokens() method returning the model's maximum output token limit
When model_max_output is 0, MUST use SESSION_OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX (32k) as fallback reservation
When context_window is 0, compaction MUST NOT trigger (return false immediately)
A configurable disable flag MUST allow skipping compaction entirely
Comparison MUST use strictly greater than (>), not greater-or-equal (>=)

CTX-005.description:
Parent story for three work streams:

1. **CTX-006**: Make Rust the single source of truth for context_window — TUI queries Rust instead of sourcing from models.dev JavaScript-side
2. **CTX-007**: Per-model configurable compaction thresholds — decouple compaction trigger from context_window, support absolute token values or percentage
3. **CTX-008**: TUI fields and NAPI bridge for compaction threshold configuration

**Problem Statement:**
- The TUI displays context_window from models.dev (JavaScript-side), but compaction uses Rust's ProviderManager::context_window(). These can disagree.
- For Opus 4.6, models.dev says 1M but the API limits to 200k without the beta header → SessionHeader shows [1M] but compaction threshold is ~968k → compaction never triggers proactively.
- Compaction threshold is mathematically coupled to context_window (threshold = context_window - min(max_output, 32k)). There's no way to configure a different compaction trigger per model.
- Known models like Claude should retain ~200k-based compaction even when 1M context becomes available.
- Custom/profile models need user-configurable compaction thresholds.

CTX-006.description:
Make Rust's ProviderManager::context_window() the single authoritative source for context window size across the entire application. The TUI must query this value from Rust rather than independently sourcing it from models.dev JSON data in TypeScript.

**Current Problem:**
- TUI gets contextWindow from NapiModelInfo.context_window (models.dev data baked into provider sections at listing time)
- Rust resolves context_window via ProviderManager::context_window() with its own priority chain
- These can disagree: models.dev says 1M for Opus 4.6, but Rust's claude::CONTEXT_WINDOW constant is 200k, and the API limits to 200k without the beta header
- The SessionHeader badge shows [1M] but compaction uses a different (and also wrong) value

**Solution:**
- After model selection, emit a Rust event (or expose NAPI query) with the resolved context_window and max_output_tokens
- TUI reads these values from Rust state, not from providerSections/models.dev data
- This ensures the displayed value, the compaction threshold, and the fill percentage all derive from the same authority
- The model selector can still show models.dev values for browsing, but the active session's context_window comes from Rust

Context fill percentage and SessionHeader badge both derive from the same Rust context_window — they can never disagree

CTX-007.description:
Decouple the compaction trigger threshold from the context window size and make it independently configurable per model. Currently, threshold = context_window - min(max_output, 32k), which is a fixed mathematical relationship. This means if models.dev says a model has 1M context, compaction triggers at ~968k — even if the practical API limit is 200k.

**Solution:**
- Add a per-model compaction threshold configuration that can be:
  (a) Absolute token value (e.g., 200000 tokens for Claude models)
  (b) Percentage of context window (e.g., 80% for unknown/custom models)
- Built-in defaults per model family:
  - Claude family: 200k tokens (retains existing behavior regardless of 1M availability)
  - Gemini family: 80% of context_window
  - OpenAI family: 80% of context_window
  - Other/unknown: 80% of context_window
- Custom/profile models: user-configurable via provider settings or custom model form
- Rust ProviderManager resolves the effective compaction threshold, replacing the current calculate_usable_context() with a threshold that considers per-model config
- The existing AUTOCOMPACT_BUFFER (50k) and SESSION_OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX (32k) constants remain for post-compaction budget calculation

examples.text: Claude Sonnet 4 with 200k context → threshold = 200k - 8k = 191,808 (legacy behavior retained, no change)
Gemini 2.5 Pro with 1M context → threshold = 800,000 (80% of 1M)
GPT-4o with 128k context → threshold = 102,400 (80% of 128k)
User sets absolute threshold of 150,000 tokens on a custom model with 200k context → compaction fires at 150k regardless of model family
User sets percentage threshold of 60% on a 200k context model → compaction fires at 120,000
Unknown model with 100k context and no family info → threshold falls through to legacy formula: 100k - 32k = 68,000
User sets threshold of 300,000 on a model with 200k context → clamped to 200k - output_reservation (168,000)
Context fill shows 50% when at 100k tokens with 200k threshold — not when at 500k tokens with 1M context

rules.text: Compaction threshold can be configured as either absolute tokens (e.g., 200000) or percentage of context window (e.g., 80%)
Resolution priority: user-configured override > built-in model family default > legacy calculate_usable_context formula
Built-in defaults: Claude family = context_window minus output reservation (legacy behavior retained); Gemini/OpenAI/others = 80% of context_window
All compaction trigger paths (pre-prompt, CompactionHook, emergency, retry) must use the same resolved threshold
Context fill percentage must be computed relative to the compaction threshold, not the raw context window
If a user-configured threshold exceeds context_window, it should be clamped to context_window minus output reservation
The ProviderManager gains a compaction_threshold() method that replaces direct calculate_usable_context() calls in the stream loop
Post-compaction budget (summarization_budget) should be relative to the threshold, not the context_window

The SessionHeader badge displays the raw context_window (e.g., [200k], [1M]) but the fill percentage is computed relative to the compaction threshold (CTX-007 Rule [4]). DISC-001.description: discover-foundation must read draft, identify next unfilled field, prompt AI with system-reminders, re-read after each fspec update-foundation command, chain to next field, validate when complete, and auto-regenerate FOUNDATION.md from foundation.json

examples.text: INITIAL RUN: Human runs 'fspec discover-foundation' → Command creates foundation.json.draft with structure → Draft has REQUIRED fields: project{name,vision,projectType}, problemSpace{primaryProblem{title,description,impact}}, solutionSpace{overview,capabilities[]}, personas[] → All fields contain [QUESTION: ...] or [DETECTED: ...] placeholders → Command emits system-reminder: 'Draft created. To complete foundation, you must ULTRATHINK the entire codebase. Analyze EVERYTHING: commands, routes, UI, tests, README, package.json. Understand HOW it works, then determine WHY it exists and WHAT users can do. I will guide you field-by-field. Field 1/9: project.name'

FIELD 1 (project.name): Command reads draft → Finds [QUESTION: What is the project name?] → Emits: 'Field 1/9: project.name. Analyze package.json name field. Confirm with human. Run: fspec update-foundation --field project.name --value <name>' → AI reads package.json, sees 'fspec' → AI asks human 'Package name is fspec, correct?' → Human confirms → AI runs 'fspec update-foundation --field project.name --value fspec' → Command detects update, re-scans draft, finds next unfilled field

FIELD 2 (project.vision): Command re-scans → Finds [QUESTION: What is the one-sentence vision?] → Emits: 'Field 2/9: project.vision (elevator pitch). ULTRATHINK: Read ALL code, understand the system deeply. What is the core PURPOSE? Focus on WHY this exists, not HOW it works. Ask human. Run: fspec update-foundation --field project.vision --value "your vision"' → AI reads README, analyzes commands (validate, format, list-features), understands it manages Gherkin specs → AI formulates: 'CLI tool for managing Gherkin specifications using ACDD' → AI asks human 'Is vision correct?' → Human confirms → AI updates field

FIELD 3 (project.projectType): Command re-scans → Finds [DETECTED: cli-tool] → Emits: 'Field 3/9: project.projectType. Auto-detected cli-tool from commander.js usage and bin field. Verify with human. Options: cli-tool, web-app, library, sdk, mobile-app, desktop-app, service, api, other. Run: fspec update-foundation --field project.projectType --value cli-tool' → AI analyzes code: sees commander.js imports, .command() calls, bin field in package.json → AI confirms: yes, this is cli-tool → AI asks human 'Detected cli-tool, correct?' → Human confirms → AI updates field → Command chains to problemSpace

FIELD 4 (problemSpace.primaryProblem): Command re-scans → Finds [QUESTION: What problem does this solve?] → Emits: 'Field 4/9: problemSpace.primaryProblem. CRITICAL: Think from USER perspective. WHO uses this (persona)? WHAT problem do THEY face? WHY do they need this solution? Analyze codebase to understand user pain, ask human. Required: title, description, impact (high/medium/low). Run: fspec update-foundation --field problemSpace.primaryProblem.title --value "Problem Title"' → AI analyzes: this is CLI for specs, users are developers, they need structured spec workflow → AI asks human 'Primary problem: Developers lack structured workflow for managing specifications?' → Human elaborates → AI updates title,description,impact

FIELD 5 (solutionSpace.capabilities): Command re-scans → Finds [QUESTION: What can users DO?] → Emits: 'Field 5/9: solutionSpace.capabilities. List 3-7 HIGH-LEVEL abilities users have. Focus on WHAT not HOW. Example: "Spec Validation" (WHAT), not "Uses Cucumber parser" (HOW). Analyze commands/features to identify user-facing capabilities. Run: fspec update-foundation --field solutionSpace.capabilities[0].name --value "Capability Name"' → AI analyzes commands: validate, format, list, create → Groups into capabilities: Spec Management, Validation, Work Unit Tracking → AI asks human → Human confirms → AI adds each capability with description

FIELD 6 (personas): Command re-scans → Finds [QUESTION: Who uses this?] → Emits: 'Field 6/9: personas. Identify ALL user types from interactions. CLI tools: who runs commands? Web apps: who uses UI + who calls API? Analyze ALL user-facing code. Ask human about goals and pain points. Run: fspec update-foundation --field personas[0].name --value "Persona Name"' → AI analyzes: CLI commands used by developers, no web UI, no API consumers → Identifies persona: "Developer using CLI in terminal" → AI asks human about goals: managing specs, following ACDD → AI asks about pain points: fragmented tools, no workflow → AI updates persona with name, description, goals, painPoints

COMPLETION: AI fills last required field → Command re-scans → ALL required fields complete (no [QUESTION:] in required fields) → Command validates draft against JSON schema → Schema validation PASSES → Command creates spec/foundation.json from draft → Command deletes spec/foundation.json.draft → Command AUTOMATICALLY runs 'fspec generate-foundation-md' (no AI action needed) → Command emits: 'Discovery complete\! Created: spec/foundation.json, spec/FOUNDATION.md. Foundation is ready. You can now run fspec commands that require foundation.' → AI can now proceed with other work

ERROR: Manual Editing → AI uses Write tool to edit foundation.json.draft directly → Command detects: draft mtime changed without fspec command → Command compares last known state vs current → Command emits ERROR in system-reminder: 'CRITICAL: You manually edited foundation.json.draft. This violates the workflow. You MUST use: fspec update-foundation --field <path> --value <value>. Reverting your changes. Draft restored to last valid state. Try again with proper command.' → Draft is restored → AI must use fspec commands

ERROR: Validation Failure → AI fills all fields → Command validates against schema → Validation FAILS: missing required field problemSpace.primaryProblem.description → Command emits: 'Schema validation failed.
