architectureNotes.text: Service worker runs a Streamable HTTP MCP server using offscreen document or chrome.sockets API for TCP listening. Alternatives: use chrome.offscreen to create a hidden page that runs the HTTP server, or use a tiny Node.js bridge process spawned alongside

Content script injects into all pages and monitors navigator.modelContext for tool registrations. Uses MutationObserver-like pattern or polls for changes. Communicates with service worker via chrome.runtime.sendMessage

Architecture layers: Content Script (WebMCP tool discovery per tab) → Service Worker (tool registry, browser control APIs, event aggregation) → MCP HTTP Server (Streamable HTTP transport with SSE for notifications) → ConnectMCP (fspec agent client)

MV3 service workers cannot open TCP ports directly. The HTTP server MUST run in either: (a) an offscreen document (chrome.offscreen API), (b) a companion Node.js native messaging host process, or (c) use the chrome.sockets API (if available in MV3). Option (b) is most reliable and follows the mcp-chrome pattern

For bidirectional events via ConnectMCP: ConnectMCP's rmcp ClientHandler has on_tool_list_changed callback. When the extension sends MCP notifications/tools/list_changed, rmcp re-fetches tools. For custom browser events, use MCP notifications with custom method names that get injected into the session via watcher_input_tx

Content scripts run in an ISOLATED WORLD — they share the page's DOM but NOT the page's JavaScript context. navigator.modelContext is only accessible from the page's MAIN world. To bridge this, use chrome.scripting.executeScript({ world: 'MAIN' }) to inject scripts into the page context. These main-world scripts communicate back via window.postMessage(), which the content script relays to the service worker via chrome.runtime.sendMessage.

Architecture layers: Main-World Injected Script (WebMCP tool discovery/invocation per tab, runs in page context) → Content Script (isolated world relay, postMessage ↔ chrome.runtime bridge) → Service Worker (tool registry, browser control APIs, event aggregation, native messaging client) → Native Messaging Host (Node.js, runs Streamable HTTP MCP server with GET-based SSE for persistent notifications) → ConnectMCP (fspec agent client)

EXT-001.description: Build a Chrome extension (Manifest V3) that leverages WebMCP (navigator.modelContext API) and exposes browser capabilities as an MCP server. The extension lives in the extension/ directory and is connectable via ConnectMCP tool using Streamable HTTP transport. It must be bidirectional: the agent can invoke browser tools AND the browser extension can fire events/notifications back to the agent session via MCP server-initiated messages (SSE channel). The extension bridges the gap between WebMCP's in-browser tool registration and fspec's ConnectMCP-based MCP client, enabling the agent to discover and call WebMCP tools registered by any website, control tabs/navigation, capture screenshots, and receive page-level events (navigation, tool registration changes, DOM mutations) as real-time notifications.

examples.text: Agent calls ConnectMCP(transport: 'http', url: 'http://localhost:19876/mcp') → extension responds with MCP initialize → tools/list returns browser_navigate, browser_screenshot, list_tabs, plus any WebMCP tools from open tabs

User navigates to a WebMCP-enabled travel site → site calls navigator.modelContext.registerTool('searchFlights', ...) → content script detects registration → extension adds webmcp__travel-demo.bandarra.me__searchFlights to MCP tool list → sends notifications/tools/list_changed to agent via SSE

Agent calls mcp__ext__browser_screenshot({tabId: 123, fullPage: true}) → extension captures full-page screenshot using chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab → returns base64 PNG image

User clicks a link that navigates to new URL → extension fires MCP notification {method: 'notifications/browser/navigation', params: {tabId: 123, url: 'https://new-page.com', title: 'New Page'}} → agent receives via SSE and can react

WebMCP-enabled site unregisters a tool via navigator.modelContext.unregisterTool('oldTool') → content script detects removal → extension removes from tool list → sends notifications/tools/list_changed → agent's next tool call reflects updated list

Agent calls webmcp__example.com__submitForm({name: 'John', email: 'john@test.com'}) → extension routes to content script → content script calls the WebMCP tool's execute() function → result returned to agent
Extension popup shows: server status (listening/stopped), port number, connected clients count, list of available tools grouped by source (native vs WebMCP per tab)

User navigates to a WebMCP-enabled travel site → site calls navigator.modelContext.registerTool({name: 'searchFlights', ...}) → main-world injected script detects registration → extension adds webmcp__travel-demo.bandarra.me__searchFlights to MCP tool list → sends notifications/tools/list_changed to agent via GET SSE stream

WebMCP-enabled site unregisters a tool via navigator.modelContext.unregisterTool('oldTool') → main-world discovery script detects removal → extension removes from tool list → sends notifications/tools/list_changed via GET SSE stream → agent's next tools/list call reflects updated list

Agent calls webmcp__example.com__submitForm({name: 'John', email: 'john@test.com'}) → extension injects main-world script via chrome.scripting.executeScript({world: 'MAIN'}) → main-world script calls the WebMCP tool's execute() function in the page context → result relayed back via postMessage → content script → service worker → native host → agent receives structured result

rules.text: The extension MUST be a Manifest V3 Chrome extension with a service worker background script, content scripts for WebMCP tool discovery, and a popup UI for connection status
The extension MUST expose a Streamable HTTP MCP server (default port 19876) that the agent connects to via ConnectMCP(transport: 'http', url: 'http://localhost:19876/mcp')
Browser-to-agent events (page navigation, WebMCP tool registration changes, console errors) MUST be sent as MCP server-initiated notifications via the SSE channel of Streamable HTTP transport
The extension MUST discover WebMCP tools registered by websites via navigator.modelContext and expose them as MCP tools namespaced as webmcp__<origin>__<toolName>
The extension MUST provide native browser control tools: navigate, screenshot, get_page_content, list_tabs, switch_tab, close_tab, click_element, fill_form, execute_script
The extension source code lives in the extension/ directory at project root with its own package.json, build system (Vite/esbuild + TypeScript), and manifest.json
Connection lifecycle: ConnectMCP connects → extension opens SSE stream for server→client notifications; ConnectMCP disconnects or session ends → SSE stream closes
The extension requires Chrome 146+ with the WebMCP for testing flag enabled (chrome://flags/#web-mcp) for WebMCP tool discovery; browser control tools work on any Chrome version

Browser-to-agent events (page navigation, WebMCP tool registration changes, console errors) MUST be sent as MCP server-initiated notifications via the GET-based SSE stream of Streamable HTTP transport (client opens GET /mcp to receive persistent server→client notifications)

The extension MUST be a Manifest V3 Chrome extension with a service worker background script, content scripts (isolated world relay), main-world injected scripts for WebMCP tool discovery/invocation, and a popup UI for connection status

Connection lifecycle: ConnectMCP connects → POST /mcp initialize handshake → GET /mcp opens persistent SSE stream for server→client notifications; ConnectMCP disconnects or session ends → DELETE /mcp → SSE stream closes

architectureNotes.text: Native host is pure Node.js with zero npm dependencies — uses only built-in http, net, crypto, path, os, fs modules. This keeps it lightweight and avoids npm install for the host process.

Chrome native messaging protocol: messages are length-prefixed (4-byte unsigned 32-bit little-endian integer) followed by raw JSON bytes. The host reads stdin in this format and writes stdout in this format. Max message size is 1MB.

The MCP Streamable HTTP server uses Node.js built-in http module. SSE streams are implemented by keeping the response open with Transfer-Encoding: chunked and writing 'data: {...}\n\n' formatted lines. Each SSE event is a JSON-RPC notification or response.

Tool call routing: when a POST /mcp tools/call arrives, the host writes a native messaging frame to stdout addressed to the extension. The host assigns a correlation ID and holds the HTTP response open until the extension replies on stdin with a matching correlation ID. This is an async request-response pattern over the native messaging channel.

assumptions: The Chrome extension ID is known at registration time — the user provides it via --extension-id flag during --register
The native host process is long-lived — Chrome keeps it alive as long as the extension has an active connectNative() port. It does not need to auto-start on system boot.
EXT-003.description: Build the Node.js native messaging host process that: (a) registers with Chrome as a native messaging host, (b) runs a Streamable HTTP MCP server on port 19876, (c) implements the full MCP lifecycle (POST initialize, GET SSE stream, POST tools/call, DELETE session), (d) communicates with the Chrome extension service worker via stdin/stdout native messaging protocol.

examples.text: Agent calls ConnectMCP(transport: 'http', url: 'http://localhost:19876/mcp') → POST /mcp with initialize → server returns {serverInfo, capabilities, protocolVersion} with Mcp-Session-Id header → tools/list returns empty list (no extension connected yet)

Extension calls chrome.runtime.connectNative('com.fspec.webmcp') → host starts, reads 4-byte length prefix + JSON from stdin → host parses as native messaging frame → when extension sends {type: 'TOOLS_CHANGED', tools: [...]}, host updates internal tool registry

Agent opens GET /mcp with Accept: text/event-stream → server responds 200 with Content-Type: text/event-stream → stream stays open → when extension sends browser event via stdin, host writes SSE data line with JSON-RPC notification → agent receives it

Agent sends POST /mcp with tools/call for browser_navigate → host writes native messaging frame to stdout for the extension → extension executes chrome.tabs.update → extension writes result back on stdin → host returns JSON-RPC result to agent
Agent sends DELETE /mcp with Mcp-Session-Id → server closes SSE stream for that session → cleans up session state → returns 200

User runs node extension/host/native-host.js --register → script detects macOS → writes com.fspec.webmcp.json to ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/NativeMessagingHosts/ with correct path and allowed_origins
POST /mcp without Mcp-Session-Id for a non-initialize request → server responds 400 Bad Request with error message
POST /mcp with invalid Mcp-Session-Id → server responds 404 Not Found (session does not exist)

rules.text: The native messaging host MUST be a standalone Node.js script that Chrome launches via chrome.runtime.connectNative('com.fspec.webmcp')
The host process communicates with the Chrome extension via stdin/stdout using Chrome's native messaging protocol (4-byte little-endian length prefix + JSON payload)
The host MUST run a Streamable HTTP MCP server on port 19876 (default) at endpoint /mcp
MCP lifecycle: POST /mcp for JSON-RPC requests (initialize, tools/list, tools/call), GET /mcp for persistent SSE notification stream, DELETE /mcp for session termination
The server MUST assign an Mcp-Session-Id header on initialize response and require it on all subsequent requests

The host MUST support a --register flag that writes the Chrome native messaging host manifest JSON to the platform-specific directory (macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/NativeMessagingHosts/)
The host MUST relay messages bidirectionally: MCP requests from HTTP clients are forwarded to the extension via stdout, and extension responses from stdin are returned to the HTTP client
The GET /mcp SSE stream MUST stay open for the duration of the session to enable server-initiated notifications (browser events pushed from extension → native host → SSE → agent)
The native host lives in extension/host/ directory with its own entry point script, separate from the extension's browser-side code
The host MUST handle multiple concurrent MCP sessions (multiple agents connecting simultaneously) by tracking session IDs

EXT-003.title: Native Messaging Host & MCP Streamable HTTP Server

userStory.action: connect to the Chrome extension's MCP server via ConnectMCP and have tool calls and notifications routed through a native messaging host
userStory.benefit: the agent can invoke browser tools and receive real-time browser events through the standard MCP protocol without Chrome service worker TCP limitations

architectureNotes.text: chrome.runtime.connectNative() in MV3 service workers returns a Port object. Messages are sent/received as plain JSON objects (Chrome handles the native messaging frame encoding/decoding). The service worker does NOT need to do 4-byte length-prefix framing — that's the native host's responsibility. The Port.postMessage() and Port.onMessage handle serialization.

Message type taxonomy: FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_REGISTERED, FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_UNREGISTERED (content→SW for tool registry updates), FSPEC_INVOKE_TOOL, FSPEC_INVOKE_RESULT (SW→content→main and back for tool invocations), FSPEC_GET_STATUS (popup→SW for status queries), TOOL_CALL (native host→SW for incoming tool calls), TOOLS_CHANGED/NOTIFICATION (SW→native host for outgoing state changes)

The sender object in chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener automatically includes sender.tab.id for content scripts. No need for content scripts to manually include tab ID — Chrome provides it. Service worker uses sender.tab.id to route responses back.

EXT-004.description: Implement the Chrome extension service worker as the central event hub: tool registry management, chrome.runtime messaging between content scripts and service worker, window.postMessage relay in content scripts (isolated world ↔ main world bridge), and native messaging client connection to the host process. Content scripts act as relay between main-world injected scripts and the service worker.

examples.text: Extension loads → service worker calls chrome.runtime.connectNative('com.fspec.webmcp') → native host stdin/stdout connection established → service worker logs 'Native messaging connected'

Native host sends {type: 'TOOL_CALL', correlationId: 'abc', method: 'tools/call', params: {name: 'browser_navigate', arguments: {url: 'https://example.com'}}} via stdin → service worker receives and routes to chrome.tabs.update handler → handler returns result → service worker writes {correlationId: 'abc', result: {url: 'https://example.com', title: 'Example'}} to native port

Content script on tab 42 receives window.postMessage({type: 'FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_REGISTERED', tool: {name: 'searchFlights', ...}}) from main-world script → content script calls chrome.runtime.sendMessage({type: 'FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_REGISTERED', tool: {...}}) → service worker receives with sender.tab.id = 42 → updates tool registry → forwards TOOLS_CHANGED to native host

Service worker needs to invoke WebMCP tool on tab 42 → sends chrome.tabs.sendMessage(42, {type: 'FSPEC_INVOKE_TOOL', correlationId: 'xyz', toolName: 'searchFlights', args: {...}}) → content script receives → posts to main world via window.postMessage → main world executes tool → result flows back: postMessage → content script → chrome.runtime.sendMessage → service worker
Native messaging port disconnects (host process dies) → service worker detects port.onDisconnect → waits 2 seconds → retries chrome.runtime.connectNative → reconnects successfully
Popup sends chrome.runtime.sendMessage({type: 'FSPEC_GET_STATUS'}) → service worker responds with {connected: true, port: 19876, toolCount: 5, nativeConnected: true}

rules.text: Service worker MUST connect to native host via chrome.runtime.connectNative('com.fspec.webmcp') on startup and maintain the connection
Service worker MUST maintain a tool registry (Map of tool name → tool metadata) updated by native host TOOLS_CHANGED messages and content script WebMCP discovery messages

Content script MUST relay messages bidirectionally: window.postMessage (main world) ↔ chrome.runtime.sendMessage (service worker) using FSPEC_WEBMCP_ prefix for main→SW and FSPEC_INVOKE_ prefix for SW→main
Service worker MUST route incoming native host tool calls to the correct tab's content script and return the result back to the native host via native messaging
All messages between service worker and native host use the 4-byte little-endian length-prefix protocol (same as EXT-003 native messaging format)
Service worker MUST handle native messaging port disconnect gracefully and attempt reconnection
Messages from content scripts MUST include the sender tab ID so the service worker can route responses back to the correct tab

Service worker MUST forward browser event notifications (from chrome.tabs.onUpdated, onCreated, onRemoved) to the native host for SSE broadcast — actual event handlers are EXT-007 scope but the forwarding mechanism is EXT-004

EXT-004.title: Service Worker & Content Script Message Routing

userStory.action: have the service worker and content scripts route messages between the native host, browser APIs, and main-world scripts
userStory.benefit: downstream features (browser control, WebMCP discovery, events, popup) can use a reliable messaging backbone without each implementing their own routing

architectureNotes.text: Tool handlers are implemented as a new module (background/browser-tools.ts) that exports a function registry (Map<string, handler>). The message router's handleNativeMessage method is updated to check the native tool registry before returning 'no handler' errors.
For tools that need to resolve 'active tab' when no tabId is given, use chrome.tabs.query({active: true, currentWindow: true}) to find the current tab. This is a promise-based API in MV3.

The NATIVE_TOOLS definition in the native host (host/lib/mcp-server.mjs) must be expanded with the 7 new tools (browser_switch_tab, browser_close_tab, browser_get_page_content, browser_click_element, browser_fill_form, browser_go_back, browser_go_forward) so tools/list returns all 11.

chrome.scripting.executeScript returns a Promise<InjectionResult[]>. The results[0].result contains the actual return value. Need to handle serialization properly — complex DOM objects cannot be returned, only JSON-serializable values.

assumptions: All Chrome extension APIs are async in MV3. Tool handlers must be async functions. The TOOL_CALL handling in the message router must become asynchronous to support awaiting Chrome API results before sending the response back to the native host.
EXT-005.description: Implement the suite of browser control MCP tools: browser_navigate, browser_screenshot, browser_get_page_content, browser_list_tabs, browser_switch_tab, browser_close_tab, browser_click_element, browser_fill_form, browser_execute_script, browser_go_back, browser_go_forward. Each tool is exposed via the MCP server and executed via Chrome extension APIs (chrome.tabs, chrome.scripting, etc).

examples.text: Agent calls browser_navigate({url: 'https://example.com'}) → service worker calls chrome.tabs.update(activeTabId, {url: 'https://example.com'}) → waits for onUpdated with status 'complete' → returns {url: 'https://example.com', title: 'Example Domain'}

Agent calls browser_screenshot({tabId: 42}) → service worker calls chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab(windowId, {format: 'png'}) → returns {content: [{type: 'image', data: 'iVBOR...', mimeType: 'image/png'}]}

Agent calls browser_list_tabs() → service worker calls chrome.tabs.query({}) → returns [{id: 1, url: 'https://example.com', title: 'Example', active: true}, {id: 2, url: 'about:blank', title: 'New Tab', active: false}]
Agent calls browser_execute_script({code: 'document.title'}) → service worker calls chrome.scripting.executeScript({target: {tabId}, func: ...}) → returns the script result as text

Agent calls browser_click_element({selector: '#submit-btn'}) → service worker injects script via chrome.scripting.executeScript → script finds element, calls click() → returns {clicked: true, selector: '#submit-btn'}
Agent calls browser_click_element({selector: '#nonexistent'}) → script cannot find element → returns MCP error {isError: true, content: [{type: 'text', text: 'Element not found: #nonexistent'}]}

Agent calls browser_fill_form({selector: '#email', value: 'test@example.com'}) → script sets input value and dispatches input+change events → returns {filled: true, selector: '#email', value: 'test@example.com'}
Agent calls browser_switch_tab({tabId: 42}) → service worker calls chrome.tabs.update(42, {active: true}) and chrome.windows.update(windowId, {focused: true}) → returns confirmation with tab info
Agent calls browser_close_tab({tabId: 42}) → service worker gets tab info first, then calls chrome.tabs.remove(42) → returns {closed: true, tabId: 42, url: 'https://example.com'}
Agent calls browser_get_page_content({tabId: 42, format: 'text'}) → returns page innerText; browser_get_page_content({format: 'html'}) → returns outerHTML
Agent calls browser_go_back() → chrome.tabs.goBack(activeTabId) → returns {navigated: true, direction: 'back'}; browser_go_forward() similarly

rules.text: Each browser control tool is registered as a native tool handler in the service worker, dispatched by the message router when a TOOL_CALL arrives from the native host with a matching tool name
browser_navigate uses chrome.tabs.update({url}) on the specified tab (or active tab if none specified) and returns the final URL and page title after load completes
browser_screenshot uses chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab() and returns the screenshot as a base64-encoded PNG data URI
browser_list_tabs uses chrome.tabs.query({}) and returns an array of tab objects with id, url, title, and active status
browser_switch_tab uses chrome.tabs.update(tabId, {active: true}) and chrome.windows.update(windowId, {focused: true}) to focus the specified tab
browser_close_tab uses chrome.tabs.remove(tabId) and returns confirmation with the closed tab's info
browser_get_page_content uses chrome.scripting.executeScript to retrieve document.title, document.URL, and DOM content (innerText or outerHTML) from the specified tab
browser_click_element uses chrome.scripting.executeScript to find an element by CSS selector and call element.click() in the page context
browser_fill_form uses chrome.scripting.executeScript to find an element by CSS selector, set its value, and dispatch input/change events
browser_execute_script uses chrome.scripting.executeScript to run arbitrary JavaScript code in the specified tab and returns the result
browser_go_back and browser_go_forward use chrome.tabs.goBack(tabId) and chrome.tabs.goForward(tabId) respectively to navigate browser history
All tool results follow MCP content format: {content: [{type: 'text', text: '...'}]} for text results or {content: [{type: 'image', data: '...', mimeType: 'image/png'}]} for screenshots
Tools that accept an optional tabId default to the current active tab if no tabId is provided
The NATIVE_TOOLS array in the MCP server must be expanded to include all 11 tools with complete inputSchema definitions so tools/list returns them all
Tool handler errors (element not found, invalid selector, tab not found) must return MCP error responses with descriptive messages, not throw uncaught exceptions

EXT-005.title: Native Browser Control Tools

userStory.action: invoke browser control tools via the MCP connection
userStory.benefit: I can navigate pages, capture screenshots, list and manage tabs, execute scripts, interact with page elements, and control browser history programmatically

architectureNotes.text: The main-world discovery script runs as a self-contained function injected via chrome.scripting.executeScript({world: 'MAIN'}). It must monkey-patch navigator.modelContext to intercept registerTool/unregisterTool calls before any page scripts run. The script maintains a Map of registered tools keyed by name, and communicates exclusively via window.postMessage with FSPEC_ prefixed message types.

The message-router.ts tool name format must change from 'webmcp__<name>' to 'webmcp__<origin>__<name>' to match the MCP namespacing convention. The origin is the hostname extracted from the page URL. The content script relay already passes origin from the main-world postMessage.

Injection is triggered by chrome.tabs.onUpdated with status 'complete' in the service worker. A new webmcp-injector.ts module handles injection via chrome.scripting.executeScript({target: {tabId}, world: 'MAIN', func: discoveryFunction}). The discovery function is the serialized form of the main-world script.

EXT-006.description: Implement WebMCP tool discovery and invocation through main-world script injection. Discovery: inject scripts via chrome.scripting.executeScript({world: 'MAIN'}) to detect navigator.modelContext.registerTool/unregisterTool calls, relay tool metadata back via postMessage → content script → service worker. Invocation: inject main-world scripts to call tool execute() functions in page context, relay results back through the same chain. Tools namespaced as webmcp__<origin>__<toolName>. Requires Chrome 146+ with WebMCP flag.

examples.text: Site at travel-demo.bandarra.me registers tool 'searchFlights' → discovery script posts {type: FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_REGISTERED, tool: {name: 'searchFlights', ...}, origin: 'travel-demo.bandarra.me'} → content script relays to SW → SW registers as 'webmcp__travel-demo.bandarra.me__searchFlights' → native host gets TOOLS_CHANGED → SSE notification to agent

Site at example.com unregisters tool 'oldTool' → discovery script posts {type: FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_UNREGISTERED, toolName: 'oldTool', origin: 'example.com'} → content script relays → SW removes 'webmcp__example.com__oldTool' from registry → TOOLS_CHANGED → SSE notification

Agent calls tools/call with name 'webmcp__example.com__submitForm' and args {name: 'John'} → SW looks up tool in registry (source: webmcp, tabId: 42) → sends FSPEC_INVOKE_TOOL to tab 42's content script → content script posts to main world → main world calls the tool's execute({name: 'John'}) → result posted back → content script relays FSPEC_INVOKE_RESULT to SW → SW returns to native host
Tool execute() throws Error('Network timeout') → discovery script catches, posts {type: FSPEC_INVOKE_RESULT, correlationId: 'xyz', error: 'Network timeout'} → SW returns error response to agent

rules.text: Main-world discovery script MUST intercept navigator.modelContext.registerTool() and unregisterTool() calls by monkey-patching the API before any page script runs

EXT-009.description:
When a website uses the WebMCP polyfill library (e.g., webmcp.dev's `new WebMCP().registerTool(...)`) instead of the native `navigator.modelContext.registerTool()` API, the fspec extension's monkey-patch interceptor never fires. Dynamically registered tools are invisible to the MCP client.

Three failure modes identified:
1. Polyfill bypass: webmcp.dev uses `WebMCP` class with its own internal registry — never touches `navigator.modelContext`
2. Injection race: MAIN-world script injected at `document_idle`/`complete` can miss tools registered during initial page script execution
3. Format mismatch: Tool entries from `TOOLS_CHANGED` may not match MCP `tools/list` expected shape

See `mcp-research.md` for full analysis, Chromium source references, and resolution plan.

Tool registered via WebMCP library can be invoked through MCP and the execute callback fires in page context
Discovery script injected twice on same page only runs once (double-injection guard)
When ModelContextTesting is available, ontoolchange fires and listTools() catches tools registered before injection

architectureNotes.text: Replace eval()-based execution in browser-tools.ts with chrome.userScripts.execute() using USER_SCRIPT world. Add ChromeUserScriptsForTools interface to deps. Call configureWorld() in service-worker.ts on startup. Add userScripts permission to manifest.json.

EXT-010.description:
browser_execute_script always returns "null" regardless of the code passed. The handler uses chrome.scripting.executeScript with a func that calls eval(codeStr), but MV3's Content Security Policy forbids unsafe-eval in the extension's isolated world. The eval() silently throws an EvalError which Chromium catches and returns null. Other browser tools (get_page_content, click_element, fill_form) work fine because they use inline function code without eval.

Fix: Replace eval()-based execution with chrome.userScripts API (Chrome 120+ configureWorld, Chrome 135+ execute). The USER_SCRIPT world is exempt from page CSP and supports configureWorld({ csp: "script-src 'self' 'unsafe-eval'" }) to allow eval. This is the same approach Violentmonkey and Tampermonkey plan for MV3. Requires adding "userScripts" permission and user must enable "Allow User Scripts" toggle.

See attached eval-csp-research.md for full analysis, Chromium source investigation, comparison of Violentmonkey/Tampermonkey approaches, and alternative solutions considered.

EXT-011.description:
The extension exposes 11 native browser control tools but is missing the ability to CREATE new tabs. It can close tabs (browser_close_tab), switch tabs (browser_switch_tab), list tabs (browser_list_tabs), and navigate existing tabs (browser_navigate) — but there is no way for the AI agent to open a URL in a new tab.

The workaround of using browser_execute_script with window.open() fails because Chrome's popup blocker blocks it (no user gesture context in the USER_SCRIPT world).

This is a clear gap: the agent can close and manage tabs but cannot create them.

Fix: Add a browser_create_tab tool that calls chrome.tabs.create(). This requires changes in two places:
1. extension/src/background/browser-tools.ts — add handler + extend ChromeTabsForTools interface with create()
2. extension/host/lib/mcp-server.mjs — add tool definition to NATIVE_TOOLS array

The chrome.tabs.create() API requires NO additional permissions beyond what the extension already has (the 'tabs' permission is already declared in manifest.json). Per Chrome docs: 'creating a new tab' does not require any permissions.

EXT-013.description:
When browser_screenshot captures a large viewport (e.g. 1728x992 on a complex page like Shorthand's editor), the base64 PNG easily exceeds 1MB. Chrome's native messaging enforces a 1MB limit on port.postMessage() in BOTH directions. When the extension tries to send the oversized screenshot result back via port.postMessage(), Chrome disconnects the native messaging port entirely. This causes: (1) the pending MCP tool call to time out after 30s, (2) the entire native messaging channel to die — all subsequent tool calls fail with 'Tool not found', and (3) reconnecting via ConnectMCP doesn't help because the native host process lost its Chrome connection.

Additionally, the native-messaging.mjs reader has a secondary bug: if an oversized message somehow arrives, line 72-74 does buffer = Buffer.alloc(0) which corrupts the stream by discarding partial data from subsequent messages.

Fix: The browser_screenshot handler in browser-tools.ts must resize and compress the PNG to a JPEG before returning it through native messaging. Target max 1568px on long edge (Claude's optimal processing size) and JPEG quality tuned to keep total message well under 1MB. Also fix the reader's oversized-message handling to skip the exact number of bytes rather than zeroing the buffer.

Very tall full-page screenshot (1568x4000) → sliced into multiple ~1000px tiles, each tile is a separate JPEG content block

Native reader encounters oversized message (>64 MiB) → skips it and processes subsequent messages correctly

Each tile must be returned as a separate image content block in the MCP result content array
The total JSON message sent through native messaging must stay well under the 1 MB host→extension limit (each tile under 800KB base64)

architectureNotes.text: Validation goes in ReadTool::call() in codelet/tools/src/read.rs, in the FileType::Image branch, after base64 encoding but before constructing ReadOutput::Image
Use a new ToolError::ImageSizeLimit variant (or reuse ToolError::Validation) with a human-readable error message — the error appears as a text tool result, never as image data in the conversation

EXT-014.description:
When the Read tool reads an image file that exceeds the LLM provider's API size limit (e.g., >5MB base64 for Claude), the image gets sent to the API, which returns a 400 invalid_request_error. Because the oversized image is now permanently embedded in the conversation history, **every subsequent API call re-sends it and fails with the same error** — the agent loop is irrecoverably broken.

This is the exact bug described in anthropics/claude-code#2939 and #20021: once an oversized image enters the context, it poisons all future requests.

**Root cause:** The Read tool (`codelet/tools/src/read.rs`) base64 encodes image files with zero size validation. The image flows through:
1. `ReadOutput::Image { data, media_type }` — unbounded base64 string
2. rig's `parse_tool_result_content()` — converts to `ToolResultContent::image_base64()`
3. Provider layer — sends to API
4. API rejects → 400 error → image stays in history → infinite loop of failures

**The fix must happen in the Read tool** because once the image enters the conversation history, it's too late. The Read tool is the last point where we can return a text error instead of image data.

**Provider-specific image limits:**
- **Claude (Anthropic):** 5MB base64 per image, max 8000×8000px (2000×2000 if >20 images in request), optimal ≤1568px long edge, 32MB total request
- **OpenAI (GPT-4o):** 50MB total payload, auto-resizes images server-side, practical ~20MB base64 per image
- **Gemini (Google):** 20MB total inline request (100MB with newer API), max 3600 images per request
- **Z.AI (GLM-4V):** 5MB per image, max 6000×6000px

**Implementation:**
1. Add image size validation in the Read tool's `FileType::Image` branch — check base64 size against a conservative universal limit (e.g., 5MB base64, the strictest across all providers)
2. When an image exceeds the limit, return a text error with the file path, actual size, and the limit — NOT the image data
3. Consider adding provider-aware limits through the facade layer so each provider can set its own max
4. The error message should be informative enough for the LLM to suggest alternatives (e.g., 'use offset/limit to read as text', 'resize the image first')

examples.text: Small PNG (500KB) → Read tool returns ReadOutput::Image normally, no validation error
Large JPEG (8MB raw, ~10.7MB base64) → Read tool returns ToolError::Validation with message containing file path, size '10.7 MB', limit '5.0 MB', and suggestion to resize
Image exactly at 3.75MB raw (~5MB base64) → Read tool returns ReadOutput::Image (boundary case, within limit)
SVG file (10MB XML text) → Read tool treats it as text and returns ReadOutput::Text, NOT ReadOutput::Image — no image size validation applied
Agent reads oversized image, gets error, tries again with different approach (e.g., bash to resize) → agent loop does NOT break, subsequent API calls succeed

rules.text: Read tool must validate image base64 size before returning ReadOutput::Image — if the base64 data exceeds 5MB (the strictest provider limit, shared by Claude and Z.AI), return a ToolError::Validation with an informative message instead of the image data
The error message must include: the file path, the actual base64 size, the limit, and a suggestion to resize the image or read it as text using offset/limit

The validation must happen BEFORE returning the image data, not after — once image data enters ToolResultContent and then conversation history, it cannot be removed and will poison all subsequent API calls
The 5MB limit applies to the raw file bytes (not the base64 string), since base64 encoding inflates size by ~33% — a 3.75MB file becomes ~5MB base64
SVG files should be exempt from image size validation — they are text-based XML and should be handled as text, not as binary image data

Three validation layers (defense-in-depth): Layer 1: Read tool (has raw bytes, most informative error). Layer 2: parse_tool_result_content (has base64, safety net for all tools). Layer 3: stream_loop user images (has base64 from bridge).

Recovery mechanism lives in stream_loop.rs error handler (around line 1379). Pattern: detect is_image_content_error() → pop last user message → call sanitize_image_content(session.messages) which walks messages backward and replaces Image content with text placeholders → emit_error() so the LLM sees what happened → break (session returns to idle, no retry)

EXT-016.description:
EXT-014 was supposed to prevent oversized images from poisoning the conversation history, but it only validates base64 byte size (5MB). The actual error from the Claude API is:

> At least one of the image dimensions exceed max allowed size: 8000 pixels

A full-page screenshot of a news site can be 15,000+ pixels tall while still being under 5MB in base64. EXT-014's size check passes, the image enters conversation history, and the session is irrecoverably broken.

**Two failures in EXT-014:**

1. **Missing pixel dimension validation**: Claude enforces max 8000×8000px per image. The Read tool only checks byte size, not pixel dimensions. Need to decode PNG/JPEG headers to extract width×height before returning ReadOutput::Image.

2. **Wrong defensive layer**: Validation is ONLY in the Read tool, but images enter conversation history through multiple paths:
   - Read tool → ReadOutput::Image → parse_tool_result_content() → ToolResultContent::Image
   - User-pasted images → stream_loop.rs line 438 → UserContent::image_base64()
   - Future MCP tools could return image data
   The LAST line of defense must be in parse_tool_result_content() (rig-core patch streaming.rs) — the chokepoint where all tool results become ToolResultContent. If an image exceeds limits there, replace it with a text error BEFORE it enters the conversation.

**Provider pixel limits:**
- Claude (Anthropic): 8000×8000px (2000×2000 if >20 images), optimal ≤1568px long edge
- OpenAI: Auto-resizes server-side (no hard pixel limit)
- Gemini: 3600 max images per request (no documented pixel limit)
- Z.AI: 6000×6000px

**Implementation plan:**
1. Add pixel dimension extraction from PNG headers (bytes 16-23: width u32 BE, height u32 BE) and JPEG SOF markers in the Read tool — zero external dependencies needed
2. In Read tool FileType::Image branch: after size check, extract dimensions and reject if either exceeds 8000px
3. In parse_tool_result_content(): before calling ToolResultContent::image_base64(), decode enough base64 to read the header and check dimensions — this is the safety net that protects against ALL image sources
4. In stream_loop.rs user image path: validate dimensions before calling UserContent::image_base64()
5. Error messages should suggest resizing (e.g., sips -Z 4000 image.png on macOS)

Corrupt PNG with invalid header → dimension extraction fails gracefully, falls back to allowing the image (don't block valid images just because header parsing failed)

Image exactly 5999×5999px → passes dimension check, proceeds to normal base64 size check (boundary case)
Normal viewport screenshot (1920×1080px, 2MB) → Read tool checks dimensions, both under 5999px, returns ReadOutput::Image normally
API returns 400 for unknown reason → error is shown to the LLM, session returns to idle, user can send next message — no automatic retry

API returns 400 with 'image dimensions exceed max allowed size' → stream_loop detects it's a content-related 400, scans recent messages for image content, replaces ToolResultContent::Image and UserContent::Image with text placeholders, emits the error so the LLM sees what went wrong, session returns to idle

rules.text: parse_tool_result_content() in rig-core streaming.rs must validate image dimensions before calling ToolResultContent::image_base64() — this is the safety net that catches ALL image sources (Read tool, MCP tools, future tools), replacing oversized images with a text error
Read tool must extract pixel dimensions from PNG headers (IHDR chunk at bytes 16-23: width/height as u32 BE) and JPEG SOF markers — no external image crate needed, just raw header parsing
User-pasted images in stream_loop.rs (line 438, UserContent::image_base64) must also be validated for dimensions before entering conversation history

The universal pixel dimension limit must be 5999px (just under 6000) as a safe default — the strictest provider limit is Z.AI GLM-4V at 6000×6000px, OpenAI GPT-5.4 also caps at 6000px in 'original' detail mode, and Claude enforces 8000px. Using 5999 covers all providers safely.

The error message for oversized dimensions must include: file path (if known), actual dimensions (WxH), the limit (5999px), and a suggestion to resize (e.g., sips -Z 4000 image.png on macOS, convert -resize 4000x4000 image.png on Linux)

Images must be validated for pixel dimensions (max 5999px on any side — the lowest common denominator across all supported providers: Z.AI 6000px, Claude 8000px, OpenAI auto-resizes) BEFORE being returned as ReadOutput::Image or converted to ToolResultContent::Image — once in conversation history, they cannot be removed

questions.answer: No. Strategy D should NOT scan src/ automatically. Instead, it should guide the AI agent through a context-driven discovery process: AI provides implementation context → Tool uses foundation.json personas → AI understands user behavior → Creates example maps → Generates features → Generates test skeletons → Links to implementation. This is outside-in BDD, not inside-out code scanning.

questions.answer: Yes. Strategy D should actively prompt with persona-based questions using system-reminders to guide AI thinking. Example: 'WHO uses this? (Check foundation.json personas)' and 'WHAT does [persona] want to accomplish?'. This provides cognitive scaffolding to help AI shift from inside-out code-thinking to outside-in behavior-thinking. Prompts should be guiding (not blocking), conditional on foundation.json existence, and include examples of good persona-driven thinking.
questions.text: @human: When AI provides implementation context (e.g., 'MusicPlayer.tsx has play/pause buttons'), should Strategy D prompt with persona-based questions like 'Which persona from foundation.json uses this feature?' or 'What does [persona] want to accomplish?'

questions.answer: Foundation.json must exist (run 'fspec discover-foundation' if missing as one-time setup). During Strategy D, when persona is needed but missing, prompt AI to add it incrementally via 'fspec add-persona <name> <description> --goal <goal>'. For granular code (APIs, functions), guide AI to identify which human persona BENEFITS (not which system calls it) using system-reminders: 'Not who calls calculateDiscount() but who benefits from accurate discounts? Answer: Shopper'. Skip feature files for pure utilities (formatDate, parseJSON) - test-only coverage.
questions.text: @human: If foundation.json is missing or has no personas, should Strategy D guide AI through creating foundation first via 'fspec discover-foundation', or allow manual persona specification for this reverse session only?

questions.answer: Yes. Strategy D should provide transformation templates via system-reminders to help AI translate implementation → behavior. Templates: (1) UI Elements → User Actions (button → 'User clicks/taps [action]', input → 'User enters [data]'), (2) State → User Expectations (useState → 'User sees [state]', loading → 'User waits for [process]'), (3) API Endpoints → User Needs (POST /orders → 'User completes order'). Templates accelerate mental shift, ensure consistency, and reinforce outside-in thinking.
questions.text: @human: Should Strategy D provide templates or prompts to help AI transform implementation details (buttons, functions, state) into user behavior descriptions (plays song, pauses playback, manages playlist)?

questions.answer: Pause for review with guided prompts. After AI creates example map, Strategy D emits system-reminder with review checklist: 'Do rules cover examples?', 'Are examples concrete?', 'All questions answered?', 'Examples map to personas?'. Then offers explicit choice: (1) Generate features now: fspec generate-scenarios, (2) Add more examples/rules. AI explicitly chooses when to generate (not automatic). Example Mapping is a conversation requiring reflection, not a form-filling exercise. Quality gate prevents garbage-in-garbage-out.
questions.text: @human: After AI creates example maps (rules, examples, questions), should Strategy D automatically generate feature files and test skeletons, or should it prompt AI to review/refine the example map first?

questions.answer: Semi-automatic with educational system-reminder. Strategy D auto-links coverage by default using 'fspec link-coverage --skip-validation' but emits system-reminder showing: (1) What was linked (scenario → test skeleton → implementation), (2) Exact command that was run (educational), (3) How to verify: 'fspec show-coverage', (4) How to fix if wrong: 'fspec unlink-coverage' then re-link manually. Balances low friction (automatic) with transparency (not a black box) and learning (AI sees the mechanism).
questions.text: @human: Should Strategy D guide AI to link test skeletons to existing implementation using 'fspec link-coverage --skip-validation' automatically, or require AI to manually create coverage links?

questions.answer: Feature-scoped sessions (multiple related files allowed). Strategy D allows multiple implementation files in one session if they deliver the SAME user-facing feature. rules.text: Strategy D guides AI agents through outside-in BDD: Context → Personas → User Behavior → Example Maps → Features → Test Skeletons → Implementation Links

Yes. Strategy D should actively prompt with persona-based questions using system-reminders to guide AI thinking. Example: 'WHO uses this? (Check foundation.json personas)' and 'WHAT does [persona] want to accomplish?'. This provides cognitive scaffolding to help AI shift from inside-out code-thinking to outside-in behavior-thinking. Prompts should be guiding (not blocking), conditional on foundation.json existence, and include examples of good persona-driven thinking.

Foundation.json must exist (run 'fspec discover-foundation' if missing as one-time setup). During Strategy D, when persona is needed but missing, prompt AI to add it incrementally via 'fspec add-persona <name> <description> --goal <goal>'. For granular code (APIs, functions), guide AI to identify which human persona BENEFITS (not which system calls it) using system-reminders: 'Not who calls calculateDiscount() but who benefits from accurate discounts? Answer: Shopper'. Skip feature files for pure utilities (formatDate, parseJSON) - test-only coverage.

Yes. Strategy D should provide transformation templates via system-reminders to help AI translate implementation → behavior. Templates: (1) UI Elements → User Actions (button → 'User clicks/taps [action]', input → 'User enters [data]'), (2) State → User Expectations (useState → 'User sees [state]', loading → 'User waits for [process]'), (3) API Endpoints → User Needs (POST /orders → 'User completes order'). Templates accelerate mental shift, ensure consistency, and reinforce outside-in thinking.

Pause for review with guided prompts. After AI creates example map, Strategy D emits system-reminder with review checklist: 'Do rules cover examples?', 'Are examples concrete?', 'All questions answered?', 'Examples map to personas?'. Then offers explicit choice: (1) Generate features now: fspec generate-scenarios, (2) Add more examples/rules. AI explicitly chooses when to generate (not automatic). Example Mapping is a conversation requiring reflection, not a form-filling exercise. Quality gate prevents garbage-in-garbage-out.

Semi-automatic with educational system-reminder. Strategy D auto-links coverage by default using 'fspec link-coverage --skip-validation' but emits system-reminder showing: (1) What was linked (scenario → test skeleton → implementation), (2) Exact command that was run (educational), (3) How to verify: 'fspec show-coverage', (4) How to fix if wrong: 'fspec unlink-coverage' then re-link manually. Balances low friction (automatic) with transparency (not a black box) and learning (AI sees the mechanism).

Feature-scoped sessions (multiple related files allowed). Strategy D allows multiple implementation files in one session if they deliver the SAME user-facing feature. IMPACT ANALYSIS for removing the projectType enum (performed via direct code search, not DeepSearch):

1. ZERO business logic depends on specific projectType values. Searched for projectType === '...', switch statements, case branches, if-checks across all of src/. Only src/commands/update-foundation.ts:163 has `case 'projectType':` which matches the SECTION NAME, not a value.

2. Consumers that read project.projectType:
   - src/commands/show-foundation.ts:130 → `Type: ${foundation.project.projectType || 'N/A'}` — displays verbatim
   - src/commands/discover-foundation.ts:265 → extracts `[DETECTED: X]` placeholder via regex (unaffected by enum removal)
   - src/generators/foundation-md.ts → does NOT reference projectType at all

3. Files that write projectType:
   - src/schemas/generic-foundation.schema.json lines 36-50 (the enum itself — REMOVE)
   - src/types/generic-foundation.ts lines 89-98 (the ProjectType union — CHANGE to `type ProjectType = string`)
   - src/utils/ensure-files.ts:208 (default 'cli-tool' — keep, still valid)
   - src/commands/discover-foundation.ts:127 (system-reminder prompt 'Options:' — change to 'Examples:')
   - src/commands/discover-foundation.ts:588 (placeholder '[DETECTED: cli-tool]' — keep, still valid)
   - src/commands/update-foundation.ts:163-166 (writes the value — ADD length validation)
   - 9 event-storm command files use `projectType: 'other' as const` for default foundation initialization — these keep working; the `as const` assertions become superfluous but remain valid TypeScript

4. Test fixtures: ~60 occurrences of `projectType: 'cli-tool'` (or 'web-app', 'library', etc.) across test files. All continue to work unchanged because these values are still valid strings.

5. Tests that specifically assert enum membership:
   - src/types/__tests__/foundation-schema.test.ts lines 129-140: tests `validProjectTypes: ProjectType[] = [...]`. NEEDS UPDATE — replace with test that any short string validates, plus minLength/maxLength boundary tests.

6. No test currently asserts that an invalid projectType enum value is rejected at schema level — verified via grep for 'projectType.*invalid|reject.*projectType'. Zero matches. So no negative tests to remove.

CONCLUSION: Removing the enum is a low-blast-radius change. Only 3 source files and 1 test file need modification (plus new tests for length-limit behavior). The remaining ~60 test fixtures work without modification.

FOUND-044.description:
Improve the foundation discovery workflow feedback loop so weaker LLMs (and humans) get immediate, actionable feedback, while also relaxing the overly-restrictive projectType enum that blocked valid project categories like 'saas-platform' and 'browser-extension'.

This addresses the friction documented in foundation-workflow-analysis.md where a 5-minute foundation setup became a 35-minute debugging session because `projectType: 'web-saas'` was silently accepted by `update-foundation` and only rejected at finalization with a misleading 'Missing required' error.

== Schema change (NEW - primary fix) ==

Change `projectType` from a 9-value enum to a freeform short string. Rationale: the enum values are purely descriptive metadata — ZERO code paths in src/ branch on specific projectType values (verified via exhaustive search). The constraint was input validation, not business logic. Relaxing it removes the original user's bug entirely (web-saas becomes valid).

Files affected:
- src/schemas/generic-foundation.schema.json lines 36-50: remove `enum`, add `minLength: 1`, `maxLength: 30`
- src/types/generic-foundation.ts lines 89-98: replace `ProjectType` union with `type ProjectType = string`
- src/commands/discover-foundation.ts line 127: change system-reminder from `Options:` to `Examples:` with a note that it's non-exhaustive and any short descriptor is valid
- src/types/__tests__/foundation-schema.test.ts lines 129-140: update to test that any short string validates, plus maxLength boundary
- Test fixtures (~60 occurrences of 'cli-tool' etc.) continue to work unchanged
- 9 event-storm command files use `projectType: 'other' as const` — these keep working; the `as const` assertions become superfluous but remain valid
- src/generators/foundation-md.ts does NOT use projectType at all — no change needed
- src/commands/show-foundation.ts line 130 displays the value verbatim — no change needed

== Remaining improvements ==

1. **Length-limit validation in `update-foundation`** — Extend `updateJsonField()` to validate `projectType` against `1 ≤ length ≤ 30` at write time. Error: `Invalid projectType: "<value>" (must be 1-30 characters, got <N>). Fix: fspec update-foundation projectType "<short-descriptor>"`.

2. **Fail-fast validation for `problemImpact`** — problemImpact remains a real enum (high/medium/low). Validate at write time with the actionable error format.

3. **`show-foundation --draft` flag** — Add `--draft` option to read `spec/foundation.json.draft`. Error clearly if draft doesn't exist.

4. **Improve `update-foundation` help text** — Change description from 'Update section content in FOUNDATION.md' to 'Update a field in foundation.json (or foundation.json.draft during discovery)'. Enumerate complete section list with no 'etc.' Note capabilities/personas use dedicated commands.

5. **Better 'draft exists' error message** — When `discover-foundation` detects an existing draft, offer three valid next steps (`--finalize`, `show-foundation --draft`, `--force`). Hard error with wrapped system-reminder, no draft content inline.

6. **Ajv enum/length error formatting at finalization** — Extend error formatter in `discover-foundation.ts` lines 336-365 to detect `err.keyword === 'enum'` AND `err.keyword === 'maxLength'`/`minLength` and emit actionable messages distinguishing invalid values from missing fields.

7. **`list-foundation-sections` standalone command** — First-class discovery mechanism for section names with JSON paths and constraints. For `projectType` shows `freeform string (1-30 characters), examples: cli-tool, web-app, saas-platform`. For `problemImpact` shows the real enum: `high, medium, low`.

CRITICAL CONSTRAINT: 100% deterministic behavior. NO fuzzy/semantic matching anywhere. No Levenshtein distance, no 'did you mean' suggestions, no similarity scoring on user input. All error messages list valid values or constraints verbatim.

See foundation-workflow-analysis.md in project root for full analysis with line-level source references.

GIT-014.description:
Add git worktree primitives for session isolation using pure gitoxide.

## Purpose

When multiple sessions work on the same codebase in parallel, they need filesystem isolation to avoid conflicts. Worktrees provide:
- Separate working directories sharing the same git object store
- Each session can have dirty state without affecting others
- Efficient storage (only working files duplicated, not .git)

## Scope (Primitives Only)

This card provides the low-level worktree operations:
- create_worktree(session_id, commit_ref) -> WorktreeInfo
- remove_worktree(session_id) -> Result
- list_worktrees() -> Vec<WorktreeInfo>

## Out of Scope (Handled Elsewhere)

- BackgroundSession integration (caller's responsibility)
- effective_cwd() method (caller's responsibility)
- Orphan cleanup (GIT-018 Session Manager)
- Merge/patch application (GIT-015)

## Optional Feature

Worktree isolation is opt-in:
- Enabled: Parallel sessions, experimental work
- Disabled: Single foreground session, read-only watchers

See: docs/architecture/multi-session-git.md

GIT-015.description:
Collect changes from session worktrees and apply them to the main worktree.

## Simplified Scope

We don't need complex git merge operations. Session worktrees use detached HEAD, so when a session completes:
1. Collect diff between session's base commit and current HEAD
2. Present diff to user for review
3. Apply changes to main worktree via git apply
4. Clean up session worktree

## Implementation

1. Add diff() method to SessionWorktree (base_commit..HEAD)
2. Add complete() method that returns SessionResult with diff
3. Add abort() method for discarding session changes
4. Add apply_session_changes() to apply patch to main worktree
5. Handle conflicts with clear error messages

## No Git Merge

This is intentionally NOT a git merge:
- User decides what to keep
- Conflicts are visible in the patch
- No merge commits created
- Clean and predictable

See: docs/architecture/multi-session-git.md

Applying session changes removes deleted files from main worktree

GIT-016.description:
Parent story controlling the migration from isomorphic-git (TypeScript) to gitoxide (gix) - a pure Rust git implementation.

## Migration Strategy

**Phase 1 - Foundation (GIT-013):** Replace isomorphic-git with gitoxide via NAPI bindings
**Phase 2 - Snapshots (GIT-017):** Replace stash-based checkpoints with ghost commits
**Phase 3 - Session Isolation (GIT-014):** Add worktree creation for BackgroundSession isolation
**Phase 4 - Session Completion (GIT-015):** Collect session changes and apply to main worktree

## Architecture

- **gitoxide (gix)**: Pure Rust git implementation, no external git binary needed
- **Ghost commits**: Point-in-time snapshots within a worktree (undo/restore)
- **Worktrees**: Filesystem isolation for parallel sessions
- **NAPI bindings**: codelet/git crate exposes Rust APIs to TypeScript

See: docs/architecture/multi-session-git.md

GIT-017.description:
Replace stash-based checkpoints with ghost commits (detached commit objects).

## What are Ghost Commits?

Ghost commits are detached git commits that:
- Capture complete working tree state (tracked + untracked files)
- Have no branch reference (invisible to git log)
- Preserve parent relationship to HEAD
- Can be restored to return to exact state
- Are auto garbage collected by git after ~2 weeks if unreferenced

## Implementation

1. Create temporary index (GIT_INDEX_FILE=/tmp/index) to avoid disturbing user's staging area
2. Read-tree HEAD into temp index
3. Add all changes to temp index
4. git write-tree to create tree object
5. git commit-tree to create detached commit (no ref update)
6. Store ghost commit SHA in checkpoint metadata
7. Restore via git restore --source <sha> --worktree .

## Migration

- Replace src/utils/git-checkpoint.ts stash operations with ghost commits
- Update TUI CheckpointViewer to work with ghost commits
- Maintain same TypeScript API surface for existing consumers

See: docs/architecture/multi-session-git.md

GIT-018.description:
Integrate git worktree isolation into BackgroundSession and provide management UI.

## Problem

GIT-014/015/017 created worktree and ghost commit PRIMITIVES, but nothing connects them to BackgroundSession. Sessions don't use worktrees, so there's nothing to manage.

## Solution

This card bridges the gap with two parts:

### Part A: Integration Layer

1. Add `isolated: bool` parameter to session creation
2. When isolated=true, create worktree via GIT-014 primitives
3. Track worktree info (path, base_commit) in session
4. Implement `effective_cwd()` → worktree path if isolated, else project root
5. Connect ghost commits (GIT-017) to session checkpoint operations
6. On session end: leave worktree for review (don't auto-cleanup)

### Part B: Management Layer

1. `list_sessions(filter?)` → derive status from active sessions + worktrees
2. `inspect_session(id)` → get diff without side effects
3. `merge_session(id)` → apply changes to main, remove worktree
4. `discard_session(id)` → remove worktree without applying
5. `prune_orphaned()` → clean worktrees with no session record

## Status Derivation (computed, not stored)

- `active` = session ID in BackgroundSession's active map
- `pending_merge` = worktree exists + NOT active + has changes
- `clean` = worktree exists + NOT active + no changes
- `orphaned` = worktree exists + no session record anywhere

## See Also

- Architecture: docs/architecture/multi-session-git.md
- Analysis: spec/attachments/GIT-018/architecture-analysis-and-scope.md

GIT-020.description:
CRITICAL BUG FIX: Isolated session file isolation is TOO RESTRICTIVE.

Current broken behavior:
- Blocks ALL paths outside the worktree (including /tmp, /Users/rquast/Desktop/, etc.)

Correct behavior:
- ALLOW paths within the worktree
- BLOCK paths within the ORIGINAL PROJECT DIRECTORY (that the worktree was created from)
- ALLOW all other paths (like /tmp, /Users/rquast/Desktop/, etc.)

The session stores both:
- `project: String` - the original project path
- `worktree_path: Option<PathBuf>` - the worktree path

The fix requires:
1. Pass BOTH worktree_path AND project_root to path validation
2. Change validation logic to only BLOCK original project, not everything outside worktree

GIT-028.description:
GIT-019 was marked done but the critical NAPI binding to actually create isolated sessions was never implemented.

## Problem

BackgroundSession has the fields ready:
- `worktree_path: Option<PathBuf>`
- `base_commit: Option<String>`
- `effective_cwd()` method

But there's no NAPI binding to create a session with `isolated=true`. The existing bindings don't accept an isolation parameter:
- `session_manager_create(model, project)`
- `session_manager_create_with_id(session_id, model, project, name)`

## Solution

Add `session_manager_create_isolated()` NAPI binding that:
1. Creates worktree via `create_worktree()` from codelet-git
2. Creates session manifest via `create_session_manifest()`
3. Creates BackgroundSession with `worktree_path` and `base_commit` populated
4. Returns session info including worktree path

## Tests

Must have actual TypeScript tests calling the NAPI binding, not just Rust source-code-grep tests.

GIT-033.description:
The @file search popup in MultiLineInput currently always searches the current working directory, without considering session isolation state.

## Problem

When a user types `@auth` in an isolated session:
- The popup searches the project root (where the TUI was started)
- But AI tools operate in `.fspec/worktrees/<session-id>/`

This means:
- User can't find files the AI created in the worktree
- User might reference files that don't exist in the worktree
- Confusing UX disconnect between what user sees and where AI works

## Solution

Reuse existing functions to check session isolation:

1. Pass sessionId to `useFileSearchInput` hook
2. Call `sessionGetEffectiveCwd(sessionId)` NAPI function which:
   - Returns worktree path for isolated sessions
   - Returns project root for non-isolated sessions
3. Pass that path to `callGlobTool(pattern, effectiveCwd, true)`
4. Handle fallback when no session exists yet (use project root)

## Existing Functions to Reuse

- `sessionGetEffectiveCwd(sessionId: string): string | null` - already in NAPI, returns effective cwd
- `sessionIsIsolated(sessionId: string): boolean | null` - checks if session has worktree

## Files to Modify

- `src/tui/hooks/useFileSearchInput.ts` - Accept sessionId, call sessionGetEffectiveCwd NAPI
- `src/tui/components/AgentView.tsx` - Pass sessionId to hook

architectureNotes.text:
Slash command handler in AgentView.tsx handleSubmit (~line 3095). Pattern: check `userMessage === '/merge-worktree'`, clear input via setInputValue('').

Flow:
1. Check `isIsolated` from useIsIsolated() sessionStore hook
   - If false → setConversation type:'status' error "This command is only available in isolated sessions", return
2. Call inspectSessionChanges(currentProjectRef.current, currentSessionId) → SessionResultJs
   - SessionResultJs: { filesChanged[], filesAdded[], filesDeleted[], diff, baseCommit }
   - If all three arrays empty → setConversation type:'status' "Nothing to merge", return (session stays open per rule [9])
3. Call mergeSessionChanges(currentProjectRef.current, currentSessionId) → MergeResultJs
   - MergeResultJs: { sessionId, filesModified[], filesAdded[], filesDeleted[] }
   - On success:
     a. Show merge summary via setConversation type:'status' (e.g. "✓ Merged: 3 modified, 1 added, 0 deleted")
     b. Close session: cleanupCurrentSessionHandler() → await destroySession(currentSessionId) → onExit()
   - On error:
     a. Check if error.message contains 'Conflict'
     b. If conflict → parse file list from error, show via setConversation type:'status', session stays open
     c. If non-conflict error → show generic error message, session stays open

Underlying Rust merge algorithm (codelet_git::merge_session in session_status.rs):
1. get_session_diff(repo_path, session_id) → compares base_commit tree vs worktree working directory to capture filesChanged, filesAdded, filesDeleted
2. apply_session_changes(repo_path, session_id) → detects conflicts by comparing base_tree vs worktree_files vs main_files. Conflict = file modified in BOTH session and main since base_commit, OR new file in session that exists in main with different content. On no conflicts: copies modified/added files to main workdir, removes deleted files, removes worktree dir. On conflict: throws GitError::ConflictError { files: Vec<String> } with worktree intact.
3. delete_manifest(session_id) → removes ~/.fspec/git-sessions/<session-id>.json

Conflict error format (as it reaches TypeScript): "Conflict detected: [\"file1.ts\", \"file2.ts\"] have been modified in both session and main worktree"

Note: mergeSession() removes the worktree on success. destroySession() separately destroys the Rust BackgroundSession, detaches work unit, clears sessionStore, and unsubscribes from stream. Both cleanups are needed.

architectureNotes.text:
Generic 'action prompt' mechanism threaded through the component stack:

1. ActionPrompt interface:
   interface ActionPrompt { message: string; onConfirm: () => void | Promise<void> }
   Note: onConfirm may be async (e.g. destroySession). The handler must await it.

2. AgentView state:
   const [actionPrompt, setActionPrompt] = useState<ActionPrompt | null>(null)
   Passes actionPrompt + setActionPrompt to both InputTransition and the merge handler context.

3. InputTransition new prop:
   actionPrompt?: ActionPrompt | null
   Also receives: clearActionPrompt: () => void (bound to setActionPrompt(null) in AgentView)

4. InputTransition rendering (when actionPrompt is set):
   <Text color='green'>✓ {actionPrompt.message}</Text> <Text dimColor>(Press Enter or Esc to close)</Text>

5. InputTransition keyboard handler (useInputCompat, priority MEDIUM):
   Enter or Escape → await actionPrompt.onConfirm(), then clearActionPrompt()
   All other keys → consumed (blocked)
   The auto-clear ensures the prompt is always cleaned up, whether onConfirm unmounts the component or not. Future callers that don't unmount get correct behavior for free.

6. MultiLineInput does NOT need changes — InputTransition short-circuits rendering before reaching MultiLineInput when actionPrompt is active (same pattern as isPaused).

7. Rendering priority (early return order in InputTransition):
   isPaused && pauseInfo → existing pause rendering
   actionPrompt → NEW action prompt rendering
   animationPhase === 'loading' → existing loading/compaction
   ... rest of existing animation phases
   isPaused takes precedence over actionPrompt. In practice they should never overlap (no tool calls during slash commands), but the ordering is safe if they do.

Rich merge summary format (added to conversation before action prompt):

✓ Merge successful

  Modified (3):
    src/auth/login.ts
    src/auth/register.ts
    src/utils/helpers.ts

  Added (1):
    src/auth/types.ts

  Deleted (0)

Conflict summary format:

⚠ Merge conflicts detected

  Conflicting files:
    src/auth/login.ts
    src/utils/helpers.ts

  These files were modified in both this session and the main worktree.
  Resolve the conflicts, then run /merge-worktree again.

Data sources: MergeResultJs.filesModified/Added/Deleted for success.

Conflict file parsing: The Rust error format uses Debug trait on Vec<String>: 'Conflict detected: ["file1.ts", "file2.ts"] have been modified in both session and main worktree'. Parse with best-effort regex to extract file paths. If parsing fails (e.g. Rust format changes), fall back to displaying the raw error.message — this is a known coupling with Rust's thiserror/Debug output and graceful degradation is acceptable.

InputTransition.tsx changes:

New props:
  actionPrompt?: { message: string; onConfirm: () => void | Promise<void> } | null
  clearActionPrompt?: () => void

Rendering priority (early return order, BEFORE loading/animation phases):
  1. isPaused && pauseInfo → existing pause rendering (unchanged)
  2. actionPrompt → NEW action prompt rendering (green message + dimColor hint)
  3. animationPhase === 'loading' → existing loading/compaction (unchanged)
  4. ... rest of existing animation phases (unchanged)

Keyboard handler: Register via useInputCompat when actionPrompt is active, priority MEDIUM.
  Enter or Escape → await actionPrompt.onConfirm(), then clearActionPrompt()
  All other keys → consumed (blocked), return true

The handler must guard against double-invocation (user presses Enter twice fast). Use a local ref isClosing to prevent re-entry:
  const isClosingRef = useRef(false);
  if (isClosingRef.current) return true;
  isClosingRef.current = true;
  await actionPrompt.onConfirm();
  clearActionPrompt?.();

Note: The await in the keyboard handler requires the handler function to be async. useInputCompat's handler type supports this — same pattern as other async handlers in the codebase.

GIT-037.description:
Improve the /merge-worktree UX so that successful merges don't immediately destroySession() and onExit() — the user never sees the merge summary because the view switches to BoardView instantly. Instead:

1. On successful merge: show a rich file-by-file summary in the conversation, then put the InputTransition into a new 'action prompt' state showing '✓ Merge complete — Press Enter to close session'. Only when the user presses Enter does the cleanup/destroy/exit sequence run.

2. On conflict: show a detailed, color-coded conflict summary in the conversation with guidance ('Resolve conflicts in this session, then run /merge-worktree again'), and return the input to normal mode.

3. On 'nothing to merge': current behavior is fine (shows message, session stays open).

This requires changes to:
- mergeWorktreeHandler.ts: Don't call cleanup/destroy/exit synchronously. Instead, set an 'action prompt' state that defers the exit.
- InputTransition.tsx: Add a new render path for 'action prompt' state (like isPaused but for merge-complete or other deferred actions).
- AgentView.tsx: Wire up the new action prompt state and the Enter-to-close callback.

Note: MultiLineInput.tsx does NOT need changes — InputTransition short-circuits rendering before reaching MultiLineInput when actionPrompt is active (same pattern as isPaused).

architectureNotes.text: In mergeWorktreeHandler.ts, when a conflict error is caught, AFTER calling addStatusMessage() for the TUI display, call ctx.injectLlmContext(buildConflictLlmContext(errorMessage, ctx.worktreePath)). The injectLlmContext callback in AgentView.tsx sets inputValue to the conflict message and flags pendingAutoSubmitRef=true. A useEffect watching [inputValue, handleSubmit] fires on the next render and calls handleSubmit(), which sends the message to the Rust session via sessionSendInput — the normal user message flow. The LLM then receives the conflict details as real user input and can act on it.

CRITICAL: persistenceAppendMessage only writes to disk (SQLite persistence layer). The live Rust session never sees it. The conflict message MUST go through sessionSendInput (the normal user input path) so the Rust agent loop processes it. The earlier approach of calling persistenceAppendMessage was fundamentally broken — the LLM had zero awareness of the conflicts because the message never reached the in-memory session.

GIT-038.description:
When /merge-worktree detects conflicts, the conflict summary (file list + guidance) is shown as a UI status message in the conversation view, but the LLM has no awareness of it because status messages don't reach the Rust session.

The fix: when merge conflicts are detected in mergeWorktreeHandler.ts, AFTER showing the visual status message, send a user message to the Rust session (via the normal handleSubmit → sessionSendInput path) containing the conflict details. The LLM receives this as real user input and can immediately read the conflicting files, resolve the conflict markers, and tell the user to run /merge-worktree again.

This uses the injectLlmContext callback which sets inputValue and flags pendingAutoSubmitRef, causing handleSubmit to fire on the next React render cycle.

rules.text: When /merge-worktree detects conflicts, the conflict details (file list, worktree path, resolution instructions) MUST be sent as a user message to the Rust session via sessionSendInput so the LLM can act on it — not just shown as a TUI status message.
The conflict message must include the worktree path so the LLM knows where to find the conflicting files (isolated sessions operate in a different working directory than the main project).
The conflict message must mention git conflict markers (<<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>>) and instruct the LLM to read each file, resolve the markers, and run /merge-worktree again after resolving.

The conflict context is sent as a user-role message via the normal handleSubmit → sessionSendInput path, not via persistenceAppendMessage or any direct NAPI injection. This ensures the Rust agent loop processes it like any other user turn.
The visual TUI status message (formatted conflict summary for the user's eyes) remains unchanged — the user message to the LLM is an ADDITIONAL action, not a replacement.
Only conflict errors trigger the user message to the LLM — successful merges, 'nothing to merge', and non-conflict errors do NOT send any message to the Rust session.

GIT-040.description:
Eliminate the worker_threads-based diff-worker.ts system by moving all diff computation to Rust via NAPI bindings. This removes the separately-bundled diff-worker.js file which is incompatible with Node.js SEA (Single Executable Application) mode, eliminates the last git CLI dependency (execSync git show), and simplifies the build pipeline.

## Current Problem

1. **SEA Incompatibility**: diff-worker.js is bundled separately by esbuild and loaded at runtime via `new Worker(path)`. In SEA mode, this file doesn't exist on the filesystem, causing MODULE_NOT_FOUND.
2. **git CLI dependency**: `getCheckpointFileDiff()` in diff.ts still uses `execSync('git show ...')` — the only remaining git CLI usage.
3. **Build complexity**: A separate esbuild step is needed just for the worker, plus worker-path.ts resolution logic.
4. **worker_threads overhead**: The worker was needed when diffing was slow JS; with Rust/gitoxide it's fast enough for direct synchronous NAPI calls.

## Solution

1. Add `get_checkpoint_file_diff(dir, filepath, checkpoint_ref)` to codelet-git (Rust)
2. Add NAPI binding for the new function
3. Replace Worker-based diff loading in FileDiffViewer.tsx and CheckpointViewer.tsx with direct NAPI calls
4. Delete: diff-worker.ts, worker-path.ts, worker-path-resolution.test.tsx
5. Remove the esbuild diff-worker step from package.json build script
6. Update the SEA build script (no longer needs to handle diff-worker)

questions.answer: Sequential execution only. Hooks for the same event run one after another in the order defined in fspec-hooks.json. This provides predictable execution order, easier debugging, and allows later hooks to depend on earlier hooks' side effects.

questions.answer: No skip mechanism. When a blocking hook fails, the command is blocked and the user must fix the issue. To bypass a hook, the user must edit spec/fspec-hooks.json to remove or disable it (more intentional than a flag). This maintains discipline and ensures hooks enforce their intended policies.

questions.answer: Always run for all work units. No matcher system. This keeps the framework simple and predictable. If users need conditional execution, they can implement it inside their hook scripts by reading the work unit context and exiting early if conditions aren't met.

questions.answer: Default timeout is 60 seconds (matching Claude Code). Hooks can override with 'timeout' field in fspec-hooks.json. Global default can be set in 'global.timeout'. When timeout is exceeded, the hook process is killed and an error is returned.

questions.answer: Plain stdout/stderr only. Exit code determines success (0) or failure (non-zero). Hook output is displayed as-is to the user. If blocking hook fails (exit != 0), fspec shows stderr in a system-reminder block for AI agent consumption. This keeps hooks simple and works with any tool.

questions.answer: No dry-run mode. Users can use 'fspec list-hooks' to see configured hooks and 'fspec validate-hooks' to validate configuration syntax. To test a hook, users can temporarily make it non-blocking or run it manually outside of fspec.

questions.answer: No chaining for any hooks. All hooks (event hooks and exit hooks) receive the original context/output via stdin. Hooks execute sequentially but independently for side effects (validation, logging, notifications). The original command output is returned to the user unchanged by hooks.
questions.text: @human: Should we support hook chaining where one hook's output becomes the next hook's input?

questions.answer: Hooks inherit the parent process environment naturally (as spawned child processes). fspec does NOT set custom FSPEC_* environment variables. Hooks receive all context via stdin as JSON. Hooks are independent programs that manage their own environment.

questions.answer: Support optional conditions in hook configuration. Hooks can specify 'condition' object with fields like 'tags', 'prefix', 'epic', 'estimateMin', 'estimateMax'. If condition doesn't match, hook is skipped. If no condition specified, hook always runs. This allows context-aware hooks without requiring logic in every script.
questions.text: @human: Should we support hook conditions (e.g., only run if estimate > 5 points, or only for @critical tagged features)?

questions.answer: Support hooks for ANY fspec command using convention: 'pre-<command-name>' and 'post-<command-name>'. Examples: pre-create-work-unit, post-add-rule, pre-link-coverage, post-generate-scenarios. Plus special lifecycle hooks: pre-start (before any command) and pre-exit (before returning output). questions.text: @human: Do you want hooks for non-transition events like create-work-unit, add-dependency, or link-coverage?
