LCP-001.description: Define the foundational data model for Local Change Protocols. Design the @LCP structured comment block grammar in a language-agnostic format (supporting JS/TS block comments, Python/Ruby hash comments, Rust doc comments, etc). Define the lcp-registry.json schema with two distinct sections: (1) risk zone configuration (manually managed glob patterns per risk level) and (2) protected files cache (derived from scanning source files). Write JSON Schema (Ajv) for registry validation. This story produces the SPECIFICATION only — no parser implementation.
LCP-001.title: LCP Data Model and Registry

LCP-002.description: Implement the @LCP comment block parser that extracts structured LCP data from source files across all supported languages (TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Rust, Ruby, Go, Java, C, C++). Implement the scan-lcp command that walks the codebase, parses all @LCP blocks, and builds/updates the protectedFiles section of lcp-registry.json. Support incremental scanning (only changed files via git diff). Detect orphaned registry entries where the source file was deleted. Implement show-lcp command to display all LCP-protected files with their constraints (text and JSON output), with optional --file flag for single-file display.
LCP-002.title: LCP Parser, Scanner, and Display

LCP-003.description: Implement commands for managing risk zone classifications: add-risk-zone, remove-risk-zone, show-risk-zones. Store risk zone configuration in lcp-registry.json with glob-based path matching for zone membership. Integrate with fspec's tag system by mapping zones to @risk-high, @risk-medium, and @risk-low tags. High-risk zones require LCP blocks; medium-risk zones recommend them; low-risk zones allow automated refactors.
LCP-003.title: Risk Zone Management

LCP-004.description: Implement validate-lcp command for structural validation of all @LCP blocks: correct YAML-like syntax, required fields present (scope, risk_level), valid risk level values, at least one constraint for high-risk files, verification commands reference real scripts. Implement audit-lcp command for completeness checking: find all files in high-risk zones missing @LCP blocks, warn for medium-risk zone files without LCP, report orphaned LCPs (files with @LCP not in any risk zone). Implement audit-lcp --fix to generate minimal skeleton @LCP blocks for compliance (not the full interactive init — that is LCP-008). Integrate LCP validation into the existing fspec check pipeline. Support both text and JSON output formats.
LCP-004.title: LCP Validation and Audit

LCP-005.description: Implement verify-lcp command that executes the verification commands listed in @LCP blocks for changed files. Detect which files changed using git diff integration. Only run verification for LCP-protected files that were modified. Leverage fspec's existing process spawning infrastructure (the hook execution engine pattern) for command execution and timeout handling rather than building a new execution engine. Report pass/fail per file per verification command. Support verifying a single file (--file flag) or all changed LCP files.
LCP-005.title: LCP Verification Engine

LCP-006.description: Integrate LCP enforcement into fspec's two-layer hook architecture. TypeScript layer: add LCP verification as a configurable pre-validating workflow hook in fspec-hooks.json, auto-suggest virtual hooks when a work unit touches files in high-risk zones, block implementing-to-validating transition if LCP verification fails. Rust agent core layer: provide a pre_tool_use hook script that checks LCP constraints before Write/Edit/ApplyPatch tools are allowed to modify protected files — this is the hard enforcement path that physically prevents AI agents from changing constrained code without running verification. Both layers use the existing hook configuration schema in fspec-hooks.json.
LCP-006.title: LCP Workflow Enforcement

LCP-007.description: Inject LCP constraints into AI agent context when interacting with protected files. Two integration points: (1) TypeScript fspec CLI layer — when fspec commands produce output about LCP-protected files, append system-reminder blocks with risk level, constraints, review requirements, and verification commands. (2) Rust agent core layer — configure session_start or pre_tool_use hooks to inject LCP context so agents have continuous awareness of constraints, not just at command output time. Format LCP data for optimal AI consumption: explicit DO NOT CHANGE directives, required verification commands, risk level warnings. Include risk zone context from LCP-003.
LCP-007.title: LCP System Reminder and Agent Guidance

LCP-008.description: Implement init-lcp command for interactive LCP block generation. Support generating LCP from work unit architecture notes (--from-work-unit flag). Support generating LCP blocks for all files matching a risk zone (--zone flag). Insert correctly-formatted comment blocks into target files using the appropriate language-specific comment syntax detected from file extension. Unlike audit-lcp --fix (which generates minimal skeleton blocks for compliance), init-lcp produces context-aware blocks with meaningful scope, constraints, and verification commands derived from the project context.
LCP-008.title: LCP Scaffold and Init

LIMITS-001.description:
Parent story for fixing the broken CTX-005 epic. The current architecture has a critical bug: ProviderManager::select_model() unconditionally stores models.dev registry values into model_context_window, which shadows provider compile-time constants. For Claude Opus 4.6, this means models.dev's 1M context is used instead of Claude's hardcoded 200k (the 1M beta header isn't even sent), making the badge show [968k] and compaction never trigger before API rejection.

**Root Causes:**
1. select_model() unconditionally overwrites model_context_window with models.dev data — provider constants become dead code
2. No provider veto mechanism — providers cannot clamp or override registry values
3. Context window resolution is fragmented across 6 providers with inconsistent patterns
4. Codex constants are hardcoded guesses (272k) for all models
5. max_output_tokens has the same override problem
6. Compaction threshold receives wrong inputs and produces wrong results

**Solution:**
1. LIMITS-001: Create ModelLimitsResolver trait giving providers veto/clamp authority
2. LIMITS-002: Implement trait for all 6 providers with correct limits
3. LIMITS-003: Fix ProviderManager resolution chain to use resolver
4. LIMITS-004: Fix compaction threshold to use corrected context_window
5. LIMITS-005: Fix badge and fill% display chain
6. LIMITS-006: Integration testing with all provider/model combinations

The trait extends LlmProvider (or is composed with it), not a separate trait hierarchy — providers implement one trait that covers both runtime operations and limits

LIMITS-002.description:
Create a ModelLimitsResolver trait that each provider implements to declare its hard limits. This gives providers the authority to clamp or override values from external registries (models.dev, Copilot API).

The trait provides:
- max_context_window(): Option<usize> — the provider's hard ceiling (e.g., Claude returns Some(200_000) until CONFIG-007 opt-in)
- max_output_tokens_limit(): Option<usize> — the provider's hard max output ceiling
- default_context_window(): usize — fallback when no registry data
- default_max_output_tokens(): usize — fallback when no registry data

The resolution function takes (registry_value, user_override, provider) and applies: user_override → clamp by provider max → registry_value → clamp by provider max → provider default.

This is a Rust-only change in codelet/providers/src/.

examples.text: Claude resolver with max_context_window=Some(200_000): registry says 1M → resolve returns 200k (clamped)
OpenAI resolver with max_context_window=None: registry says 128k → resolve returns 128k (trusted)
User override of 500k on Claude (max 200k): resolve returns 200k (user override clamped by provider max)
No registry data, no user override for Codex: resolve returns 272k (provider default)
OPENAI_CONTEXT_WINDOW env var set to 256000: OpenAI resolver uses this as the env-derived default, overriding compile-time 128k
Codex resolver returns should_send_max_output_tokens()=false — API rejects this parameter

rules.text: The trait must provide max_context_window() returning Option<usize> — providers return Some(limit) to clamp, None to trust registry
The trait must provide max_output_tokens_limit() returning Option<usize> — same semantics as max_context_window()
The trait must provide default_context_window() and default_max_output_tokens() — used when no registry data exists

A standalone resolve_model_limits(registry_value, user_override, resolver) function must implement the priority chain: user_override → clamp by provider max → registry → clamp by provider max → default
The trait must live in codelet/providers/src/ as a new file (model_limits.rs) — it is part of the provider abstraction, not the CLI
The trait should optionally provide should_send_max_output_tokens() -> bool (default true) — Codex needs to return false since its API rejects max_output_tokens
Env var overrides (OPENAI_CONTEXT_WINDOW, etc.) must be handled inside the resolver, not scattered across provider constructors and manager fallbacks

LIMITS-003.description:
Implement the ModelLimitsResolver trait for each provider:

1. **Claude** — max_context_window = Some(200_000), max_output_tokens_limit = Some(8_192). Until CONFIG-007 (1M opt-in) is implemented, Claude MUST clamp to 200k regardless of what models.dev reports. When CONFIG-007 lands, this becomes Some(1_000_000) for Tier 4 users.

2. **OpenAI** — max_context_window = None (trusts registry), defaults = 128k/4k. Env var overrides (OPENAI_CONTEXT_WINDOW, OPENAI_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS) become part of the resolver, not scattered across provider constructor + manager fallback.

3. **Gemini** — max_context_window = None (trusts registry), defaults = 1M/8k. Gemini's API genuinely supports the advertised context window.

4. **Codex** — max_context_window = None, defaults = 272k/4k. The max_output_tokens field should NOT be sent to API (Codex rejects it). Add a should_send_max_output() method returning false.

5. **Z.AI** — max_context_window = None, defaults = 128k/8k. Straightforward implementation.

6. **Copilot** — max_context_window = None, defaults = 200k/4k. Gets real limits from live /models endpoint which feeds into registry path.

Each implementation must have unit tests verifying the clamp behavior.

LIMITS-004.description:
Refactor ProviderManager to use the ModelLimitsResolver trait instead of the current fragmented resolution.

**Current broken flow:**
select_model() → stores models.dev value unclamped → context_window() returns it → provider constant is dead code

**New flow:**
select_model() → stores models.dev value → context_window() resolves via ModelLimitsResolver → provider can clamp

**Changes:**
1. ProviderManager::context_window() must call resolve_model_limits() which applies the resolver's clamp
2. ProviderManager::max_output_tokens() same treatment
3. select_model() can continue storing raw registry values, but resolution clamps them
4. set_model_direct() (Codex/profile path) works the same way — resolver clamps user values too
5. override_model_limits() (NAPI path) — user overrides are clamped by provider max
6. Remove the scattered env var reads from provider_constant_context_window() — move them into the resolver
7. Remove the duplicate env var reads from OpenAI provider constructor

**Critical invariant:** After this change, context_window() for Claude Opus 4.6 MUST return 200,000 (not 1,000,000), and compaction threshold MUST be ~192k (not 968k).

This is a Rust change in codelet/providers/src/manager.rs.

GPT-4o: select_model stores 128k → context_window() returns 128k (no clamp needed, OpenAI trusts registry)

DeepSearch sub-agent inherits parent's clamped context_window (200k for Claude), not the raw 1M

architectureNotes.text: Combine nanobrowser's full-page DOM tree building (buildDomTree.js ~1500 LOC injected into page) with LocatorKit's precision selector ranking. Key architecture: (1) Inject JS into page via CDP to walk DOM, detect interactivity, assign highlight indices. (2) Build structured tree with DOMElementNode/DOMTextNode classes. (3) Generate ranked selectors per element with match count validation. (4) Return token-efficient tree representation to LLM. Reference implementations: nanobrowser/chrome-extension/public/buildDomTree.js and LocatorKit/contentScript.js

Nanobrowser's interactivity detection is the most comprehensive found: checks cursor style (30+ cursor types), HTML tag semantics, ARIA roles, event listeners (getEventListeners + fallback to onclick attributes), heuristic signals (class names like btn/clickable, data-toggle attributes), and contenteditable. Also handles nested interactive elements via isElementDistinctInteraction() to avoid double-highlighting parent+child.

LocatorKit's selector generation is best-in-class for stability: ranks candidates by source (data-testid > id > aria-label/role > class > nth-of-type > fallback), validates uniqueness via querySelectorAll match counts, filters Tailwind/Bootstrap utility classes with 50+ regex patterns, detects dynamically-generated IDs (high digit ratio, long hex strings), and builds nth-of-type chains as last resort for uniqueness.

REVISED APPROACH (after studying agent-browser): Instead of nanobrowser's heavyweight 1500-LOC DOM tree builder, adopt agent-browser's lightweight ref-based pattern. Core: (1) browser_scan_page tool runs via chrome.scripting.executeScript in ISOLATED world, uses TreeWalker for O(n) traversal, detects interactive elements (buttons, links, inputs, ARIA roles, cursor:pointer, contenteditable). (2) Each interactive element gets a numeric ref (e1, e2...) stored in extension memory with its CSS selector. (3) Output is an indented accessibility-tree-like notation, NOT raw HTML. (4) Existing browser_click_element and browser_fill_form accept refs (@e1) in addition to CSS selectors. (5) browser_diff_page shows what changed since last scan (Myers diff). This is 10x simpler than nanobrowser while being equally effective for AI agents.

agent-browser uses Playwright's ariaSnapshot() to get the accessibility tree, which is unavailable in Chrome Extension context. Our scan must build an equivalent representation using TreeWalker + ARIA role detection + computed style checks, but targeting the same output format: indented tree with role, name, and [ref=eN] annotations. Key difference: agent-browser stores refs as getByRole() Playwright locators; we store refs as CSS selectors (since we interact via chrome.scripting.executeScript + querySelector). The ref map lives in the service worker memory, scoped per tabId, and is invalidated on tab navigation events (already tracked by browser-events.ts).

browser-use research findings (2026-03-06): browser-use (~80k stars) replaced their original buildDomTree.js injection with a pure CDP approach using 4 parallel data sources: DOMSnapshot.captureSnapshot (layout/bounds/paint order/computed styles), Accessibility.getFullAXTree (roles/names), DOM.getDocument (structure), and DOMDebugger.getEventListeners (JS click handlers). This CDP approach is NOT usable in our Chrome Extension context (requires chrome.debugger which shows a banner to the user), but their ClickableElementDetector heuristics and serialization patterns are the most battle-tested in the ecosystem and should be adopted as design patterns.

Interactivity detection heuristics to adopt from browser-use's ClickableElementDetector: (1) Label wrapper detection — has_form_control_descendant() with max_depth=2 for label>span>input patterns; skip labels with 'for' attribute. (2) AX property signals — 'focusable', 'editable', 'settable' mean interactive; 'checked', 'expanded', 'pressed', 'selected' only exist on interactive widgets. (3) Search element heuristics — detect class/id containing 'search', 'magnify', 'glass', 'lookup', 'find'; check data-* attributes. (4) Icon-size heuristics — 10-50px elements with class/role/data-action/aria-label are likely interactive icons. (5) Aria-disabled/aria-hidden early exit — skip these immediately. Since we cannot use CDP's getEventListeners, our fallback is: onclick/onmousedown/onkeydown attributes + cursor:pointer + tabindex, which covers ~90% of cases.

Bounding box propagation pattern from browser-use's DOMTreeSerializer: PROPAGATING_ELEMENTS = [a, button, div[role=button], div[role=combobox], span[role=button], span[role=combobox], input[role=combobox]]. When a propagating parent element fully contains a child (99% containment threshold), the child is excluded from interactive element list. This prevents double-counting in patterns like text and . In our content script implementation, use getBoundingClientRect() on parent and child to compute containment ratio.

Attribute inclusion for scan output (from browser-use's DEFAULT_INCLUDE_ATTRIBUTES, adapted for token efficiency): Include in tree notation ONLY when present: type, checked, selected, expanded, pressed, disabled, required, placeholder, min, max, minlength, maxlength, step, pattern, accept, multiple, inputmode, autocomplete, aria-expanded, aria-checked, contenteditable, level (for headings). Exclude from tree notation (too noisy): class, style, data-* (except data-testid), event handlers. This keeps scan output under ~2000 tokens for typical pages while giving the AI enough context to interact correctly.

LOCATE-001.description:
Parent story for transforming the fspec WebMCP Chrome Extension into a fully-fledged browser companion for AI agents. Encompasses renaming/rebranding, DOM scanning with accessibility-tree output, ref-based element interaction, page diffing, advanced interactivity heuristics, and comprehensive skill documentation. Inspired by agent-browser's snapshot/ref pattern, browser-use's interactivity detection, and LocatorKit's selector generation.

Delivered scope (LOCATE-002 through LOCATE-008): Extension rename, ref state management, DOM scanning core (browser_scan_page), ref resolution in click/fill tools, page diff tool (browser_diff_page), advanced interactivity heuristics (label wrappers, bounding box propagation, compound controls, search elements, icon detection, dynamic class filtering), and MCP tool definitions with skill documentation.

Future scope (not delivered): Shadow DOM/iframe traversal, hash-based element re-identification across page navigations.

examples.text: AI calls find_in_page on a Google search results page → receives numbered tree: [0]<input name=q>search query />, [1]<a href=...>First result />, etc.
AI wants to click element [5] → system resolves index to CSS selector and XPath, executes click via CDP
Page has Tailwind classes like 'flex mt-4 px-6 rounded-lg' → selector generation filters these out and uses semantic class 'login-form' instead
Page has a button inside a shadow DOM web component → buildDomTree enters shadow root and assigns highlight index to the button
AI requests detailed context for element [3] → receives JSON with: preferred CSS selector, alternate selectors, XPath, nearest heading, label text, bounding box, match counts
Page has 200+ elements but only 35 are interactive → token-efficient output only includes the 35 interactive elements plus visible text context
Element is behind a modal overlay → isTopElement check via elementFromPoint detects it's occluded and marks it as non-interactive
After page navigation, AI needs to find same 'Submit' button → hash comparison (branch path + attributes + xpath) re-identifies it even if highlight index changed

Full scan→interact→diff cycle: AI calls browser_scan_page → gets tree: [e1] button "Login" [e2] textbox "Email" [e3] textbox "Password" → AI calls browser_fill_form with selector @e2 and value 'user@test.com' → AI calls browser_fill_form with selector @e3 → AI calls browser_click_element with selector @e1 → AI calls browser_diff_page → sees '+ heading "Dashboard"' / '- button "Login"' confirming login succeeded

Scan output is token-efficient accessibility tree format: '- heading "Sign In" [level=1]
  - textbox "Email" [ref=e1]
  - textbox "Password" [ref=e2]
  - button "Submit" [ref=e3]
- region "Footer"
  - link "Forgot Password" [ref=e4]' — structural elements without refs are included for context but the AI only interacts via ref'd elements
Navigation bar has Home → only one ref assigned to the parent, children (span, svg) are NOT given separate refs because parent fully contains them (bounding box propagation)
Form has → label wrapping a checkbox is detected as single interactive element (depth-limited descendant check finds the input), 'for'-less label wrapper gets the ref, not the inner input separately

Page has <input type='date'> which renders with internal year/month/day spinners in shadow DOM → scan shows single ref: '- textbox "Date of birth" [ref=e5] [type=date] [min=1900-01-01] [max=2026-12-31]' — the internal spinner sub-components are collapsed into the parent input

Signup form scan includes validation attributes: '- textbox "Email" [ref=e1] [type=email] [required] [pattern=.+@.+\..+]\n  - textbox "Password" [ref=e2] [type=password] [required] [minlength=8] [maxlength=128]\n  - textbox "Age" [ref=e3] [type=number] [min=13] [max=120] [step=1]' — AI can fill correctly without trial-and-error

Page has a <div class='search-icon magnify' data-action='toggle-search'> with no ARIA role or onclick → heuristic matching detects search-related class names and data attributes, assigns a ref as interactive element

rules.text: Page must be represented as a structured element tree with numeric indices for each interactive element (nanobrowser approach), not just raw HTML or screenshots
Each interactive element must have a unique highlight index that remains stable within a single page state snapshot
Selectors must be ranked by reliability: data-testid > id > aria-label/role > class-based > nth-of-type > fallback, with match count validation (LocatorKit approach)
Interactivity detection must combine cursor style, tag name, ARIA roles, event listeners, and heuristic signals (contenteditable, dropdown toggles)
Visibility checking must account for CSS display/visibility/opacity, viewport bounds, occlusion via elementFromPoint, and scroll position
Utility/framework CSS classes (Tailwind, Bootstrap spacing/layout classes) must be filtered from selector generation to produce stable selectors
Element context must include: nearest heading, label text, ancestor snippets, and text content — not just tag name and attributes
Shadow DOM and iframe elements must be traversable — elements inside shadow roots and cross-origin iframes should be discoverable
Output format must be token-efficient — indented tree notation [index]<tag attr>text /> for page-wide views, detailed JSON for single element queries
Elements must be re-identifiable across page navigations using hash-based comparison (branch path + attributes + xpath hash like nanobrowser)

The AI workflow must follow agent-browser's proven pattern: scan → interact → re-scan. browser_scan_page captures the current state, the AI uses refs to interact, then scans again to verify. Refs are ephemeral per-scan, not persistent across page changes.

browser_click_element and browser_fill_form must accept ref syntax (@e1, @e5) as selector values, resolving them from the stored ref map before executing — maintaining backward compatibility with raw CSS selectors
A browser_diff_page tool must show what changed between the last scan and current page state using text diff (additions/removals), so the AI can verify that its actions had the intended effect

Interactive parent elements (links, buttons, role=button divs) must 'claim' fully-contained children — if a parent contains , only the parent gets a ref, not the children (browser-use's bounding box propagation pattern prevents double-counting)

Label elements (<label>) wrapping form controls must be detected with depth-limited descendant check (max 2 levels: label > span > input) — labels with 'for' attribute must be skipped to avoid double-activating the target input (browser-use's Ant Design pattern)

Compound HTML5 controls (date, time, datetime-local, range, number, color, file inputs) must be represented as a single interactive element — their internal shadow DOM sub-components (spinners, calendar dropdowns, color swatches) must NOT be exposed as separate refs

Re-identification hashing must filter dynamic/transient CSS classes before hashing — state classes like 'focus', 'hover', 'active', 'loading', 'expanded', 'collapsed', 'highlighted', 'entering', 'leaving' must be excluded to produce stable hashes across UI state changes (browser-use's DYNAMIC_CLASS_PATTERNS approach)

Scan output must include validation-relevant attributes for form elements: pattern, min, max, minlength, maxlength, step, accept, multiple, inputmode, autocomplete, required — so the AI can fill forms correctly without trial-and-error (browser-use's DEFAULT_INCLUDE_ATTRIBUTES insight)

Non-semantic elements used as search controls (divs/spans with class/id containing 'search', 'magnify', 'glass', 'lookup', 'find', or data-* search attributes) must be detected as interactive via heuristic matching, even without ARIA roles or onclick attributes

architectureNotes.text: Pure TypeScript module at extension/src/background/ref-state.ts. Uses Map<number, TabScanState> as internal state. No chrome.storage — in-memory only for sub-millisecond reads. Service worker restart clears state naturally (correct behavior — stale refs should require re-scan). Wire into existing browser-events.ts via import + clearTabScanState calls in onUpdated and onRemoved handlers.

LOCATE-003.description:
Create a centralized ref-state.ts module in extension/src/background/ that stores the scan state per tab — ref→selector mappings, tree text for diffing, and timestamps. Wire it into browser-events.ts for automatic invalidation on navigation (changeInfo.url) and tab close (onRemoved). This module is the foundation for all scan/ref/diff tools.

Key interfaces: TabScanState { refs: Map<string, RefEntry>, treeText: string, timestamp: number }, RefEntry { selector: string, role: string, name: string }. Exports: setTabScanState(), getTabScanState(), clearTabScanState(), resolveRef(). State is in-memory in the service worker, scoped per tabId.

examples.text: Set scan state for tab 42 with 3 refs (e1→button, e2→textbox, e3→link), then getTabScanState(42) returns the exact same refs, treeText, and timestamp
resolveRef(42, 'e2') returns { selector: '#email', role: 'textbox', name: 'Email' } after a scan, but returns undefined for unknown ref 'e99'
Tab 42 has scan state, tab 99 has different scan state — clearTabScanState(42) removes only tab 42's state, getTabScanState(99) still returns its data
Tab 42 navigates to a new URL (changeInfo.url fires) → clearTabScanState(42) is called → getTabScanState(42) returns undefined, forcing re-scan
Tab 42 is closed (onRemoved fires) → clearTabScanState(42) is called → no memory leak from accumulated scan states of closed tabs
getTabScanState(999) for a tab that was never scanned returns undefined (not an error)

rules.text: State is stored in-memory in the service worker as a Map<number, TabScanState> keyed by tabId
setTabScanState stores refs map, treeText, and timestamp for a given tabId
getTabScanState returns the stored state or undefined if no scan exists for that tabId
clearTabScanState removes the state for a given tabId without affecting other tabs
resolveRef is a convenience wrapper that looks up a ref key (e.g. 'e1') from the stored state for a tab and returns the RefEntry or undefined
Tab navigation (changeInfo.url in tabs.onUpdated) must trigger clearTabScanState to invalidate stale refs
Tab close (tabs.onRemoved) must trigger clearTabScanState to clean up memory
Each tab maintains independent state — operations on one tab never affect another tab's scan state

LOCATE-003.title: Ref State Management Module

userStory.action: have scan state persisted per-tab in the service worker
userStory.benefit: the scan→interact→verify workflow has consistent ref resolution and automatic invalidation on navigation

architectureNotes.text: Two-file implementation: (1) scanPageDOM injected function lives in browser-tools.ts as the browser_scan_page handler — it uses chrome.scripting.executeScript() ISOLATED world to inject a TreeWalker-based scanning function. (2) Ref assignment and tree formatting happen in the service worker handler after the injected function returns raw element data. The handler stores refs via setTabScanState() from ref-state.ts (LOCATE-003). The injected function must be serializable (no closures over external state) since it runs in page context.

LOCATE-004.description:
Implement the browser_scan_page tool that scans the active tab's DOM for interactive elements and returns a structured accessibility-tree-like output with ephemeral refs. This is the core scanning engine.

The tool injects a scanning function via chrome.scripting.executeScript() in the ISOLATED world. The function uses TreeWalker for O(n) DOM traversal, element.matches() for interactivity detection (a[href], button, input, textarea, select, [role=button], [role=link], [role=checkbox], [role=radio], [role=tab], [role=menuitem], [role=option], [role=switch], [role=textbox], [role=combobox], [role=searchbox], [role=slider], [role=spinbutton], [contenteditable], [tabindex], summary, details), element.checkVisibility() + getBoundingClientRect() for visibility filtering, and getComputedStyle() for cursor:pointer + pointer-events:none checks.

CSS selector generation uses ranked strategy: data-testid > id > unique attribute combo > nth-child path. Dynamic/generated IDs (high digit ratio, hex strings) are excluded.

Output format matches agent-browser's accessibility tree notation:
- heading "Sign In" [level=1]
  - textbox "Email" [ref=e1]
  - textbox "Password" [ref=e2] [type=password]
  - button "Sign In" [ref=e3]

Tool accepts: tabId (optional), interactive (boolean, default true), selector (CSS selector to scope scan). Returns: tree text + metadata (url, title, viewport, element count, ref count).

examples.text: Login page scan: page has h1 'Sign In', email input, password input, submit button, 'Forgot Password' link — returns tree with heading for context, 4 interactive elements with refs e1-e4, metadata shows 4 interactive elements
Page with hidden elements: div with display:none containing a button, and a visible button — only the visible button gets a ref, hidden button is filtered out
Dynamic ID filtering: button with id='btn-abc123def' (hex-like) uses fallback selector instead of #btn-abc123def; button with id='submit-btn' uses #submit-btn
Interactive mode false: scan returns ALL elements including paragraphs, divs, spans — no interactive filtering, no refs assigned
Scoped scan: selector='form.login' scopes TreeWalker to only traverse within that form element, returning only elements inside it
Aria-label name extraction: input with aria-label='Search products' shows as 'textbox "Search products" [ref=e1]' instead of showing placeholder text
Parent claiming children: Home — only the gets a ref as 'link "Home" [ref=e1]', children are not separately listed
Disabled/hidden exclusion: button with aria-disabled='true' and div with aria-hidden='true' containing a link — neither gets a ref
Form validation attributes: input[type=email][required][pattern=.+@.+] shows as 'textbox "Email" [ref=e1] [type=email] [required] [pattern=.+@.+]'
Cursor pointer heuristic: div with no role/onclick but cursor:pointer via CSS — detected as interactive and gets a ref
Ref state integration: after scan, setTabScanState is called with refs map, tree text, and timestamp — resolveRef(tabId, 'e1') returns the correct RefEntry
Error: invalid tabId returns MCP error result; restricted page (chrome://) returns error explaining page cannot be scanned

Selector ranking: element with data-testid='email' gets selector [data-testid="email"]; element with only id='email-input' gets #email-input; element with no id gets attribute combo like input[type="email"][name="email"]

rules.text: Scanning uses TreeWalker for O(n) DOM traversal, skipping SCRIPT/STYLE/NOSCRIPT nodes and their children via FILTER_REJECT

Interactive elements detected via combined selector: a[href], button, input, textarea, select, ARIA role widgets, [contenteditable], [tabindex], summary, details — plus heuristic checks for cursor:pointer and onclick/onmousedown/onkeydown attributes
Visibility filtering uses element.checkVisibility() for CSS display/visibility/opacity checks, plus getBoundingClientRect() for zero-size filtering
Elements with aria-disabled=true, aria-hidden=true, or pointer-events:none are excluded from interactive elements
CSS selector generation uses ranked strategy: data-testid > id (excluding dynamic IDs) > unique attribute combo > nth-child path
Dynamic IDs are excluded from selector generation: IDs with >30% digits, >8 chars that look hex-like, or matching patterns like r-[hash], ember[digits], react-[hash]
Output format is an indented accessibility tree: role "name" [ref=eN] [attr=value] — structural elements (headings, regions) included for context without refs, interactive elements get refs
Refs are assigned by the service worker handler (e1, e2, ...) and stored via setTabScanState from ref-state.ts — NOT in the injected scanning function
Accessible name extraction priority: aria-label > aria-labelledby > placeholder > value > alt > title > direct text content (trimmed, max 80 chars)
Role extraction uses implicit role mapping (button→button, a[href]→link, input[type=text]→textbox, h1-h6→heading, etc.) with explicit role attribute always overriding
Tool accepts optional parameters: tabId (defaults to active tab), interactive (boolean, default true — filters to only interactive elements), selector (CSS selector to scope scan to a DOM subtree)
Metadata returned alongside tree text includes: url, title, viewport dimensions, total element count, and interactive ref count

Validation-relevant attributes included in output when present: type, checked, selected, expanded, pressed, disabled, required, placeholder, min, max, minlength, maxlength, step, pattern, accept, multiple, inputmode, autocomplete, level (for headings)
Interactive parent elements (links, buttons, role=button) that fully contain children should claim the children — only the parent gets a ref, not the contained spans/imgs/svgs

LOCATE-004.title: DOM Scanning Core — browser_scan_page Tool

userStory.action: scan the active tab's DOM for interactive elements and structural context
userStory.benefit: understand the page layout and interact with elements using ephemeral refs

architectureNotes.text: Add resolveRef import from ./ref-state at top of browser-tools.ts. Ref resolution is a ~10-line prefix check at the top of each handler, after resolveTabId. Direct import is appropriate since ref-state is an internal extension module.

LOCATE-005.description:
Add @ref resolution to browser_click_element and browser_fill_form handlers. When the selector argument starts with '@' (e.g. '@e3'), resolve it from the ref map via resolveRef(tabId, ref) before passing to the existing click/fill logic. Raw CSS selectors (not starting with '@') pass through unchanged — 100% backward compatible.

Implementation is a ~10-line prefix check at the top of each handler:
1. Check if selector starts with '@'
2. Strip '@' prefix to get ref key (e.g. 'e3')
3. Look up in ref-state.ts via resolveRef(tabId, refKey)
4. If not found, return error: 'Ref @e3 not found. Run browser_scan_page first.'
5. If found, use the stored CSS selector for the rest of the handler

examples.text: Click with @e1 after scan → resolves to the CSS selector stored for e1 and clicks it
Fill form with @e3 after scan → resolves to the CSS selector stored for e3 and fills the value
Click with @e99 (nonexistent ref) → returns error: 'Ref @e99 not found. Run browser_scan_page first to scan the page.'
Click with @e1 on tab with no prior scan → returns error (no scan state exists)
Click with raw CSS '#submit' → passes through unchanged, existing click logic executes
Fill form with raw CSS 'input[name=email]' → passes through unchanged, existing fill logic executes
Click with 'div@e1' (@ in middle) → treated as raw CSS selector, NOT as a ref

rules.text: Selectors starting with '@' are resolved from the ref map via resolveRef(tabId, refKey)
Raw CSS selectors (not starting with '@') pass through unchanged — 100% backward compatible
If ref is not found, return error suggesting to run browser_scan_page first
The '@' prefix is stripped to get the ref key (e.g. '@e3' → 'e3')
Only browser_click_element and browser_fill_form gain ref resolution (they are the only tools accepting selectors)
'@' is not a valid start character for CSS selectors, so there is no ambiguity

LOCATE-005.title: Ref Resolution in Click and Fill Tools

userStory.action: use @ref shortcuts in browser_click_element and browser_fill_form
userStory.benefit: interact with scanned elements without knowing their CSS selectors

architectureNotes.text: Myers diff algorithm implemented in separate module (myers-diff.ts) — ~80 lines, pure function, no Chrome dependencies
Handler registered in browser-tools.ts alongside existing browser_scan_page — reuses resolveTabId, scripting.executeScript, scanPageDOM, formatAccessibilityTree
Context lines use 1 unchanged line before/after each change group — separated by '...' ellipsis when gap >1 unchanged lines

assumptions: Diff always runs the scanner with the same parameters (interactive=true, no scope) as the default browser_scan_page to ensure comparable trees
LOCATE-006.description:
Implement the browser_diff_page tool that shows what changed on the page since the last browser_scan_page call. Uses a simplified Myers diff algorithm on the line-level tree text.

Workflow:
1. Run the same scanning function as browser_scan_page on the current tab
2. Retrieve the previous scan's tree text from ref-state.ts (getTabScanState)
3. Run line-level text diff (additions, removals, unchanged)
4. Update the stored state with the new scan (so the next diff compares against this one)
5. Return unified diff format with change stats

Output format:
  - heading "Sign In" [level=1]
  - textbox "Email" [ref=e1]
- - button "Sign In" [ref=e3]
+ - button "Signing in..." [ref=e3] [disabled]

Changes: 1 addition, 1 removal, 2 unchanged

The diff algorithm operates on plain text lines — no need for a full AST diff. A simplified Myers diff (~80 lines) computes the shortest edit script between two line arrays.

Tool accepts: tabId (optional). Returns: diff text + stats { additions, removals, unchanged, changed: boolean }. If no previous scan exists, returns the full current tree as all additions.

examples.text: Button text changes after click: 'Sign In' → 'Signing in...' with disabled added — shows 1 addition, 1 removal, N unchanged
Identical pages scanned twice — diff returns 0 additions, 0 removals, changed: false
New elements appear (e.g., form validation errors after submit) — multiple additions, 0 removals
Elements removed (e.g., modal closed) — 0 additions, multiple removals
No previous scan exists — returns full current tree as all additions with note 'No previous scan to compare against'
Complete page navigation (all content changed) — all old lines removed, all new lines added
Empty page (no elements) — handles gracefully with 0 changes

rules.text: Diff uses simplified Myers algorithm on line-level tree text for minimum edit distance
Reuses the same scanning function as browser_scan_page (scanPageDOM + formatAccessibilityTree)
Previous scan state retrieved from ref-state.ts (getTabScanState); new scan updates stored state
If no previous scan exists, return full current tree as all additions with explanatory note
Output format uses unified diff: unchanged lines have no prefix, additions prefixed with '+ ', removals with '- '
Returns DiffStats: { additions, removals, unchanged, changed: boolean }
Only include changed regions with context lines (1-2 unchanged lines around changes) for token efficiency
Tool accepts optional tabId parameter (defaults to active tab)

LOCATE-006.title: Page Diff Tool — browser_diff_page

userStory.action: see what changed on the page since the last scan
userStory.benefit: I can verify my actions had the intended effect in the scan→interact→verify workflow

architectureNotes.text: Heuristics are implemented in two places: (1) the testable helper module dom-scanner-helpers.ts exports named functions for unit testing, (2) the scanPageDOM function in scan-page-dom.ts has inlined copies of the same logic since it runs in page context via chrome.scripting.executeScript(). A new file dom-scanner-heuristics.ts holds the exported helper functions to keep dom-scanner-helpers.ts under 300 lines. The bounding box propagation (heuristic 2) replaces the existing shouldClaimChildren with a post-processing pass using getBoundingClientRect containment. The filterDynamicClasses function is used during selector generation for stable hashing, not during interactivity detection.

LOCATE-007.description: Enhance the DOM scanning function with battle-tested interactivity detection heuristics from browser-use and nanobrowser. These handle the long tail of edge cases that basic CSS selector matching misses. Heuristics to implement: 1. **Label wrapper detection** — has_form_control_descendant() with max_depth=2 for patterns like (Ant Design). Labels with 'for' attribute are skipped (they proxy to the external input). Labels wrapping form controls get the ref, not the inner input. 2. **Bounding box propagation** — PROPAGATING_ELEMENTS = [a, button, div[role=button], div[role=combobox], span[role=button], span[role=combobox], input[role=combobox]]. When a propagating parent fully contains a child (99% containment threshold via getBoundingClientRect()), the child is excluded from the interactive element list. Prevents double-counting in patterns like text. 3. **Compound control collapsing** — HTML5 date, time, datetime-local, range, number, color, file inputs are represented as single interactive elements. Their internal shadow DOM sub-components (spinners, calendar dropdowns) are NOT exposed as separate refs. 4. **Search element heuristics** — Detect non-semantic search controls: divs/spans with class/id containing 'search', 'magnify', 'glass', 'lookup', 'find', or data-* search attributes. architectureNotes.text: Multi-phase scan: (1) getAllFrames discovers frames, (2) main frame scanPageDOM detects <iframe> elements and records their position/depth, (3) per-frame executeScript with frameIds runs scanPageDOM in each iframe, (4) service worker merges results — main frame tree + iframe subtrees spliced at the correct positions. Refs assigned per-frame with f{frameId}e{N} prefix for non-main frames. RefEntry gains frameId field so click/fill targets the right frame.

getAllFrames() returns MORE fields than documented in research: per Chromium IDL (web_navigation.json), each frame object includes: errorOccurred (boolean), processId (integer), frameId (integer), parentFrameId (integer), url (string), documentId (string), parentDocumentId (string, optional), documentLifecycle (enum: prerender/active/cached/pending_deletion), frameType (enum: outermost_frame/fenced_frame/sub_frame). The documentId and frameType fields are particularly useful — documentId enables precise correlation with InjectionResult.documentId, and frameType distinguishes sub_frame from the main frame without relying on frameId===0.

Chrome 133+ behavior change: Since Chrome 133, chrome.scripting.executeScript uses match_origin_as_fallback by default (PSA from Chrome Extensions DevRel, Jan 2025). This means executeScript now injects into MORE frames by default, including about:blank and sandboxed srcdoc frames that previously required explicit match_origin_as_fallback. This improves iframe scanning coverage automatically. Source: groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/chromium-extensions/c/D8DcJARVM90

LOCATE-009.description:
Extend browser_scan_page, browser_click_element, browser_fill_form, and browser_diff_page to discover and interact with elements inside iframes. Currently all scanning is scoped to the top-level frame only — elements inside same-origin and cross-origin iframes are invisible to the AI agent.

Chrome's chrome.scripting.executeScript API supports targeting specific frames via frameIds and discovering all frames in a tab via chrome.webNavigation.getAllFrames(). Same-origin iframes can also be scanned by the top-level injection walking into contentDocument. Cross-origin iframes require separate executeScript calls per frameId.

The scan output should nest iframe content under the iframe element in the accessibility tree, with refs that encode the frameId so click/fill can target the correct frame. Example: refs like 'f2e5' meaning frame 2, element 5.

examples.text: Page with Stripe payment iframe: scan returns main frame elements (e1, e2) plus iframe content as nested children (f5e1 'Card Number', f5e2 'Expiry', f5e3 'CVC', f5e4 'Pay'). AI fills card fields using @f5e1, @f5e2, @f5e3 and clicks @f5e4.
Page with no iframes: scan returns only main frame elements with simple refs (e1, e2, e3) — 100% backward compatible, no behavioral change
Click on iframe element using @f5e4: resolveRefSelector parses 'f5e4' → frameId=5, elementRef='e4', looks up CSS selector, then executeScript targets frameIds: [5] to click within the iframe
Ad-heavy page with 25 iframes: maxFrames=10 limits scanning to the 10 largest/most relevant frames, remaining iframes show as 'iframe [skipped]' in the tree

Nested iframes (iframe inside iframe): getAllFrames returns all frames at all depths with parentFrameId chain. Tree shows nested indentation correctly. Refs use the direct frame's ID (f12e1), not the parent chain

Sandboxed iframe with sandbox='allow-same-origin' (no allow-scripts): executeScript in ISOLATED world still succeeds — scanPageDOM runs and returns elements. The iframe appears in tree with its content. The sandbox attribute only blocks MAIN world scripts, not extension content scripts.

rules.text: manifest.json must include 'webNavigation' permission to enable chrome.webNavigation.getAllFrames() for frame discovery
Frame discovery uses chrome.webNavigation.getAllFrames() to enumerate all frames in a tab — returns frameId, parentFrameId, url for each frame including nested iframes
chrome.scripting.executeScript with frameIds targets specific frames — works for both same-origin AND cross-origin iframes because the extension has <all_urls> host permission
Main frame refs remain backward-compatible (e1, e2, e3). Iframe refs use frame-prefixed format: f{frameId}e{N} (e.g. f5e1 = frame 5, element 1). The @ prefix works for both: @e1 and @f5e3
RefEntry must gain a frameId field (0 for main frame) so click/fill can target the correct frame via chrome.scripting.executeScript({ target: { tabId, frameIds: [frameId] } })
Iframe content appears nested under the iframe element in the accessibility tree output — the tree shows the iframe's src/name, then indented children from the frame scan
A maxFrames parameter (default 10) limits the number of iframes scanned to prevent timeout on ad-heavy pages. Same-origin and larger iframes are prioritized over small cross-origin ones
browser_diff_page must produce diffs on the merged multi-frame tree. Frame additions/removals (iframes dynamically created or destroyed) appear as tree-level changes

CRITICAL CORRECTION (from Chromium source review): Sandboxed iframes WITHOUT allow-scripts CAN be scanned via chrome.scripting.executeScript in ISOLATED world (the default). The sandbox attribute only blocks MAIN world scripts. Extension content scripts in ISOLATED world bypass sandbox restrictions. This was confirmed by Chromium bug 355256366 (fixed Chrome 130) and the Chrome 133 PSA that made match_origin_as_fallback the default for executeScript. Rule [6] claim about sandbox-no-scripts skipping is WRONG for our use case.

Non-scannable frames must be skipped gracefully: chrome-extension:// and chrome:// URLs. about:blank frames should be scanned if they have content (same-origin JS-populated). about:srcdoc frames (url='about:srcdoc') should always be scanned. Sandboxed iframes WITHOUT allow-scripts CAN still be scanned because executeScript runs in ISOLATED world which bypasses sandbox script restrictions (only MAIN world is blocked). The iframe element always appears in the tree regardless.

Frame-to-DOM correlation uses a two-pass injection approach: (1) First pass: inject a marker into each frame via executeScript({ frameIds: [fid], func: (id) => { window.__fspec_frameId = id; }, args: [fid] }), setting a global variable with the frameId. (2) Second pass: parent frame scan detects all <iframe> elements. For same-origin iframes, reads iframe.contentWindow.__fspec_frameId for exact frameId→DOM mapping. For cross-origin iframes (where contentWindow access is blocked by SOP), falls back to matching iframe.src against getAllFrames().url — cross-origin duplicates with identical URLs are rare and use document order as tiebreaker.

architectureNotes.text: Three-Layer Lock Architecture: Layer 1 (Inter-Process) = proper-lockfile with mkdir strategy for cross-process coordination; Layer 2 (In-Process) = Readers-writer pattern using promises and queues for concurrent reads; Layer 3 (Atomic Writes) = Temp file + rename for POSIX atomic write guarantees

LockedFileManager Singleton Pattern: Single instance coordinates all in-process locks via Map<string, number> for read counts and Set<string> for write locks, with separate waiting queues (Array<() => void>) for blocked readers and writers

proper-lockfile Configuration: stale=10000ms (10 second timeout for crashed processes), retries={retries:10, minTimeout:50ms, maxTimeout:500ms} for exponential backoff, realpath=false for symlink support and performance
Affected Files: work-units.json (230+ work units, high contention), foundation.json, tags.json, prefixes.json, epics.json, example-map.json, fspec-hooks.json - ALL must use LockedFileManager

Process 1 acquires write lock on work-units.json and crashes mid-write - proper-lockfile's stale lock detection (10 second timeout) allows Process 2 to acquire lock after timeout, preventing permanent deadlock

Command writes to work-units.json using atomic pattern: (1) writes to work-units.json.tmp.abc123, (2) renames to work-units.json - If crash occurs during step 1, original file is intact; if during step 2, rename is atomic

Reader 1 and Reader 2 both call fileManager.readJSON('work-units.json') - Both acquire in-process read locks simultaneously (readers-writer pattern), both acquire proper-lockfile locks with retry, both read file concurrently

Writer calls fileManager.writeJSON('work-units.json', data) while Reader is active - Writer waits for Reader's in-process read lock to release, then acquires exclusive write lock, prevents read-during-write corruption

Command refactoring minimal change: Replace 'const data = await ensureWorkUnitsFile(cwd); ... await writeFile(file, JSON.stringify(data, 2))' with 'await fileManager.transaction(file, async (data) => { ... })' - same 400 lines of mutation logic unchanged

Transaction rollback on error: 'await fileManager.transaction(file, async (data) => { if (\!valid) throw new Error("bad"); data.x = 1; })' - Error thrown, no write occurs, file unchanged, error propagates to command catch block

Multi-file sequential transactions: 'await fileManager.transaction(workUnitsFile, async (data) => { data.workUnits[id] = newWorkUnit; }); await fileManager.transaction(epicsFile, async (data) => { data.epics[epicId].workUnits.push(id); });' - If second fails first committed, run fspec repair-work-units to fix

Debug metrics output: 'FSPEC_DEBUG_LOCKS=1 fspec update-work-unit-status AUTH-001 done' logs '[LOCK] Acquired WRITE lock on work-units.json (waited 2ms, held 15ms, retries 0)' - helps diagnose performance issues and lock contention

questions.text: @human: Should the file locking system handle network filesystems (NFS, SMB) or only local filesystems?

questions.answer: Throw error immediately with clear message. The retry logic (10 retries with exponential backoff) already provides sufficient resilience. After retries exhausted, command should fail fast with actionable error message suggesting user check for stuck processes.
questions.text: @human: What should happen if lock acquisition fails after all retries - throw error immediately or offer user option to retry/abort?

questions.answer: Always read from disk for consistency. Caching introduces cache invalidation complexity and potential stale reads in concurrent scenarios. File I/O performance is acceptable (3-5ms reads) and correctness is more important than speed.
questions.text: @human: Should LockedFileManager cache file contents to reduce disk I/O, or always read from disk for consistency?

questions.answer: Incremental migration is safer. Phase 1: Create LockedFileManager + refactor ensure-files.ts. Phase 2: Migrate high-risk commands (update-work-unit-status, create-story). Phase 3: Migrate remaining commands. Phase 4: TUI store. This allows testing at each phase.

rules.text: File locking MUST use three-layer architecture: (1) proper-lockfile for inter-process coordination, (2) readers-writer pattern for in-process optimization, (3) atomic write-replace for safe writes
Multiple readers can read the same file concurrently (readers-writer pattern allows parallel reads)
Only ONE writer can modify a file at a time (exclusive write lock blocks all readers and other writers)
All file writes MUST use atomic write-replace pattern (write to temp file + rename) to prevent partial writes
proper-lockfile MUST use stale lock detection (10 second timeout) to prevent deadlocks from crashed processes
Lock acquisition MUST use retry logic with exponential backoff (10 retries, 50-500ms timeout range)
LockedFileManager MUST be a singleton to ensure in-process lock coordination across all file operations
All JSON file operations (work-units.json, tags.json, foundation.json, etc.) MUST use LockedFileManager
Read-modify-write operations MUST use transaction() method to ensure atomicity of the entire operation
Lock release MUST happen in finally block to prevent lock leaks on errors

YES - Support network filesystems. proper-lockfile's mkdir strategy is atomic on both local and network filesystems (NFS, SMB). No additional implementation cost, works in CI/CD and team environments.

Throw error immediately after 10 retries with exponential backoff (50-500ms, ~5 seconds total). Simple, clean error message: 'Failed to acquire file lock. Check for stuck fspec processes.' Exit code 1.

NEVER cache file contents. Always read from disk for consistency. Files are small (~200KB max), reads are fast (~3-5ms), caching adds complexity and risk of stale data across processes. Correctness > speed.

Optional debug metrics via FSPEC_DEBUG_LOCKS environment variable. Logs lock acquisition time, wait time, retries, hold duration. Ties into LOG-001 logging infrastructure. Silent by default, verbose when debugging.

All-at-once migration (NOT incremental). MUST work 100% perfectly the first time. Complete implementation: LockedFileManager + refactor utilities + refactor all ~50 commands + refactor TUI store + comprehensive tests. No partial states, no gradual rollout.
ensure* functions use read-lock-first pattern: attempt read with READ lock, on ENOENT upgrade to WRITE lock with double-check before creating file
READ locks released immediately after JSON.parse() completes - data is in memory, lock no longer needed, allows other operations to proceed
transaction() method uses mutation-based API: callback receives data, mutates in place, returns void - fileManager writes mutated data automatically on completion
transaction() errors cause rollback: if callback throws error, no write occurs and file remains unchanged - error propagates to caller for proper logging and exit codes

Multi-file operations use sequential transactions (not atomic): each file gets separate transaction, if later transaction fails earlier transactions already committed - acceptable due to denormalized data, defensive querying, and repair utilities

Debug metrics enabled via FSPEC_DEBUG_LOCKS environment variable: logs lock type, file path, wait time, hold duration, retry count - silent by default, verbose when debugging - ties into LOG-001 logging infrastructure when available

LOG-004.description: App::bootstrap spawns a logs_task that calls debug!() on every received LogRecord. BroadcastLogLayer captures that debug event without a target filter and rebroadcasts it via logs_tx, which the logs_task then re-debugs — infinite recursive amplification with one layer of escaped quotes added per round-trip. Result: ~8GB log files per day, severe disk pressure, and unreadable diagnostics. Fix: filter target 'codelet_fspec_tui::app::bootstrap' (and any descendant) in BroadcastLogLayer::on_event so the cycle breaks at the source.

rules.text: BroadcastLogLayer must drop events whose target is the TUI bootstrap subscriber that re-emits broadcast records, preventing infinite recursion

architectureNotes.text: ConnectMCP tool uses rmcp crate (same as Codex) for MCP JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio transport (TokioChildProcess) and Streamable HTTP transport (StreamableHttpClientTransport). Protocol version: 2025-11-25

MCP lifecycle per connection: spawn/connect → initialize handshake (protocolVersion, capabilities, clientInfo/serverInfo) → notifications/initialized → tools/list → cache tools on session. MCP spec 2025-11-25 section: Lifecycle

Tool routing: mcp__<server>__<tool>(args) → split on '__' → lookup server in session.mcp_connections → send JSON-RPC {method: 'tools/call', params: {name: '<tool>', arguments: args}} → return content array from response

Server-initiated messages handled via rmcp ClientHandler trait: notifications/tools/list_changed → re-fetch tools/list + inject notification; notifications/resources/updated → inject notification; sampling/createMessage → inject into session via watcher_input_tx, route LLM response back as sampling result

Ephemeral session state: session.mcp_connections: HashMap<String, McpConnection> where McpConnection holds RmcpClient, cached Vec<Tool> from tools/list, server InitializeResult, optional child PID. Tool list assembled fresh each LLM call: built_in_tools + mcp_connections.flat_map(tools)

rmcp API: handler.serve(transport) does full initialize handshake (sends InitializeRequest with ClientInfo, receives ServerInfo, sends InitializedNotification). Returns RunningService<RoleClient, H> where peer() provides list_all_tools(), call_tool(), list_all_resources(), etc. ClientHandler trait has on_tool_list_changed, on_resource_updated, create_message, on_logging_message callbacks

The sampling/createMessage round-trip uses a dedicated oneshot channel: create_message handler creates oneshot pair, injects SamplingRequest(params, oneshot_tx) via watcher_input_tx, the agent_loop processes it as a special WatcherInput variant that captures the LLM response and sends it through oneshot_tx, handler awaits oneshot_rx and returns CreateMessageResult to rmcp

MCP tools are injected into the LLM via a generic McpToolWrapper that implements rig::tool::Tool trait. Each provider's create_rig_agent() accepts an optional Vec<McpToolWrapper> parameter and appends them to the agent builder. Since create_rig_agent() is called fresh each turn inside agent_loop, newly connected MCP tools appear immediately in the next turn

MCP-001.description: Implement Dynamic MCP — an architecture where MCP server connections are established through a ConnectMCP tool call at runtime, rather than static config files at session startup. The agent decides when to connect, receives structured feedback on success or failure, and gains typed MCP tools dynamically mid-session. Uses the rmcp crate for native MCP protocol handling. Server-initiated messages (notifications, sampling requests) are injected into the session via watcher_input_tx. Skills can describe ConnectMCP calls, enabling multi-server workflows that are impossible with static MCP (Codex, OpenCode).

examples.text: Agent calls ConnectMCP(name: 'github', transport: 'stdio', command: 'npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-github') → tool spawns child process, sends JSON-RPC initialize request (protocolVersion: '2025-11-25', capabilities, clientInfo), receives server capabilities with tools: {listChanged: true}, sends notifications/initialized, then calls tools/list → caches tool definitions (name, description, inputSchema per MCP spec) → returns structured result to LLM listing server name, protocol version, and discovered tools

LLM calls mcp__github__create_issue({owner: 'org', repo: 'project', title: 'Bug fix'}) → tool routes to cached github connection → sends JSON-RPC tools/call with {name: 'create_issue', arguments: {...}} → MCP server returns {content: [{type: 'text', text: 'Created issue #42'}], isError: false} → tool returns content to LLM as tool result

ConnectMCP(name: 'db', transport: 'stdio', command: 'python3 db-mcp-server.py') fails because python3 is not installed → tool catches spawn error and returns structured failure to LLM with stderr output → LLM can reason about the failure and suggest 'python3 is not installed, try: brew install python3'

Skill file describes two ConnectMCP calls (github stdio server + sonarqube HTTP server) → agent executes skill, connects both mid-session → tools/list from each server returns tool definitions with inputSchema → agent now has typed tools from both servers (mcp__github__*, mcp__sonar__*) and uses them in a multi-server workflow → session ends, both child processes killed

Connected MCP server sends JSON-RPC notification {method: 'notifications/tools/list_changed'} → ClientHandler callback fires → tool re-calls tools/list to refresh cached tool definitions → injects '[MCP:github] Server tools list changed — refreshed 5 tools' into session via watcher_input_tx → next LLM API call includes updated tool schemas

MCP server sends sampling/createMessage request with {messages: [{role: 'user', content: {type: 'text', text: 'Analyze this code...'}}], maxTokens: 500} → injected into session as input for the LLM to process → LLM response routed back through the connection as the sampling result

Agent calls ConnectMCP(action: 'list') → returns 'Connected MCP servers: github — connected 5m ago, 5 tools, 12 calls; sonar — connected 2m ago, 3 tools, 0 calls' → Agent calls ConnectMCP(action: 'disconnect', name: 'github') → connection closed, child process killed → returns '✓ Disconnected: github (was connected 5m, 12 tool calls made)' → mcp__github__* tools removed from next LLM turn

ConnectMCP(name: 'slow-server', transport: 'stdio', command: 'node slow-mcp.js', timeout: 5) → server starts but does not respond to initialize within 5 seconds → tool kills the process and returns structured error: '✗ Failed to connect: slow-server — Timeout: MCP handshake not completed within 5s. Process started (PID 48291) but did not respond.' → LLM can reason about the timeout and suggest increasing it or checking the server

rules.text: ConnectMCP is a tool call — the agent calls it to establish MCP server connections at runtime (Dynamic MCP), not through config files at startup (Static MCP)
ConnectMCP uses the rmcp crate to speak native MCP JSON-RPC — it spawns the server process (stdio) or opens HTTP connection, performs the initialization handshake, and calls tools/list

On success, ConnectMCP returns a structured tool result listing the server name, protocol version, and all discovered tools with their schemas — these tools then become callable as mcp__<server>__<tool> in subsequent LLM turns
On failure, ConnectMCP returns a structured error (runtime not found, handshake timeout, auth required) so the LLM can reason about it, suggest fixes, or try alternatives
MCP connections are ephemeral — cached on the session as a HashMap<String, McpConnection>, gathered fresh each LLM API call, no persistent registry or lifecycle manager
Server-initiated MCP messages (notifications, sampling requests, resource updates) are injected into the session via watcher_input_tx so the LLM sees them
MCP tool calls (mcp__<server>__<tool>) are routed through the cached connection — look up server in session.mcp_connections, forward via client.call_tool()
Connection lifecycle is tied to the session — when session ends, all McpConnections are dropped and child processes killed
Skills can describe ConnectMCP calls inline — enabling multi-server workflows where the agent connects to each MCP server as needed during skill execution
ConnectMCP tool call — agent decides when to connect dynamically. No auto-start, no config files.

For sampling/createMessage: inject as session input, LLM responds, response returned via the rmcp ClientHandler. The MCP spec defines this as a server→client request — our ClientHandler impl handles the round-trip natively.

ConnectMCP calls tools/list during initialization and returns the discovered tools to the LLM. Server capabilities are negotiated during the initialize handshake. No separate manifest needed — the MCP protocol handles discovery natively.

ConnectMCP supports three actions: connect (default — establish new server connection), disconnect (tear down named connection, kill child process), and list (show all active connections with tool counts and uptime)

ConnectMCP enforces a configurable timeout (default 10 seconds) for the initialization handshake — if the server does not complete initialize within the timeout, the process is killed and a structured timeout error is returned to the LLM
Config file support for pre-declaring MCP servers is V2 scope — the agent would read a config and call ConnectMCP for each entry. V1 has no config file; all connections are explicit tool calls
MCP tool names are namespaced as mcp__<server>__<tool> — the double-underscore prevents collisions between servers that expose tools with the same name, and between MCP tools and built-in tools

ConnectMCP connect action accepts optional env (HashMap<String,String>) for stdio transport passed to Command::envs(), and optional headers (HashMap<String,String>) for HTTP transport passed to StreamableHttpClientTransport. These enable passing API tokens, credentials, and auth headers to MCP servers

architectureNotes.text: File structure: src/migrations/ with index.ts (runner), registry.ts (version tracking), types.ts (interfaces), migrations/ subfolder for individual migration files, __tests__/ for tests
Migration interface: {version: string, name: string, description: string, up: (data) => data, down?: (data) => data}. Each migration has unique version number.
Registry pattern: migrations array in registry.ts exports all migrations in version order. getMigrationsToApply(currentVersion, targetVersion) returns migrations to run.
Auto-migration integration: ensureWorkUnitsFile() in src/utils/ensure-files.ts calls ensureLatestVersion(cwd, CURRENT_VERSION) before returning data
Backup naming: work-units.json.backup-{version}-{timestamp} (e.g., work-units.json.backup-0.7.0-1738329600000). Stored in same directory as work-units.json.
Version comparison: Use semver-compatible compareVersions(v1, v2) function. Returns -1 (v1 < v2), 0 (equal), or 1 (v1 > v2).
Migration history structure in work-units.json: migrationHistory: [{version: '0.7.0', applied: '2025-01-31T12:00:00Z', backupPath: 'spec/work-units.json.backup-0.7.0-1738329600000'}]
Error handling: Migration failure throws error with migration version, does NOT automatically restore backup. User can manually restore from backup file if needed.
Console output: Use chalk.yellow for warnings, chalk.blue for migration names, chalk.green for success, chalk.red for errors, chalk.dim for backup paths. Show progress for each migration.
Transaction safety: Each migration runs atomically - backup created first, then migration up() called, then data saved. If up() throws, data is not saved.
Version field location: Add 'version' field at root level of work-units.json (same level as 'workUnits' and 'states'). Default to undefined for old files (treated as v0.6.0).
Manual command structure: 'fspec migrate' with options: --version X.Y.Z (migrate to specific version), --status (show migration info), --rollback (undo last migration if down() exists)

assumptions: Support optional down() function for rollback, but not required for all migrations. Document as 'probably not needed' for most cases.
Keep all backup files indefinitely. No auto-deletion. Users can manually delete old backups from spec/ directory if disk space is concern.

architectureNotes.text: Config layer: Extend ProfileConfig in src/utils/provider-config.ts with optional customModels: CustomModelDefinition[]. Add CustomModelDefinition interface with fields: id (string, required), displayName (string, optional), facade ('openai'|'codex'|'claude'|'gemini'|'zai', optional), contextWindow (number, optional), maxOutputTokens (number, optional), reasoning (boolean, optional), hasVision (boolean, optional). Add loadCustomModels() and saveCustomModel() functions.

Model initialization: In loadProfileSections() (src/tui/services/modelInitializationService.ts), after the /v1/models fetch, load custom models from the profile config and merge them into localModels[]. Custom models override auto-discovered ones with matching IDs. If only custom models exist, the section should NOT have isUnreachable: true. Custom models get their NapiModelInfo built from CustomModelDefinition fields.

NAPI boundary: Extend sessionSetModelProfile NAPI binding to accept optional facadeOverride parameter (string or null). In Rust set_model_direct (codelet/providers/src/manager.rs), add facade_override: Option<String> field on ProviderManager. The agent loop in session_manager.rs checks facade_override before matching on current_provider to select tool facades.

Facade dispatch: The facade override ONLY affects tool definition selection (which facades are registered for the agent). It does NOT change the HTTP transport — profile models always use the OpenAI-compatible HTTP client. This mirrors Copilot's pattern where behavior facades control tool schemas independently from the HTTP layer. In practice: facade_override='gemini' means the agent gets GeminiReadFileFacade etc. tool schemas, but the actual API call goes through the OpenAI endpoint with OpenAI wire format.

TUI Model Selector: Add custom model form mode to useModelSelectorState hook. Keybind 'a' on a profile section header → opens add form. Keybind 'e' on a custom model → opens edit form (pre-filled). Keybind 'd' on a custom model → shows delete confirmation. Form fields: Model ID (required), Display Name, Facade (dropdown: default/openai/codex/claude/gemini/zai), Context Window, Max Output, Reasoning toggle, Vision toggle. Reuse ProviderSettings form pattern with arrow key navigation.

ModelSelection type: Extend ModelSelection interface (src/tui/types/provider.ts) with optional facade?: string field.
